title: Accountants and auditors
rationale: Accounting work is predominantly digital and rule-based — examining financial records, computing taxes, preparing reports — placing core tasks squarely in AI's path, with tools already automating reconciliation, tax prep, and audit sampling; however, judgment-intensive work like forensic investigation, advisory, and CPA sign-off responsibilities temper the score. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper accounting unlocks latent demand from small businesses and individuals who currently forgo proper accounting and advisory services, but statutory requirements (audits, tax filings) represent largely fixed demand that won't multiply with lower cost. The occupation will survive but shift substantially from compliance and record-keeping toward advisory, analysis, and AI oversight, displacing workers who don't move up the value chain — a classic restructure profile.

title: Actors
rationale: Much of acting output is delivered as digital media — film, TV, voiceover, commercials, and background/extra work — all of which generative AI video and voice synthesis can increasingly produce without human performers; BLS itself flags AI replacement in subfields. Live theater and theme park performance retains an irreplaceable human-presence premium, but that covers only a minority of roles, keeping disruption at the high end. Elasticity for human actors is low: while cheaper production will expand total content volume, that expanded content will disproportionately use synthetic performers rather than hiring more humans, and audience demand for named, authentic human stars is concentrated among a small elite rather than the broad workforce. High disruption plus limited demand absorption for human performers points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.

title: Actuaries
rationale: Actuarial work is almost entirely digital and cognitive—compiling data, statistical modeling, pricing risk, and writing reports—all squarely in AI's path, with modern ML already outperforming traditional actuarial models in many pricing and reserving tasks. Demand elasticity is low: the volume of insurance policies, pensions, and regulatory filings requiring actuarial analysis is driven by market size and regulation, not by the cost of actuarial labor, so 10x cheaper analysis mostly means fewer analysts per book of business rather than 10x more risk assessment (though some expansion in enterprise risk management and new insurance products exists). Professional certification requirements and regulatory sign-off obligations will slow displacement and preserve a senior credentialed core, but junior analytical headcount is vulnerable. High disruption combined with low-to-moderate elasticity places this in the replace category, despite BLS's optimistic projection which predates full accounting of generative AI capabilities.

title: Administrative services and facilities managers
rationale: The knowledge-work portions—recordkeeping, scheduling, compliance documentation, procurement tracking, and records/information management—are squarely in AI's path and already being automated, but core duties like supervising staff, physically monitoring building safety, overseeing maintenance crews, and responding on-call to facility emergencies require human presence and judgment on the ground. Elasticity is low because organizations need a roughly fixed amount of facilities oversight tied to their physical footprint; making administration 10x cheaper doesn't mean companies consume 10x more facilities management, and productivity gains likely mean fewer administrative managers per organization. With moderate disruption concentrated in the admin/records side and demand largely tied to building stock rather than cost, the occupation is resilient overall, though records and information managers specifically face restructuring pressure.

title: Adult basic and secondary education and ESL teachers
rationale: The core work — language instruction, lesson planning, assessment, and personalized practice — is precisely what AI tutoring systems now do well, and ESL/literacy instruction is among the most directly substitutable teaching domains since apps already deliver adaptive language learning at near-zero cost. While latent demand for language learning and basic skills is enormous, that demand is increasingly captured by AI tutors and apps directly rather than by hiring more human teachers, and the occupation depends on shrinking public funding and declining enrollment (BLS already projects -14%). The classroom presence and community-connection elements provide some resilience, but they don't anchor enough of the job to offset substitution. High disruption combined with demand that flows to software rather than headcount makes this a replace scenario.

title: Advertising sales agents
rationale: The core workflow — prospecting, drafting proposals and contracts, preparing sales presentations, pricing estimates, and account correspondence — is digital and language-based, squarely in AI's path; moreover, programmatic ad platforms already automate ad placement itself, disintermediating the human sales role for a growing share of the market. Elasticity is low because total ad spending is set by client marketing budgets, not by the cost of the sales intermediary; making agents 10x more productive doesn't cause businesses to buy meaningfully more advertising, it just means fewer agents (or self-serve platforms) handle the same spend. BLS already projects a 6% decline before accounting for accelerating AI capabilities. High disruption combined with inelastic demand points clearly to replacement, with residual human roles concentrated in complex, high-value relationship accounts.

title: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers
rationale: Nearly all core tasks—campaign planning, market research analysis, copy and creative evaluation, media buying, pricing strategy—are digital and cognitive, and generative AI plus programmatic ad tools already automate much of the content creation and ad placement these managers oversee, though negotiation, client relations, and team leadership retain human elements. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper campaign production lets small businesses and startups consume far more marketing, but consumer attention is finite and marketing spend is partly zero-sum competition for share, capping total demand expansion. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 5, the occupation restructures—managers who orchestrate AI-driven campaigns and focus on strategy and stakeholder management will thrive, while those anchored to hands-on campaign execution and traditional media buying face displacement. The BLS's own projected decline for advertising and promotions managers due to automated ad placement already signals this shift.

title: Aerospace engineering and operations technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on: installing instruments, building test rigs, calibrating physical equipment like wind tunnels, and assembly-line quality assurance — tasks requiring physical presence and mechanical skill that AI cannot perform. AI meaningfully assists the knowledge portions (running simulations, recording and analyzing test data, troubleshooting diagnostics), warranting a moderate disruption score. Elasticity is moderate-to-high because cheaper testing and satellite launches, drone growth, and new aircraft types are actively expanding aerospace activity, as reflected in the 8% projected growth. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the digital periphery while the physical core remains human work.

title: Aerospace engineers
rationale: Aerospace engineering is predominantly computational knowledge work — CAD design, simulation, aerodynamic and structural analysis, documentation, and compliance verification — all squarely in AI's path, though physical prototyping, testing, and safety-critical certification keep humans essential in the loop. Elasticity is moderate: falling launch costs, commercial space, and drones show real latent demand for aerospace products, but the industry is constrained by enormous capital requirements, defense budgets, FAA/regulatory certification timelines, and security clearance bottlenecks that prevent demand from scaling freely with cheaper engineering labor. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 5, the occupation restructures: AI-driven design and simulation tools will substantially shift required skills toward systems integration, verification, and AI-tool orchestration, displacing engineers who don't adapt while rewarding those who do.

title: Agricultural and food science technicians
rationale: The core work — collecting and preparing physical samples, operating lab and farm equipment, maintaining sterile environments, and inspecting foodstuffs — requires hands-on presence in labs, plants, and fields, though AI can meaningfully assist with data analysis, report writing, and anomaly detection in test results, warranting a moderate disruption score. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster testing could expand food safety monitoring and agricultural research throughput somewhat, but demand is largely tied to regulatory requirements and production volumes rather than being cost-suppressed. Because AI primarily augments the analytical periphery while the physical sampling and testing core remains human-dependent, the occupation is resilient over the next decade.

title: Agricultural and food scientists
rationale: Agricultural and food scientists do substantial knowledge work — data analysis, experiment design, literature review, and report writing — where AI tools (including AI-driven genomics, crop modeling, and formulation optimization) already add value. However, the core work is anchored in physical experimentation: lab tests, field sampling, plant/animal trials, and facility inspections that require real-world presence and cannot be compressed by AI, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is moderate — cheaper research would expand R&D into more crops, food products, and sustainability challenges, but demand is capped by trial timelines, regulatory processes, and funding constraints rather than analysis costs. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI accelerates the analytical layer while the empirical, hands-on core remains human-dependent.

title: Agricultural engineers
rationale: Agricultural engineering mixes AI-exposed design and analysis work (CAD, simulation, systems modeling) with substantial physical presence — inspecting equipment on farms, overseeing construction, testing machinery in labs, and adapting designs to messy real-world agricultural conditions. AI will accelerate the design and computational portions, but the core role requires on-site judgment, integration across biology, machinery, and environment, and PE-licensed sign-off. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper engineering could unlock more precision-agriculture, automation, and sustainability projects among farms that currently can't afford custom engineering, though the tiny occupational base and farm capital constraints limit expansion. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the knowledge-work portions without displacing the field-intensive core.

title: Agricultural workers
rationale: Agricultural work is overwhelmingly physical — planting, harvesting, herding, lifting, and machine operation in unpredictable outdoor environments — where language-model AI has little direct reach; the relevant threat is robotics and mechanization, which proceeds slowly and mainly shifts labor toward equipment operation rather than AI-driven task replacement. Demand for food is fundamentally inelastic — cheaper farm labor does not make people consume dramatically more agricultural output, so productivity gains from automation translate into fewer field workers, as BLS's projected decline reflects. AI may assist peripherally with crop monitoring, breeding records, and precision agriculture planning, but the core hands-on labor is untouched. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient to AI specifically, even though long-run mechanization pressures headcount.

title: Air traffic controllers
rationale: Air traffic control is fully cognitive and digital in nature, which puts it theoretically in AI's path, but extreme safety-criticality, FAA certification requirements, legal accountability for human decision-making, and the decades-long timeline of aviation system upgrades (as seen with NextGen) mean AI will function as decision-support rather than replacing the human-in-the-loop within 10 years. Demand elasticity is very low: the number of controllers needed is driven by air traffic volume and airspace structure, not the cost of controller labor, so productivity gains (like NextGen already demonstrates) simply let each controller handle more traffic rather than expanding total demand. BLS projections of just 1% growth despite rising air traffic confirm that efficiency gains suppress headcount rather than expand output. With moderate disruption capped by regulation and safety culture, the occupation is resilient over the 10-year horizon, though longer-term automation pressure is real.

title: Biological technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on: setting up and maintaining lab equipment, preparing physical biological samples, running wet-lab experiments, and fieldwork — tasks requiring physical presence that AI cannot perform directly. AI meaningfully assists the knowledge portions (data analysis, report writing, experiment documentation) and lab automation is advancing, but robotic replacement of general-purpose bench work remains limited within a 10-year horizon. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper and faster analysis would expand research throughput (biotech, synthetic biology, drug discovery have deep latent demand), though headcount is capped by physical lab capacity and research funding. With disruption at 4, this occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the analytical periphery while the wet-lab core persists.

title: Boilermakers
rationale: Boilermaker work is almost entirely physical — welding, assembling, and repairing large vessels in cramped, dangerous, unpredictable environments — placing it far outside AI's current or near-term reach; AI touches only peripheral tasks like blueprint interpretation or inspection scheduling. Demand is inelastic: boiler installation and maintenance is driven by industrial infrastructure needs, and even if labor were cheaper, factories wouldn't buy meaningfully more boilers (indeed, demand is structurally declining with the shift away from coal). With disruption at 1, the occupation is clearly resilient to AI, though it faces headwinds from energy transition rather than automation.

title: Bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks
rationale: Nearly every core task — posting transactions, coding entries, reconciling accounts, producing standard reports — is routine digital processing that AI and automated accounting software can already perform at high accuracy, placing this occupation squarely in AI's direct path. Demand for bookkeeping is largely fixed by the number of businesses and regulatory record-keeping requirements; making it 10x cheaper doesn't cause firms to consume 10x more bookkeeping, though modest expansion may occur among small businesses that previously skipped formal books. BLS already projects a 6% decline even before accounting for recent AI advances, and productivity gains will translate mostly into fewer clerks rather than more output. High disruption combined with inelastic demand makes 'replace' the clear category, with significant headcount contraction expected.

title: Broadcast, sound, and video technicians
rationale: The occupation is a mix of physical work — rigging lights, running cables, setting up and tearing down equipment for live events — and digital work like mixing, editing, and signal management. AI already automates much of the digital portion (auto-mixing, mastering, automated broadcast switching, AI-driven camera and lighting control), but the hands-on setup and live-event presence that dominates the largest sub-occupation (audio/video technicians) remains out of AI's reach. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper production expands content creation, corporate AV, and streaming, but demand for live-event and broadcast staffing is bounded by the number of events and stations, and BLS notes automation is already reducing per-production headcount. With disruption at the moderate level, the core work is reshaped only at the edges, making 'resilient' the appropriate category despite flat projected growth.

title: Budget analysts
rationale: Nearly all core tasks—consolidating budgets, reviewing proposals for compliance, variance analysis, forecasting, and drafting explanatory reports—are structured digital and language-based work squarely in the path of current AI tools. Elasticity is low because organizations need one budget process regardless of cost; making budget analysis 10x cheaper doesn't lead governments or firms to produce 10x more budgets, and public-sector headcount is tied to appropriations rather than demand for analysis. Some modest expansion in program evaluation and cost-benefit work is possible, but structural and institutional constraints cap it. High disruption combined with fixed, price-insensitive demand points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.

title: Bus drivers
rationale: The core task—physically operating a large vehicle on public roads—is in the path of autonomous driving technology, and fixed routes make buses relatively favorable automation targets, but deployment over the next 10 years will be slow due to safety regulation, capital costs of fleet replacement, and the non-driving duties (supervising children, assisting disabled passengers, maintaining order) that require a human onboard. Elasticity is low: bus ridership is driven by population, school enrollment, and transit policy rather than the cost of the driver, so even dramatically cheaper operation would expand service only modestly (some route expansion in underserved areas). Because AI touches the periphery today and full driver replacement remains beyond the 10-year window for most fleets—especially school buses, the majority of the occupation—the occupation is resilient in this timeframe, though longer-term autonomy risk is real.

title: Butchers
rationale: Butchery is almost entirely hands-on physical work — cutting, deboning, wrapping, and handling carcasses in cold environments — where AI language and analysis tools are irrelevant to the core tasks; only peripheral duties like inventory tracking and ordering could be assisted by AI. Automation risk comes from industrial robotics in slaughterhouses rather than AI software, and even that struggles with the variability of animal carcasses. Demand for meat cutting is tied to meat consumption, which is largely fixed regardless of labor cost, and the trend toward pre-packaged products caps any expansion. With minimal disruption to the core work, the occupation is clearly resilient to AI over the next decade.

title: Calibration technologists and technicians
rationale: Core calibration work is hands-on: physically inspecting, adjusting, and testing instruments in plants and labs, requiring dexterity and on-site presence. AI can assist with documentation, scheduling, and diagnostic analysis, and self-calibrating devices pose some automation pressure, but the physical adjustment of diverse equipment against standards remains human work. Demand is tied to installed instrument bases and regulatory/quality requirements — it's relatively fixed rather than cost-suppressed, so cheaper calibration wouldn't dramatically expand consumption. With low disruption to the physical core, the occupation is resilient, consistent with BLS's projected modest growth.

title: Cardiovascular technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work is physically hands-on: positioning patients, attaching electrodes, assisting with catheterization, monitoring during surgery, and lifting patients who need assistance. AI meaningfully affects the analytical portion — algorithms already interpret EKGs and can flag abnormalities faster than technicians — but preparation, patient interaction, and procedural assistance remain firmly human, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is moderate: an aging population and cheaper, faster diagnostics would expand cardiac screening volumes, but testing is gated by physician referrals, insurance coverage, and facility capacity. Because disruption stays well below the knowledge-work threshold, the occupation is resilient, with AI enhancing the interpretive workflow rather than displacing the bedside role.

title: Career and technical education teachers
rationale: CTE teaching centers on hands-on demonstration of physical trades — welding, auto repair, culinary work — plus in-person supervision of tools, equipment, and safety in workshops, which AI cannot perform. AI meaningfully assists the knowledge-work periphery (lesson planning, grading, tutoring on theory), but the core experiential instruction remains physical, yielding moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper instructional support could expand vocational training access, but school budgets, enrollment trends, and physical facility constraints cap growth. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — AI augments prep work but does not reshape the shop-floor teaching that defines the job.

title: Carpenters
rationale: Carpentry is overwhelmingly physical, hands-on work in unpredictable environments — measuring, cutting, installing, and repairing structures on varied jobsites — which is far outside AI's reach for the foreseeable future. AI touches only peripheral tasks like bidding, estimating, blueprint interpretation, and scheduling, particularly for the 27% who are self-employed. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper construction planning could unlock some latent demand for renovation and building, but demand is more constrained by materials, land, financing, and labor costs than by knowledge-work costs. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is clearly resilient; the larger long-term threat is prefabrication and robotics, not AI software.

title: Cartographers and photogrammetrists
rationale: The core work is almost entirely digital — analyzing satellite imagery, extracting features, integrating GIS data, and producing map visualizations — and AI already excels at automated feature extraction from imagery, photogrammetric processing, and generative map design, putting nearly all daily tasks in AI's direct path. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper geospatial products would unlock more mapping for urban planning, disaster response, autonomous navigation, and commercial applications, but 41% of employment sits in local government where budgets rather than latent demand constrain hiring, and much routine mapping demand is already served by big-tech platforms. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the occupation survives but shifts toward supervising AI pipelines, validating outputs, and specialized geospatial analysis rather than manual map production. Workers who remain traditional map producers face displacement, fitting the restructure category.

title: Cashiers
rationale: The core work — scanning items, processing payments, handling returns — is routine transaction processing already being displaced by self-checkout, mobile payments, e-commerce, and AI-powered computer-vision checkout-free stores; only peripheral tasks like bagging, age verification, and customer assistance require physical presence. Demand is highly inelastic: cheaper checkout does not make consumers shop meaningfully more, so productivity gains flow directly to headcount reduction, as reflected in BLS's projected -10% decline. With high disruption to core tasks and near-zero latent demand to absorb efficiency gains, this occupation fits squarely in the replace category.

title: Chefs and head cooks
rationale: The core work of chefs and head cooks is fundamentally physical and sensory — cooking, tasting, supervising a live kitchen, handling food quality — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like inventory management, scheduling, menu ideation, and social media promotion, warranting a low disruption score. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper administrative overhead could marginally expand restaurant viability, but demand for chefs is driven by dining-out demand and physical throughput, not knowledge-work costs. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is clearly resilient; BLS projections of 7% growth reinforce that human culinary leadership remains in demand.

title: Chemical engineers
rationale: Much of a chemical engineer's work — process simulation, design calculations, cost estimation, regulatory documentation — is digital and increasingly AI-assisted, but the core role remains anchored to physical plants, safety oversight, on-site troubleshooting, and hands-on validation of processes that AI cannot perform remotely. Elasticity is moderate: demand is tied to physical chemical production capacity, which is capital-intensive and constrained by industrial demand and offshoring, though cheaper process design could accelerate R&D in areas like sustainable materials and biotech. With disruption at 6, AI reshapes the analytical portions but not the physically grounded core, so the occupation is resilient — engineers who adopt AI simulation and design tools will be more productive without headcount collapsing.

title: Chemical technicians
rationale: The core work — setting up and maintaining lab instruments, preparing chemical solutions, handling physical samples, and troubleshooting production equipment — requires hands-on presence that AI cannot replicate, though lab automation and robotics may erode some routine testing over time. AI meaningfully assists the peripheral knowledge work: data interpretation, report writing, and experimental documentation. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper, faster testing could expand demand for quality control, environmental monitoring, and R&D throughput, but physical lab capacity and regulatory testing requirements limit explosive growth. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the analytical portion while the manual laboratory core remains intact.

title: Chemists and materials scientists
rationale: AI is transforming the computational side of chemistry — molecular modeling, literature synthesis, candidate screening (e.g., AI-driven materials discovery), and report writing — but the core work still requires physical laboratory experimentation, synthesis, instrument operation, and validation that AI cannot perform, keeping disruption at the high-moderate boundary. Elasticity is high because faster, cheaper discovery cycles unlock substantial latent R&D demand in batteries, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, and advanced materials, where the bottleneck is discovery cost and speed rather than saturated demand. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands in resilient: AI dramatically accelerates hypothesis generation and analysis, but hands-on experimental verification anchors the role. Chemists who master AI-assisted computational tools will be more productive, while overall headcount is likely stable or growing as R&D output expands.

title: Childcare workers
rationale: Childcare is almost entirely hands-on physical and emotional labor — supervising safety, feeding, diapering, and in-person play — that AI cannot perform; at most it assists with peripheral tasks like record-keeping, curriculum ideas, and parent communications. Elasticity is moderate at best: demand is constrained by birth rates, regulated staff-to-child ratios, and the fundamentally in-person nature of care, so AI-driven cost reductions in admin work would barely lower total service cost or unlock much latent demand. With disruption near the floor, the occupation is resilient — its projected decline stems from demographics and cost structure, not AI displacement.

title: Chiropractors
rationale: The core of chiropractic work is hands-on physical manipulation of the spine and joints, which AI cannot perform; only peripheral tasks like scheduling, record-keeping, marketing, imaging interpretation, and treatment planning are touched by AI tools. Elasticity is modest — chiropractic demand is driven by patient conditions, insurance coverage, and consumer preferences rather than the cost of cognitive labor, so AI-driven productivity gains in admin work would not dramatically expand headcount, though lower practice overhead could modestly grow small practices. With disruption clearly low, the occupation is resilient: AI may streamline back-office operations and diagnostic imaging review, but the manual, in-person nature of adjustments keeps the core role intact.

title: Civil engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: A substantial share of this role's tasks — CAD drafting, cost estimation, report writing, data analysis, and file management — sits squarely in AI's path, and generative design and AI-assisted drafting tools are already compressing this work. However, the core also includes field surveys, materials and soil testing, and on-site construction inspection, which require physical presence at unpredictable jobsites and anchor the occupation against full digital disruption. Elasticity is limited: infrastructure spending is driven by government budgets, politics, and physical construction costs rather than technician labor costs, so cheaper technical support work won't unlock dramatically more projects. With disruption at the 6 boundary — the digital half gets automated but the field half persists — the occupation is resilient, though the drafting-heavy roles within it will shrink and the job will tilt toward inspection and field work.

title: Civil engineers
rationale: A substantial portion of civil engineering — CAD design, structural calculations, cost estimation, permit documentation, code compliance checks — is digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and generative design tools are already emerging. However, the core role also requires physical site presence for construction oversight, surveying verification, and problem resolution, plus PE licensure and legal liability for sign-off that keeps humans in the loop, capping disruption at moderate-high. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design could unlock more infrastructure and private development projects, but total demand is largely constrained by government funding cycles and construction costs, not engineering fees. With disruption at 6, the occupation is resilient — AI will reshape the design office but not eliminate the fieldwork, accountability, and project management core.

title: Claims adjusters, appraisers, examiners, and investigators
rationale: The core work — reviewing documents, evaluating photos of damage, estimating repair costs, checking policy coverage, and flagging fraud — is precisely what AI already does well; insurers are actively deploying computer vision for auto/property estimates and ML for claims triage and fraud detection, leaving only complex on-site inspections and contentious negotiations for humans. Elasticity is very low because claims volume is driven by the number of insured losses (accidents, disasters, illnesses), not by the cost or speed of processing them — making claims handling 10x cheaper does not generate 10x more claims. BLS already projects a 5% decline, and AI-driven productivity gains will translate directly into fewer adjusters and examiners needed per claim. High disruption combined with structurally fixed demand places this squarely in the replace category.

title: Clinical laboratory technologists and technicians
rationale: Core work involves physical handling of biohazardous specimens, operating and maintaining lab equipment, and hands-on procedures like staining and slide preparation, which AI cannot perform — though AI-based image analysis (cytology, hematology, microbiology) and automated result interpretation will meaningfully absorb the analytical portion of the job, warranting a moderate disruption score. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster diagnostics would expand testing volume (genetic testing, preventive screening, aging population), but automation of high-throughput lab workflows means added volume doesn't scale linearly with headcount. With disruption at 5, the occupation remains resilient — AI reshapes the interpretive periphery and speeds workflows, but specimen handling, quality control, and equipment operation keep humans central to the lab.

title: Coaches and scouts
rationale: The core of coaching — running practices, motivating athletes, hands-on skill instruction, in-game leadership — requires physical presence and human relationships that AI cannot replicate, though AI already assists meaningfully with the analytical portions like video breakdown, opponent scouting, performance data analysis, and training program design. Scouting is more exposed since talent evaluation increasingly relies on data and video analytics, but final assessments still involve in-person observation and relationship-building with athletes and families. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper AI-assisted analysis and training tools could expand personalized coaching to more youth and recreational athletes, but team rosters, school programs, and league structures cap headcount growth. With disruption at 4, this occupation is resilient — AI augments the analytical periphery while the interpersonal and physical core remains firmly human.

title: Community health workers
rationale: The core of this work is in-person outreach, home visits, relationship-building, culturally grounded trust, and advocacy within communities — activities that depend on physical presence and human rapport that AI cannot substitute. AI can assist with peripheral tasks like case documentation, resource lookup, translation, and care coordination logistics, but these are a minority of the job. Elasticity is moderate-to-high since demand is currently constrained by public health funding rather than saturation, and cheaper coordination could extend services to underserved populations, though budget and grant structures cap expansion. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — BLS projections of 11% growth reinforce that headcount is expanding regardless of AI.

title: Compensation and benefits managers
rationale: The core work — analyzing wage and benchmark data, monitoring regulations, modeling pay structures, preparing budgets and presentations — is almost entirely digital and analytical, squarely in AI's current path; only vendor negotiation and staff supervision require human judgment and relationships. Demand is structurally capped: it scales with organizational headcount, not with the cost of comp analysis, and companies won't consume 10x more compensation planning if it becomes cheaper — instead they will consolidate the function or outsource it to AI-enabled HR consulting platforms, a trend BLS already notes. With flat projected employment even before aggressive AI adoption, productivity gains translate directly into fewer managers needed per organization. High disruption plus inelastic demand places this occupation in the replace category.

title: Compensation, benefits, and job analysis specialists
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — benchmarking pay against market surveys, cost analysis, writing job descriptions, classifying positions, drafting compliance reports — are structured, digital, language-and-data work squarely in AI's current capability path; tools already automate salary benchmarking and job description generation. Demand is tied to an organization's headcount and regulatory obligations, not the cost of the analysis itself: companies won't consume 10x more compensation studies if they become cheaper, though some latent demand exists for more frequent pay-equity reviews and better benefits optimization. Regulatory complexity keeps some human oversight, but productivity gains will largely translate to fewer specialists per organization, with work consolidating into fewer HR generalist or manager roles. High disruption combined with structurally capped demand fits the replace category.

title: Compliance officers
rationale: Core compliance tasks — monitoring regulatory changes, drafting policies, conducting audits, reviewing documents, and writing reports — are language- and rules-intensive knowledge work squarely in AI's path, though onsite inspections, trainings, and investigations retain a human element. Elasticity is moderate: compliance is largely a cost center whose demand is set by regulation rather than price, capping expansion, but cheaper compliance enables continuous monitoring, broader risk coverage, and proper programs at smaller firms, while regulatory complexity (AI governance, data privacy, ESG) keeps growing. Human accountability and sign-off requirements preserve the role, but the skill set shifts from manual review and documentation toward overseeing AI-driven monitoring systems, judgment calls, and stakeholder-facing investigation work. This fits restructure: the occupation persists, but workers who don't adapt to AI-augmented workflows will be displaced.

title: Computer and information research scientists
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — algorithm design, coding experiments, data analysis, literature review, and paper writing — are digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and frontier AI systems are already being used to accelerate research itself, warranting a high disruption score. Elasticity is high because demand for computational research is essentially open-ended: cheaper research capacity means more problems get explored in AI, security, robotics, and science, and the AI boom itself is driving a projected 20% employment growth. The frontier-research nature of the work means AI acts as a force multiplier for scientists pursuing an expanding problem space rather than a substitute for a fixed output. High disruption combined with high demand elasticity makes this a clear augment case.

title: Computer and information systems managers
rationale: The core work is knowledge-based — analyzing IT needs, cost-benefit assessment, project planning, and reporting — all directly assisted by AI today, though people management, vendor negotiation, and organizational leadership remain human-centric, keeping disruption at 7 rather than higher. Elasticity is moderate: organizations will consume more IT capability as it gets cheaper (more systems, more AI deployment, more cybersecurity), which sustains demand for oversight, but manager headcount scales with team size, and AI-driven productivity may flatten IT departments and reduce management layers. The occupation persists but shifts substantially — from directing large human teams toward orchestrating AI systems, vendors, and hybrid human-AI workflows — making restructure the right fit for high disruption with moderate elasticity.

title: Computer hardware engineers
rationale: Hardware design is predominantly digital knowledge work conducted in EDA tools—schematic capture, RTL design, simulation, verification, and layout—and AI is already materially embedded in this workflow (e.g., AI-driven chip floorplanning and design-space optimization), though physical prototyping, lab testing, and manufacturing oversight temper full automation. Elasticity is high because demand for custom silicon and embedded systems is currently constrained by design cost and long development cycles; cheaper, faster design would unlock far more application-specific chips, IoT devices, and custom accelerators, and the AI boom itself is a massive demand driver for new hardware. With high disruption absorbed by expanding output—each engineer shipping more designs—the occupation fits the augment category, consistent with BLS projecting above-average growth.

title: Computer network architects
rationale: Network design, configuration, documentation, and traffic analysis are largely digital, cognitive tasks squarely in AI's path — AI can already generate network configurations, analyze performance data, and draft architecture plans, though physical deployment, vendor coordination, and hands-on troubleshooting in server rooms retain a human component. Elasticity is moderate: AI adoption, cloud expansion, and edge computing create real growth in network complexity and demand for infrastructure work, but organizations need networks proportional to their operations, not 10x more networks just because design gets cheaper. The occupation will persist and grow with infrastructure demand, but the skill mix shifts toward AI-assisted design, automation orchestration, and strategic architecture decisions, making restructure the best fit.

title: Computer programmers
rationale: The core tasks — writing, testing, and debugging code from specifications provided by others — are fully digital and squarely in AI's strongest current capability zone; coding assistants already automate exactly this translation-of-design-into-code work. While demand for software overall is highly elastic, that expanded demand flows to software developers and engineers who own design and architecture, not to pure implementers; when AI handles implementation directly from a developer's specification, the intermediary programmer role is bypassed rather than multiplied. BLS already projects a 6% decline, and AI accelerates the trend of higher-skilled tasks shifting to developers while routine coding is automated. High disruption (9) combined with low role-specific elasticity (4) places this occupation in the replace category, even though adjacent occupations like software developer face a very different, augmentation-oriented outlook.

title: Computer support specialists
rationale: The core work — diagnosing problems via chat/phone/email, walking users through fixes, documenting tickets — is language-based, procedural knowledge work squarely in AI's path; chatbots and AI agents already resolve a large share of tier-1 tickets, and BLS itself cites automation as the driver of projected decline. Elasticity is low because support demand is derived from problems occurring, not suppressed by cost: cheaper support doesn't make users consume 10x more troubleshooting, and AI simultaneously reduces incident volume through self-healing systems and embedded AI assistants that solve issues before a ticket is filed. Physical hardware setup and on-site network work preserve a residual human role, but that's a minority of the 880k jobs. High disruption with inelastic demand means productivity gains convert directly to headcount reduction, fitting the replace category.

title: Computer systems analysts
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — requirements analysis, cost-benefit studies, system design, data modeling, documentation, testing, and light programming — are digital and language-based work squarely in AI's current path; AI tools can already draft specifications, generate diagrams, and write manuals. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper systems analysis unlocks demand as more organizations (especially small firms) can afford custom IT integration and AI adoption itself creates new systems work, but demand is capped by organizational change-management capacity rather than pure analysis throughput. The stakeholder-liaison and organizational-context portions remain human, but analysts who don't shift toward AI orchestration, architecture judgment, and business translation will be displaced. High disruption with moderate elasticity fits restructure.

title: Concierges
rationale: A significant share of concierge tasks — recommendations, reservations, travel arrangements, answering inquiries — are language-based and already being absorbed by apps and AI assistants, but the core value in residential and senior-living settings is physical presence, package handling, greeting, and high-touch personal service that AI cannot replicate. Elasticity is low: cheaper concierge-style information doesn't lead buildings or hotels to hire more concierges; instead, informational functions get automated or consolidated into front-desk roles, and demand is tied to building counts rather than service cost. The occupation persists because its in-person hospitality core remains human, even as the knowledge portion erodes (already visible in declining hotel concierge employment). With disruption at a moderate 5, the occupation is resilient, though tilted toward the residential/senior-care segments where human presence is the product.

title: Conservation scientists and foresters
rationale: Core work involves substantial fieldwork — site visits, fire suppression, walking rugged terrain, physically assessing timber and land conditions — which AI cannot perform, though AI meaningfully accelerates the analytical portions like GIS mapping, remote sensing analysis, management plan drafting, and regulatory compliance documentation. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis could expand conservation monitoring and land management coverage, but employment is dominated by government budgets and land-use policy rather than service cost, capping expansion. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the office and analytical side while the field-based core, stakeholder negotiation, and hands-on land management remain fundamentally human work.

title: Construction and building inspectors
rationale: Core work requires physical presence at construction sites—climbing ladders, crawling through attics, using testing equipment on plumbing and electrical systems—which AI cannot replicate, though AI meaningfully assists with plans examination, code compliance checking, report writing, and remote inspection via drones and computer vision. Elasticity is low because inspection volume is driven by construction activity and regulatory mandates, not by inspection cost; making inspections 10x cheaper does not cause society to demand 10x more inspections, and BLS already projects slight decline partly from remote inspection tools. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient: the hands-on inspection core persists while AI trims the office-based portions like plan review and documentation.

title: Construction equipment operators
rationale: Operating heavy machinery is fundamentally physical work in unpredictable outdoor environments, though autonomous and semi-autonomous equipment (GPS-guided grading, remote-operated dozers) is beginning to emerge in controlled settings like mining, warranting a low-but-not-minimal disruption score over the next decade. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper earthmoving could enable more infrastructure and construction projects, but demand is largely driven by public spending, land development cycles, and permitting rather than operator labor costs. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient — AI touches jobsite planning and machine assistance features, but skilled operators remain essential for the core work through the 10-year horizon.

title: Construction laborers and helpers
rationale: The work is almost entirely physical and site-based — hauling materials, digging trenches, operating jackhammers, assembling scaffolding — in unpredictable outdoor environments that remain far beyond AI and near-term robotics capabilities. AI may marginally affect scheduling, site logistics, or safety monitoring, but these are peripheral to the core manual tasks; prefabrication and construction robotics pose a longer-term threat but not a meaningful one within 10 years. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper construction would unlock substantial latent demand for housing and infrastructure, but that dynamic barely applies since AI cannot make this labor cheaper. With disruption near the minimum, this occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS's projected 7% growth.

title: Construction managers
rationale: A significant share of the role — cost estimating, scheduling, budgeting, contract interpretation, and progress reporting — is digital and already being transformed by AI-powered project management and estimation tools. However, the core of the job requires physical presence on unpredictable job sites: supervising subcontractors, responding to emergencies, coordinating with inspectors, and making real-time judgment calls that depend on seeing physical conditions and managing people face-to-face. Elasticity is moderate — cheaper management could enable more and smaller projects to get professional oversight, but total construction volume is constrained by land, capital, materials, and labor rather than management costs. With disruption capped at moderate levels by the irreducibly physical, relational nature of site supervision, the occupation is resilient; AI will make managers more productive on the paperwork side without displacing the role.

title: Cooks
rationale: Cooking is fundamentally physical, hands-on work requiring dexterity, taste, smell, and real-time coordination in a chaotic kitchen environment — tasks far outside AI's language and analysis capabilities, though kitchen robotics and automation pose a modest longer-term threat in standardized fast-food settings. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper prepared food would expand dining-out demand somewhat, but food consumption is bounded and much of the cost structure is ingredients and real estate, not labor productivity. With disruption clearly low, the occupation is resilient; AI may assist with inventory, ordering, and menu planning at the periphery, while automation risk is concentrated in the fast-food segment (already projected to decline) rather than in skilled restaurant cooking.

title: Correctional officers and bailiffs
rationale: The core work — physically supervising people in custody, restraining individuals, conducting searches, escorting prisoners, and maintaining courtroom order — requires human presence in unpredictable, often dangerous physical situations that AI cannot perform. AI may assist with peripheral tasks like report writing, surveillance monitoring, and contraband detection, but these are secondary to the hands-on security role. Elasticity is low because demand is driven by incarceration rates and criminal justice policy, not cost — cheaper supervision would not lead society to incarcerate more people, and policy trends actually favor decarceration. With minimal disruption to core tasks, this occupation is resilient to AI, though it faces headcount decline from policy shifts unrelated to technology.

title: Cost estimators
rationale: Cost estimation is almost entirely digital knowledge work — reading blueprints, extracting quantities, pricing labor and materials, and producing reports — all tasks squarely in AI's path, and takeoff/estimation software integrated with BIM is already automating much of it (BLS itself cites software productivity as driving projected decline). Demand for estimates is tied to the underlying volume of construction and manufacturing projects, which doesn't expand just because estimating gets cheaper; contractors may bid on somewhat more jobs, but total project volume caps demand. With high disruption and low elasticity, productivity gains translate directly into fewer estimators needed, consistent with the projected -4% employment decline, making 'replace' the fitting category.

title: Court reporters and simultaneous captioners
rationale: The core task — converting speech to accurate text in real time — is precisely what modern AI speech recognition does well and continues to improve at rapidly, making this occupation almost entirely digital and directly in AI's path; only edge cases like accuracy certification, speaker attribution in chaotic settings, and legal admissibility slow full automation. Demand is largely inelastic: the number of trials, depositions, and broadcast hours does not multiply because transcription gets cheaper, and while captioning coverage would expand (more content captioned), that expanded demand would be served by AI itself rather than by more human stenographers. Regulatory requirements for certified human reporters in courts provide a temporary buffer, but this is a legacy protection rather than genuine demand growth. High disruption combined with fixed underlying demand puts this squarely in the replace category, with existing pipeline shortages likely masking the contraction in official projections.

title: Craft and fine artists
rationale: This occupation splits sharply: illustrators, cartoonists, and digital artists face severe disruption from generative image AI, while ceramicists, glassblowers, sculptors, furniture makers, and other craft artists do fundamentally physical, hands-on work where AI is peripheral — averaging to moderate disruption. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because the value of fine and craft art derives from human authorship, scarcity, and provenance; making image generation 10x cheaper floods the market with commodity visuals but doesn't expand demand for original human-made works, and may actually depress commercial illustration income. The physical, authenticity-driven core of the occupation keeps it resilient overall, though the illustration segment specifically faces replacement-level pressure and workers there will need to reposition around distinctive personal style and physical media.

title: Credit counselors
rationale: The core tasks — gathering financial data, assessing income and debt, calculating budgets, drafting repayment plans, and explaining options — are language-based knowledge work squarely in AI's current path; chatbots and financial planning tools can already perform much of this analysis and client education. Demand elasticity is low: while latent demand for financial guidance exists among people who can't afford advice, AI will largely serve that demand directly through consumer-facing apps rather than through more counselors, and much of current employment is tied to fixed institutional needs like college financial aid offices whose demand tracks enrollment, not counseling cost. The empathetic, trust-building element in debt crises preserves some human roles, but not enough to offset automation of the analytical core. High disruption with capped demand expansion points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.

title: Customer service representatives
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — answering questions by phone/chat/email, processing orders and returns, updating accounts, logging interactions — are language-based digital work that current AI chatbots and voice agents already handle at scale, making this one of the most directly exposed occupations. Elasticity is low because demand for customer support is derived from the volume of problems and inquiries customers have, not from its price; making support cheaper does not make people contact support 10x more, so productivity gains flow straight to headcount reduction. Companies are actively deploying AI agents to deflect contacts, and BLS already projects decline even before full AI adoption. High disruption with inelastic demand makes this a clear replace scenario, with human roles retained mainly for escalations and complex or regulated inquiries.

title: Dancers and choreographers
rationale: Dancing is fundamentally embodied physical performance requiring live human presence, athleticism, and years of physical training — AI cannot substitute for a body on stage, though AI-generated video and motion synthesis may compete at the margins in digital media (music videos, virtual performances) and assist choreographers with routine visualization. Demand for live performance is driven by cultural funding, ticket sales, and audience appetite rather than production cost, so productivity gains from AI tools would unlock only modest additional demand. Because core work remains almost entirely physical and audience-facing, the occupation fits squarely in the resilient category, with the main long-term risk being displacement of screen-based dance work by synthetic media rather than disruption of live performance.

title: Data scientists
rationale: Data science is almost entirely digital knowledge work — data cleaning, coding, model building, visualization, and report writing are all squarely in AI's path, and current AI tools already automate large portions of these tasks (code generation, automated ML, natural-language querying of data). However, demand for data-driven insight is heavily suppressed by cost and scarce expertise: as analysis gets 10x cheaper, far more decisions, datasets, and organizations (especially smaller ones) get rigorous analysis, and BLS already projects 34% growth. The occupation will shift toward problem framing, business judgment, and validating AI-generated analysis, with productivity gains absorbed by expanding demand. High disruption paired with high elasticity makes this a classic augment case.

title: Database administrators and architects
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — writing SQL, tuning performance, designing schemas, configuring backups, and managing permissions — are digital and squarely in AI's path; AI copilots and autonomous cloud databases (self-tuning, self-patching) already automate much of routine DBA work. Elasticity is moderate: data volumes and AI adoption drive real growth in data infrastructure needs (favoring architects), but cloud consolidation means fewer administrators serve more companies, capping headcount expansion — BLS itself projects -1% for DBAs vs. +9% for architects. The occupation survives but skills shift decisively from routine maintenance toward architecture, data governance, security, and AI-pipeline design, making restructure the right category: workers who move up the stack thrive, while those doing routine administration face displacement.

title: Delivery truck drivers and driver/sales workers
rationale: Core work is physical: driving in urban environments, loading and carrying packages to doorsteps, and face-to-face customer interaction. AI already assists with routing, dispatch, and paperwork, and autonomous driving poses a longer-term threat, but the last-fifty-feet problem (carrying goods from vehicle to door) and unpredictable delivery conditions keep the driver essential over the 10-year horizon. Elasticity is moderate-to-high — e-commerce and on-demand delivery demand keeps expanding as delivery gets cheaper and faster, as reflected in BLS's 8% projected growth. With disruption at 4, this occupation is resilient: AI optimizes the periphery but does not replace the core physical work in the coming decade.

title: Dental and ophthalmic laboratory technicians and medical appliance technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on fabrication—shaping, polishing, and repairing physical appliances—which AI cannot perform directly, though the design phase is being rapidly digitized via CAD/CAM software, AI-assisted design of crowns and lenses, and 3D printing that automates portions of the workflow. Demand elasticity is low because consumption is tied to biological need (people don't get 10x more dentures or eyeglasses if prices drop), with only modest latent demand from underserved populations and cosmetic dentistry. The moderate disruption score reflects that automation (more than AI per se) is squeezing routine fabrication tasks, but the physical, dexterity-intensive core keeps this occupation resilient rather than restructured, consistent with BLS's roughly flat employment projection.

title: Dental assistants
rationale: Dental assistants' core work is overwhelmingly physical and chairside — sterilizing instruments, handing tools to dentists, suctioning, positioning x-ray equipment, and comforting patients — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, recordkeeping, and billing, which are a minor fraction of the job. Elasticity is modest: demand for dental care is driven by demographics and insurance coverage rather than cost of assisting labor, though cheaper practice operations could marginally expand access. With disruption clearly low, the occupation is resilient, consistent with BLS's faster-than-average projected growth.

title: Dental hygienists
rationale: The core work — scaling teeth, applying sealants, taking x-rays, hands-on cleaning in a patient's mouth — is fine-motor physical labor that AI cannot perform; this is the canonical low-disruption example. AI may assist peripherally with x-ray interpretation, charting, and documentation, but these are minor portions of the job. Elasticity is modest: cheaper preventive care could unlock some latent demand (underserved populations, expanded state scope-of-practice), but dental visits are constrained by insurance, chair time, and habits, so demand won't explode with productivity gains. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — BLS projects faster-than-average growth driven by demographics, not technology.

title: Dentists
rationale: The core of dentistry is hands-on procedural work — drilling, filling, extracting, placing appliances — requiring fine dexterity in a patient's mouth, which AI and current robotics cannot replicate at scale. AI meaningfully assists peripheral tasks like radiograph interpretation, diagnosis support, treatment planning, appliance design (CAD/CAM), and practice administration, but these are minority-share tasks that mostly augment rather than displace the dentist. Elasticity is modest: demand is somewhat constrained by cost and insurance coverage, so cheaper care could unlock some latent demand, but people won't consume dramatically more dental procedures and workforce growth is capped by licensure and training pipelines. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI changes the tools, not the job.

title: Desktop publishers
rationale: Desktop publishing is entirely digital work — importing text and graphics, adjusting layouts, formatting pages — all of which generative AI and automated layout tools can already perform or dramatically accelerate. Demand for standalone layout specialists is inelastic: cheaper layout doesn't create meaningfully more publication demand, and any expanded design output flows to writers, marketers, and designers using AI tools directly rather than to dedicated desktop publishers. The occupation was already declining pre-AI as its tasks were absorbed by adjacent roles and templated software, and AI accelerates that consolidation. High disruption with very low elasticity makes this a clear replace case.

title: Diagnostic medical sonographers
rationale: The core work is physically operating a transducer on a patient's body, positioning patients, and adjusting in real time based on anatomy — hands-on tasks AI cannot perform, though AI increasingly assists with image optimization, automated measurements, and preliminary anomaly flagging. Elasticity is moderate-to-high: ultrasound is already the cheap, radiation-free, first-line imaging modality, and AI-guided acquisition could expand point-of-care ultrasound use, though reimbursement and physician ordering patterns cap runaway growth. Because the disruption score is moderate — AI reshapes the analysis periphery but not the hands-on scanning core — the occupation is resilient, consistent with BLS's projected 13% growth driven by an aging population.

title: Diesel service technicians and mechanics
rationale: The core work — inspecting, disassembling, and repairing heavy diesel engines and vehicle systems — is fundamentally physical, requiring dexterity, strength, and hands-on presence in unpredictable shop and roadside environments. AI meaningfully assists the diagnostic portion (interpreting fault codes, predictive maintenance, technical manual lookup), which is a real but peripheral share of daily tasks, warranting a low disruption score. Demand for fleet maintenance is driven by freight volume and vehicle fleet size, not repair cost — cheaper diagnostics won't cause trucks to need dramatically more repairs, and electrification poses a structural headwind, keeping elasticity low. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient: AI sharpens troubleshooting but does not reshape the wrench-turning core.

title: Dietitians and nutritionists
rationale: A substantial share of the work — meal plan generation, educational materials, documentation, nutrient analysis — is digital and language-based and already in AI's path, but the core of clinical practice is behavior-change counseling, motivational interviewing, and coordination in hospitals and care facilities, which depends on human trust and licensed accountability. Elasticity is moderate: personalized nutrition guidance has large latent demand as costs drop, but much of that demand may be absorbed directly by consumer AI apps rather than translating into more dietitian jobs, and clinical volumes are tied to patient counts and reimbursement rules. With disruption at the boundary (6), the occupation lands as resilient: AI restructures the informational and planning tasks while the counseling and clinical core keeps humans central, consistent with BLS's projected above-average growth.

title: Drafters
rationale: Drafting is almost entirely digital knowledge work — converting sketches and specifications into CAD/BIM drawings — which sits directly in the path of generative design tools, AI-assisted CAD, and automated drawing generation from text or rough inputs; this drives a high disruption score. Elasticity is low because demand for technical drawings is derived from the volume of construction and manufacturing projects, which is constrained by capital budgets and physical activity, not by drafting cost; cheaper drafting mostly means engineers and architects generate drawings themselves rather than more drawings being commissioned. BLS already projects flat-to-declining employment precisely because CAD/BIM productivity gains reduce headcount. With disruption at 8 and elasticity at 3, this occupation fits the replace category, with the intermediary role between designer and drawing largely absorbed by software.

title: Drywall installers, ceiling tile installers, and tapers
rationale: Drywall installation and taping is almost entirely physical, hands-on work in unpredictable construction environments — lifting heavy panels, working on stilts and scaffolds, applying and sanding compound — which is far outside current AI capabilities; AI may only assist with peripheral tasks like material estimation and scheduling. Demand is tied to construction and remodeling activity, not the cost of this specific labor, so even large productivity gains (which would come from robotics, not AI software) would not unlock dramatic new consumption of drywall work. Elasticity is low-to-moderate since cheaper finishing could shift some construction choices at the margin but demand is fundamentally capped by building volume. With disruption near the minimum, the occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Economists
rationale: Economists' core tasks — data collection, statistical modeling, forecasting, report writing, and presenting findings — are almost entirely digital and language/quantitative work squarely in AI's path; current AI tools already assist with econometric coding, literature synthesis, and drafting analysis. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper economic analysis would let more businesses and smaller agencies consume forecasting and policy evaluation, but demand is capped by government budgets (over half of employment), slow institutional adoption, and the fact that policy decisions don't multiply just because analysis is cheap. The role survives because judgment, credibility, and communication with policymakers remain human-anchored, but the skill set shifts heavily toward AI-augmented modeling and interpretation, displacing those who don't adapt — a classic restructure profile.

title: Editors
rationale: Editing is almost entirely digital language work — proofreading, rewriting for clarity, fact-checking, and style enforcement are precisely what current LLMs already do well, putting the core copy-editing tasks squarely in AI's direct path; only high-level judgment work (story selection, managing writers, editorial ethics) is harder to automate. Elasticity is limited: while cheaper editing unlocks some latent demand (self-published authors, small content shops), much of the productivity gain is captured by writers using AI directly and skipping professional editors, and legacy publishing markets are structurally shrinking. The demand expansion that does occur in content volume is largely absorbed by AI tools rather than human editors. With disruption of 8 and elasticity of 4, this fits 'replace' — headcount contraction is likely, with survivors concentrated in senior editorial judgment and management roles.

title: Electrical and electronic engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work — assembling prototypes, calibrating instruments, soldering circuitry, physically testing and repairing equipment — requires hands-on presence with physical hardware, keeping disruption moderate. AI meaningfully assists the knowledge-work portions (drafting diagrams, analyzing test data, writing reports, troubleshooting via diagnostic reasoning), but cannot perform bench work on physical components. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper electronics prototyping and testing could expand hardware development activity, though manufacturing automation partially offsets this. With disruption at 4, this occupation is resilient — AI augments the analytical periphery while the hands-on core remains human work.

title: Electrical and electronics engineers
rationale: Much of the core work — circuit design, simulation, modeling, documentation, and requirements analysis — is digital knowledge work done in CAD/EDA software where AI copilots (schematic generation, HDL assistance, automated verification) are already materially useful, though physical testing, lab prototyping, and manufacturing oversight temper full automation. Elasticity is high because demand for electrical design is suppressed by engineering cost and scarcity: electrification, grid modernization, semiconductors, robotics, and consumer electronics represent enormous latent demand that cheaper, faster design cycles would unlock. Even BLS projects above-average growth, and productivity gains will likely be absorbed by more products and infrastructure being designed rather than fewer engineers. This fits 'augment': each engineer produces dramatically more while headcount holds or grows.

title: Electrical and electronics installers and repairers
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — disassembling equipment, replacing components, testing with physical instruments — which AI cannot perform; AI mainly assists diagnostics (fault isolation via sensor data, repair manuals, and predictive maintenance) and record-keeping, so disruption stays low. Elasticity is moderate: faster, cheaper diagnostics would shift some repair-vs-replace decisions toward repair and grid expansion supports demand, but total equipment stock and disposable-part trends cap how much extra repair work would be consumed. Since the physical repair itself remains human work and AI touches only the diagnostic periphery, the occupation is resilient, consistent with BLS's flat employment projection.

title: Electrical power-line installers and repairers
rationale: The core work — climbing poles, stringing cable, operating bucket trucks, and repairing high-voltage equipment in all weather — is physical, hazardous, and requires unpredictable real-world presence, keeping AI's impact confined to peripheral tasks like outage prediction, drone-assisted inspection, and dispatch optimization. Elasticity is moderate-to-high given genuine growing demand from grid expansion, EV adoption, and electrification, but line work volume is driven by infrastructure needs rather than the cost of the labor itself. With disruption clearly at the low end, this occupation is resilient; BLS projections of much-faster-than-average growth reinforce that AI poses no meaningful threat to headcount here.

title: Electricians
rationale: Electrician work is overwhelmingly physical and site-specific — running wire, installing fixtures, working in crawl spaces and at heights — which AI cannot perform; the rubric explicitly cites electricians as a 2-3 example. AI helps at the periphery with blueprint interpretation, diagnostics, scheduling, code lookup, and quoting, but the core work requires hands-on presence in unpredictable environments. Demand is actually growing due to electrification, EV charging, data centers, and renewables, so any productivity gains would be readily absorbed. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — AI touches administrative and diagnostic edges without reshaping the trade.

title: Electro-mechanical and mechatronics technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work — assembling, calibrating, soldering, repairing hydraulic/pneumatic and robotic equipment on factory floors — is fundamentally physical and requires manual dexterity in unpredictable industrial environments, keeping disruption low; AI mainly assists peripheral tasks like diagnostics, reading schematics, and writing test reports. Elasticity is moderate-to-high because expanding factory automation and robotics deployment creates growing demand for humans who install and maintain that equipment — ironically, AI-driven automation elsewhere increases the installed base these technicians service. However, AI-powered predictive maintenance and self-diagnosing machines partially offset that expansion. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient: the hands-on core remains human work even as diagnostic tools improve.

title: Elementary, middle, and high school principals
rationale: AI can meaningfully assist with the administrative portions of the job — scheduling, budget management, report preparation, and student achievement data analysis — but the core work is in-person leadership: managing staff, disciplining students, ensuring physical safety, and building trust with parents and the community. These duties require physical presence, authority, and interpersonal judgment that AI cannot substitute. Elasticity is very low because the number of principal positions is structurally capped at roughly one per school, so productivity gains cannot expand headcount; demand tracks student enrollment and school budgets, not the cost of administrative work. With moderate disruption confined to the periphery and demand fixed by school count, this occupation is resilient.

title: Elevator and escalator installers and repairers
rationale: The core work is intensely physical and hands-on — assembling heavy equipment, working in shafts, replacing cables and motors — with human presence required in unpredictable field environments; AI helps only peripherally with diagnostics (smart elevators with predictive maintenance sensors) and scheduling/records. Demand is structurally tied to building construction and the installed base of elevators requiring code-mandated maintenance, so even if diagnostics became 10x cheaper, the number of elevators needing physical service wouldn't expand much. With disruption well below the threshold, this is a resilient occupation where AI-driven predictive maintenance may modestly shift work toward troubleshooting but leaves headcount and core skills largely intact.

title: Emergency management directors
rationale: AI can materially assist with the knowledge-work portions—drafting emergency plans, analyzing hazard data, damage assessments, grant applications, and public communications—but the core of the job is real-time crisis leadership, interagency coordination, on-call incident command, and accountable decision-making under stress, which requires trusted human presence and political authority. Demand is structurally capped: each jurisdiction or organization needs roughly one director regardless of how cheap planning becomes, and public-sector budgets rather than task cost determine headcount. Some latent demand exists (small counties that currently fold the role into fire/police chiefs might afford dedicated capacity), but it is limited. With moderate disruption confined to the planning and paperwork periphery, this occupation is resilient.

title: EMTs and paramedics
rationale: EMT and paramedic work is fundamentally physical and requires unpredictable real-world presence: responding to accident scenes, lifting and moving patients, administering hands-on treatment, and transporting people in ambulances — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only the periphery, such as documentation, dispatch triage, and decision support for EKG interpretation or treatment protocols. Demand elasticity is low because emergency medical incidents are driven by accidents, illness, and demographics rather than price — cheaper service does not generate 10x more emergencies, though an aging population supports steady growth. With minimal disruption to core tasks, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Entertainment and recreation managers
rationale: AI can assist with the administrative portions of this job — scheduling programs, drafting budgets, analyzing customer feedback, and staff rostering — but the core work involves on-site facility oversight, in-person customer engagement, safety inspection, and managing frontline staff in unpredictable physical settings. These duties require constant human presence and interpersonal leadership, keeping disruption moderate. Demand for recreation and entertainment is growing with wellness trends and is somewhat cost-sensitive, so moderate expansion is plausible, but headcount is tied to physical facilities and programs rather than cheap digital output. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient: AI streamlines the office work but leaves the core role intact.

title: Environmental engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work — collecting field samples, operating and maintaining sampling equipment, handling hazardous materials, and inspecting facilities in person — requires physical presence in unpredictable environments, though AI and automated sensors will increasingly handle the documentation, data analysis, and compliance-reporting portions. Demand is largely driven by regulatory mandates and remediation project budgets rather than cost, so cheaper analysis unlocks only modest additional monitoring work; the BLS itself notes automated testing may limit headcount growth. Because AI touches record-keeping and lab analysis but not the hands-on fieldwork core, this occupation is resilient, though flat employment reflects gradual sensor-driven productivity gains rather than AI displacement.

title: Environmental engineers
rationale: A large share of the work — preparing reports, permit documentation, data analysis, and design calculations — is digital and squarely in AI's path, but core duties like site inspections, remediation oversight, fieldwork, and PE-licensed sign-off require physical presence and legal accountability that AI cannot assume, keeping disruption at the moderate-high boundary.
