Elasticity is moderate: demand is largely driven by regulation and public infrastructure budgets rather than cost, though cheaper engineering could unlock more remediation projects and compliance work for smaller entities. With disruption at 6, the occupation is resilient — AI will accelerate the documentation-heavy portions, but licensed judgment, field verification, and stakeholder coordination remain the human core.

title: Environmental science and protection technicians
rationale: The core work — field inspections, collecting air/soil/water samples, setting up monitoring equipment, and lab sample handling — requires physical presence at unpredictable real-world sites, which AI cannot replicate; however, AI meaningfully assists the report writing, data analysis, and compliance documentation portions, plus automated remote sensors reduce some manual monitoring needs. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper environmental monitoring could expand demand somewhat (more sites monitored, more frequent testing), but total demand is largely driven by regulatory mandates and government budgets rather than cost. Since the hands-on field and lab core remains intact while AI only accelerates the analytical periphery, this occupation is resilient.

title: Environmental scientists and specialists
rationale: A large share of the work—analyzing environmental data, drafting compliance reports, NEPA documentation, and preparing presentations—is knowledge work directly in AI's path, but core tasks like site assessments, sample collection oversight, stakeholder engagement, and regulatory judgment calls require physical presence and contextual expertise, keeping disruption at the high end of moderate. Demand is driven largely by regulatory mandates and government budgets rather than price, though cheaper analysis could unlock more voluntary corporate sustainability work and small-business compliance consulting, yielding moderate elasticity. Because the field/investigative core and the trust-based advisory role are not fully absorbable by AI, the occupation lands as resilient—though the desk-work portions will be heavily augmented and report-writing productivity expectations will rise substantially.

title: Epidemiologists
rationale: The core of epidemiological work—statistical analysis, study design, data pipeline management, report and grant writing—is digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, with modern tools already accelerating data cleaning, modeling, and literature synthesis; only fieldwork, sample collection, and community outreach require physical presence. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis could expand disease surveillance, real-time outbreak modeling, and hospital infection-control programs, but demand is heavily dependent on public funding, so government budgets cap how much latent demand gets absorbed. The occupation will persist—BLS even projects strong growth—but the skill mix shifts toward AI-augmented analytics, field investigation, and communication, displacing those who remain purely routine analysts. High disruption with mid-range elasticity places this in restructure.

title: Exercise physiologists
rationale: Core work involves hands-on physiological testing, in-person supervision of exercise with medically at-risk clients, and physical measurement of vitals — tasks requiring human presence, though AI can meaningfully assist with program design, medical history analysis, and interpreting test data. Elasticity is moderate: growing chronic disease prevalence and cheaper personalized exercise prescription could expand access, but AI fitness apps also compete directly with the program-design portion, and clinical referrals cap demand growth. Because disruption is moderate — AI augments planning but cannot conduct stress tests or physically supervise rehabilitation — the occupation is resilient, consistent with BLS's above-average growth projection.

title: Farmers, ranchers, and other agricultural managers
rationale: Farm and ranch management mixes cognitive tasks—market analysis, crop planning, financial records, disease monitoring—where AI and precision-agriculture tools already assist, with substantial physical, on-site work like equipment maintenance, herding, and harvest oversight that AI cannot perform. The knowledge-work portion is genuinely disruptable, but the core requires unpredictable real-world presence on the land, capping disruption at moderate. Demand elasticity is low because food consumption is largely fixed; productivity gains historically drive farm consolidation and fewer operators rather than more farming, as BLS projections of continued decline confirm. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient—AI will sharpen decision-making at the margins but not reshape the fundamental nature of running a farm.

title: Fashion designers
rationale: A large share of the core work—trend research, sketching, CAD design, colorway variation, and virtual prototyping—is digital and squarely in the path of generative image and 3D design tools, which can already produce concept designs, virtual samples, and trend forecasts in minutes. However, the tactile aspects (fabric selection, fit adjustments, sample evaluation, production oversight) keep it from being fully digital, capping disruption at 7. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design enables faster fashion cycles, more micro-brands, and mass customization, but total apparel consumption is bounded by consumer spending and design labor is a small fraction of garment cost, so demand won't expand 10x. The occupation survives but shifts substantially toward AI-assisted ideation, curation, and production coordination—designers who master these tools thrive while pure sketchers are displaced, fitting the restructure category.

title: Film and video editors and camera operators
rationale: The editing half of this occupation is almost entirely digital — AI-powered auto-editing, scene detection, color grading, and generative video tools are already reshaping post-production workflows — while camera operation retains a physical, on-location component that partially anchors the score, yielding a blended disruption of 7. Demand for video content is substantial and cheaper production unlocks more corporate, social, and marketing video, but generative video increasingly substitutes for footage capture entirely rather than just accelerating human work, capping elasticity at moderate. The occupation will survive, but skill requirements shift heavily toward AI-assisted post-production, prompt-driven generation, and creative direction; editors and operators who master these tools will absorb the expanded content demand while those doing routine cutting or standard studio shoots face displacement. This high-disruption, moderate-elasticity profile fits restructure.

title: Financial analysts
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — evaluating financial data, examining statements, modeling valuations, studying trends, and preparing written reports — are digital, cognitive, and language-based, placing the work squarely in AI's path; LLMs and quantitative tools can already draft research reports, screen securities, and run risk analyses. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis means more assets, smaller companies, and more scenarios get actively analyzed, but the total pool of investable capital and client relationships caps how much extra analysis the market absorbs, and much of finance is zero-sum. With disruption at 8 and elasticity at 5, the occupation restructures — analysts who shift toward AI-augmented judgment, client interaction, and strategy will thrive, while those doing routine data gathering and report writing face displacement.

title: Financial clerks
rationale: Financial clerks perform almost entirely routine digital processing — calculating bills, updating records, verifying documents, processing claims and payroll — tasks squarely within current AI and automation capabilities, warranting a very high disruption score. Demand for these back-office functions is fixed by the volume of underlying business transactions; making billing or payroll processing 10x cheaper does not lead organizations to consume 10x more of it, so productivity gains flow directly to headcount reduction. BLS already projects a 5% decline (with payroll clerks at -17%) before fully accounting for generative AI's document-processing capabilities. High disruption combined with inelastic demand makes this a clear replace case.

title: Financial examiners
rationale: The core work — reviewing balance sheets, loan documentation, meeting minutes, and writing safety-and-soundness reports — is almost entirely digital document analysis and report writing, squarely in AI's path; AI can already flag risky assets, detect compliance anomalies, and draft examination reports. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper examination could enable continuous monitoring instead of periodic exams and broader coverage of fintechs and smaller institutions, but total demand is ultimately set by regulatory mandates rather than market price, capping expansion. The occupation will persist because regulators require accountable human judgment and onsite verification, but the skill set shifts toward supervising AI-driven surveillance, handling complex judgment calls, and interpreting new regulations. This high-disruption, moderate-elasticity profile fits restructure.

title: Financial managers
rationale: The core work — preparing financial statements, forecasting, monitoring compliance, analyzing market trends — is almost entirely digital and cognitive, squarely in AI's path, though the managerial layer of accountability, stakeholder judgment, and executive advising retains a human component, yielding a disruption score of 7. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper financial analysis lets more mid-sized firms afford sophisticated treasury, risk, and FP&A functions, but each organization needs only a bounded amount of financial oversight and fiduciary sign-off, capping expansion at 5. The occupation will survive but shift toward AI-supervised judgment, risk interpretation, and strategic advising rather than report production, with fewer analysts to manage beneath them. This combination of high disruption and moderate elasticity fits the restructure category.

title: Fire inspectors
rationale: The core work — physically inspecting buildings, sorting through fire debris, patrolling forests, testifying in court, and interviewing witnesses — requires on-site human presence and legal authority that AI cannot replicate; AI mainly assists with code lookup, report writing, blueprint review, and evidence analysis. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because inspection demand is driven by building stock, fire incidence, and regulatory mandates rather than cost, though wildfire risk assessment could expand with cheaper tools. With disruption at 3, the occupation is clearly resilient: AI streamlines documentation and analysis but does not reshape the hands-on inspection and investigation core.

title: Firefighters
rationale: Firefighting is almost entirely physical, hazardous, and requires unpredictable real-world presence — entering burning buildings, rescuing victims, providing hands-on medical care — none of which AI can perform. AI may assist at the margins with dispatch optimization, wildfire prediction, drone reconnaissance, and incident report writing, but these are peripheral to core duties. Demand is driven by emergency incidence and public-safety staffing mandates, not cost or speed, so productivity gains would not meaningfully expand or contract headcount. With minimal disruption to the core work, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Fishing and hunting workers
rationale: The core work — hauling nets, setting traps, operating vessels in dangerous conditions, sorting and storing catch — is almost entirely physical and performed in remote, unpredictable environments where AI has no direct role; AI marginally improves fish-finding sonar, navigation, and catch reporting, which are already mechanized peripheral tasks. Demand is inelastic because it is capped by biology and regulation: fishing quotas, catch shares, and hunting licenses hard-limit output regardless of how cheap or efficient the work becomes. Even dramatic productivity gains would translate into fewer workers hitting the same quotas, not more fish caught. With minimal disruption and structurally constrained demand, the occupation is resilient to AI even as it slowly declines for non-AI reasons like stock management and aquaculture competition.

title: Fitness trainers and instructors
rationale: The core work — demonstrating exercises, correcting form in real time, motivating clients through physical presence, and ensuring safety — is fundamentally hands-on and interpersonal; AI fitness apps can generate workout plans and track progress, but these touch only the programming and admin periphery while in-person accountability remains the primary value proposition clients pay for. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper program design and admin could let trainers serve more clients, and health/wellness demand has substantial room to grow (as BLS's 12% projection reflects), though gym-based coaching hours are inherently constrained. With low disruption regardless of elasticity, this occupation is resilient — AI may even complement trainers by handling planning while humans deliver motivation and technique correction.

title: Flight attendants
rationale: Flight attendants' core work is physically present, in-cabin service and safety response—emergency evacuations, first aid, managing unruly passengers, serving food—none of which AI can perform; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, report writing, and passenger communication. Elasticity is largely moot since federal regulations mandate minimum attendant-to-passenger ratios, tying headcount directly to flight volume rather than productivity; cheaper 'flight attendant work' doesn't unlock latent demand for more of it. With disruption well below the threshold and legally mandated staffing, this occupation is resilient, consistent with BLS's projected 9% growth driven by air travel demand.

title: Flooring installers and tile and stone setters
rationale: The core work — removing old flooring, leveling surfaces, cutting materials, spreading adhesives, and setting tile in unpredictable residential and commercial environments — is almost entirely physical and manual, placing it well outside AI's current or near-term reach; AI helps only peripherally with measurement, estimating, layout visualization, and scheduling. Elasticity is modest since demand is tied to construction and renovation cycles rather than the cost of installation labor, though somewhat cheaper renovation could unlock some latent home-improvement demand. With disruption near the minimum, the occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS projections of faster-than-average growth.

title: Floral designers
rationale: The core work — physically arranging perishable flowers, processing shipments, and setting up displays at events — is hands-on and manual, keeping disruption low; AI touches only peripheral tasks like order-taking, design inspiration, inventory, and marketing. Demand for flowers is driven by occasions (weddings, funerals, holidays) and gifting norms rather than cost of design labor, so productivity gains would not unlock much latent demand; the occupation already faces structural decline from e-commerce consolidation. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient to AI even though it faces non-AI headwinds like online ordering and grocery-store competition.

title: Food and beverage serving and related workers
rationale: The core work — preparing and carrying food, clearing and setting tables, stocking stations, and in-person hospitality — is physical and requires unpredictable real-world presence, keeping disruption low. AI does touch the periphery: order-taking, payment, and reservations are already being automated via kiosks, apps, and AI drive-thru voice systems, which pressures fast food counter workers and hosts specifically, but bussing, serving, and room delivery remain outside AI's reach absent mature general-purpose robotics. Elasticity is modest — dining out demand responds somewhat to price but is bounded by how much people eat and discretionary income, so cheaper service labor wouldn't unlock explosive consumption. With disruption well below the threshold, this large occupation is resilient, though the ordering/host sub-tasks will gradually shift toward self-service technology.

title: Food preparation workers
rationale: Food preparation is almost entirely physical, hands-on work — chopping, slicing, cleaning, lifting — in unpredictable kitchen environments where AI language and analysis tools are irrelevant to core tasks. The occupation faces pressure from kitchen automation robotics and pre-processed ingredient supply chains, but not from AI in any meaningful sense over the next decade. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: demand for prepared food is tied to dining habits and population, not suppressed by prep-labor costs, so productivity gains would mostly reduce headcount rather than expand output. With disruption near the minimum, this occupation is resilient to AI even though it faces modest structural decline from other forces.

title: Food processing equipment workers
rationale: Core work is physical machine tending — loading equipment, monitoring temperatures, cleaning, and lifting ingredients — which AI language and analysis tools cannot perform; the main threat is traditional industrial automation and sensor-driven process control, which erodes headcount gradually rather than through AI disruption of cognitive tasks. Elasticity is low because food consumption is tied to population and caloric needs, so cheaper processing does not meaningfully expand total demand for these workers. AI may assist peripheral tasks like batch record-keeping and quality monitoring, but the hands-on core remains. Low disruption places this occupation in the resilient category, though long-run robotics/automation (distinct from AI) remains a slow-moving pressure.

title: Food service managers
rationale: The administrative slice of this job — scheduling, inventory ordering, payroll, budgeting, sales forecasting — is squarely in AI's path and is already being automated by restaurant management software, driving a moderate disruption score. However, the core of the role is physical and interpersonal: supervising kitchen and floor staff in real time, inspecting food safety compliance, handling upset customers, and stepping in during rushes, none of which AI can perform. Elasticity is modest because demand for managers scales with the number of physical dining establishments, which is driven by consumer dining habits rather than the cost of management labor. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — AI streamlines the back-office periphery while the on-site leadership core remains human.

title: Forensic science technicians
rationale: A substantial portion of the work—crime scene evidence collection, physical sample handling, chain-of-custody procedures, lab equipment operation, and courtroom testimony—requires human presence and legal accountability that AI cannot replace. AI does meaningfully assist the analytical portions: pattern matching in ballistics and fingerprints, DNA analysis interpretation, and report drafting, which drives a moderate disruption score. Elasticity is moderate: crime lab backlogs are notoriously large, so faster, cheaper analysis would absorb latent demand, but total demand is capped by crime rates and government budgets rather than being unbounded. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient—AI accelerates the lab and reporting work but the core evidence-handling and testimonial functions remain human.

title: Forest and conservation workers
rationale: The work is almost entirely physical and outdoor — planting seedlings, clearing brush, cutting trees, spraying pesticides, and fire suppression in remote, unpredictable terrain where AI language and analysis tools are largely irrelevant. The main technological pressure comes from robotics and remote sensing (e.g., automated tree counting), not AI-driven cognitive automation, and BLS already projects modest decline from that mechanization. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: demand is set by public land budgets, timber markets, and wildfire needs rather than by service cost, though rising wildfire risk provides some offsetting demand. With disruption at 1, the occupation is clearly resilient to AI even as slow mechanization trims headcount.

title: Fundraisers
rationale: Much of fundraising is knowledge work squarely in AI's path: donor prospect research, crafting appeal messages, drafting grant and campaign materials, managing donor databases, and running digital/social media campaigns are already being transformed by AI tools. However, major-gift solicitation, event hosting, and long-term donor relationship cultivation remain fundamentally interpersonal, capping disruption at high but not extreme. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper fundraising lets more small nonprofits professionalize their development efforts, but the total pool of philanthropic dollars is finite, so productivity gains can't be absorbed indefinitely by more giving. The occupation will survive but shift toward relationship management and strategy, with AI handling research, writing, and campaign mechanics — a classic restructure profile.

title: Funeral service workers
rationale: The core work — comforting grieving families in person, preparing and transporting bodies, embalming, and coordinating physical ceremonies — is hands-on, emotionally sensitive, and requires physical presence, so AI touches only peripheral tasks like paperwork, obituary drafting, scheduling, and insurance filings. Demand elasticity is very low because funeral demand is fixed by the death rate; making services cheaper or faster does not cause society to consume more funerals, and trends like cremation already compress spending. With disruption at 3, the occupation is resilient: AI streamlines administrative overhead but the human, ceremonial, and physical core remains intact.

title: Gambling services workers
rationale: The core work of dealing cards, running table games, and managing casino floors is fundamentally in-person hospitality and entertainment — customers at physical casinos are paying for human interaction and atmosphere, which AI does not replace. The real threat is online gambling substitution (a channel shift, not AI performing the dealer's tasks), and AI touches only peripheral areas like surveillance, scheduling, and player analytics. Elasticity is low because demand for in-person gambling is driven by regulation, licensing, and consumer entertainment preferences rather than the cost of dealer labor; making dealers more productive would not meaningfully expand table game demand. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient to AI even as it faces structural pressure from online betting platforms.

title: General maintenance and repair workers
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — fixing plumbing, electrical, HVAC, machinery, and building components in unpredictable real-world environments that AI and robotics cannot handle in the next decade. AI touches only the periphery: diagnostic assistance, work-order management, parts ordering, and predictive maintenance scheduling. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper diagnostics and better preventive maintenance could expand demand somewhat, but total maintenance need is largely driven by building stock, not price. With disruption at 2, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: General office clerks
rationale: The core tasks — typing and formatting documents, data entry, filing, preparing bills, answering routine phone inquiries, scheduling — are precisely the routine digital and language-based work that current AI tools already handle well; only minor physical tasks like sorting mail or greeting visitors resist automation. Demand for clerical support is derived from the fixed administrative overhead of organizations, and making it 10x cheaper doesn't lead offices to consume 10x more filing or phone answering — productivity gains flow directly to headcount reduction, as BLS's projected -7% decline (predating full generative AI absorption) already suggests. With high disruption and inelastic demand, this occupation faces significant contraction as AI and self-service tools absorb the work. The 'replace' category clearly fits.

title: Genetic counselors
rationale: The core work — collecting family histories, evaluating genetic data for risk, documenting sessions, and explaining test results — is largely cognitive and language-based, and AI variant-interpretation tools and LLM-generated patient education materials are already directly in its path; only the empathetic counseling of distressed clients resists automation, yielding high disruption. Elasticity is high because genetic testing volume is exploding while only ~4,000 counselors exist nationally — access to counseling is severely rationed by workforce scarcity and cost, so cheaper, faster risk interpretation would unlock enormous latent demand as genomic medicine expands into cancer, pharmacogenomics, and routine care. With AI handling interpretation and documentation, each counselor can serve far more patients in a market that is demand-constrained, making augment the right fit.

title: Geographers
rationale: The core work — GIS analysis, satellite imagery interpretation, spatial data modeling, map creation, and report writing — is almost entirely digital and squarely in AI's path, with AI-powered remote sensing analysis and automated cartography already advancing rapidly; only fieldwork and stakeholder engagement resist automation. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper geospatial analysis has genuine latent demand in business, climate adaptation, and infrastructure planning, but 68% of geographers work for the federal government where headcount is budget-driven rather than demand-driven, capping expansion. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the occupation restructures — geographers who shift toward directing AI-driven geospatial pipelines, validating outputs, and framing policy-relevant questions will thrive, while those doing routine GIS production and data compilation face displacement.

title: Geological and hydrologic technicians
rationale: Core work is a mix of physical fieldwork — installing equipment, collecting mud and water samples in remote locations — and lab/office analysis; AI and automated sensors can meaningfully speed up the data compilation, mapping, and report-writing portions, and drones already threaten some exploration tasks, but the hands-on sampling and equipment maintenance remain human work. Demand is tied to resource extraction budgets, federal funding, and regulatory monitoring requirements rather than the cost of technician labor, so cheaper analysis would not dramatically expand the volume of sites monitored or samples collected. With moderate disruption confined to the desk-based half of the job and structurally constrained demand, the occupation is resilient — though flat headcount and sensor automation mean modest attrition on the margins.

title: Geoscientists
rationale: Geoscientists split time between fieldwork (sample collection, surveys, remote-site travel), laboratory testing, and office analysis; AI meaningfully accelerates the analytical portions — interpreting seismic and remote sensing data, building geologic models, drafting maps and reports — but the field and lab components require physical presence and cannot be automated. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis could expand demand for resource exploration, hazard assessment, and environmental monitoring, but total demand is tied to energy markets, regulation, and government budgets rather than analysis costs. Because core work remains anchored in physical data collection and site-specific judgment, disruption stays at moderate levels, making 'resilient' the fitting category even as the office-based skill set shifts toward AI-augmented interpretation.

title: Glaziers
rationale: Glazier work is almost entirely physical and hands-on — lifting, cutting, fitting, and securing heavy glass at varied jobsites, often at height, in unpredictable real-world conditions where AI has no direct role. AI may marginally assist with peripheral tasks like estimating, scheduling, or reading digital blueprints, but the core installation work is untouched for the foreseeable horizon. Elasticity is low-moderate since demand is driven by construction cycles and building stock rather than the cost of glazier labor itself. With minimal disruption to core tasks, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Graphic designers
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — layout, illustration, logo creation, photo editing, iterating on client feedback — are fully digital and squarely in the path of generative image and design AI, which already produces production-quality output for routine work; only client relationship management and high-level creative direction resist automation. Demand for visual content is genuinely elastic (cheaper design means more brands, campaigns, and content get professionally designed), but much of that expanded demand will be captured by non-designers self-serving with AI tools rather than flowing back to designers, and BLS already flags AI reducing freelance contracting. This caps elasticity at moderate: some segments (brand strategy, complex multi-channel campaigns) expand, while commodity design work evaporates. High disruption with moderate elasticity fits restructure — the occupation survives, but shifts toward creative direction, brand strategy, and AI-tool orchestration, displacing designers who compete on routine production work.

title: Grounds maintenance workers
rationale: Grounds maintenance is almost entirely physical, outdoor work — mowing, pruning, planting, applying chemicals — performed in unstructured, variable environments where AI language and analysis tools are largely irrelevant; robotic mowers may automate some routine mowing but cannot handle the diverse manual tasks that define the job. Elasticity is modest: cheaper landscaping would unlock some additional demand from homeowners and municipalities, but demand is fundamentally tied to physical land area and property budgets rather than being cost-suppressed at scale. With disruption at 1, this occupation is clearly resilient — AI touches only peripheral scheduling, routing, and plant-diagnosis tasks while the core work remains human hands and equipment outdoors.

title: Hand laborers and material movers
rationale: Core tasks — lifting, carrying, packing, cleaning, feeding machines — are almost entirely physical, so language-model AI has little direct impact; the real threat is warehouse robotics and automated sorting, which AI accelerates but which still faces cost and dexterity barriers in unstructured environments, warranting a low-moderate disruption score. Demand elasticity is low: the volume of freight moved, groceries bagged, and trash collected is driven by consumption and population, not by the cost of manual labor, so productivity gains from automation mostly reduce headcount per facility rather than expand total demand. Some sub-segments (machine feeders, packers) are already projected to decline as robots absorb routine handling, while stockers and order fillers grow with e-commerce. Because AI itself touches only the periphery of this hands-on work over a 10-year horizon, the occupation is resilient, though gradual robotic substitution will erode the most repetitive niches.

title: Hazardous materials removal workers
rationale: The core work — physically removing asbestos, lead, mold, and radioactive materials in protective suits, confined spaces, and disaster zones — is manual, hazardous, and requires unpredictable real-world presence, keeping AI relevance to peripheral tasks like recordkeeping, compliance documentation, and contamination testing analysis. Robotics may eventually assist in extreme environments like nuclear decommissioning, but general-purpose hazmat abatement in varied old buildings is far from automatable. Demand is driven by regulatory mandates, the fixed stock of contaminated sites, and sporadic remediation funding rather than cost — cheaper service wouldn't meaningfully expand the volume of hazardous material needing removal. With low disruption to the core physical work, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Health and safety engineers
rationale: The knowledge-work portions — reviewing plans against regulations, drafting safety programs, analyzing incident data, and preparing compliance documentation — are squarely in AI's path, but the core work requires physical presence: inspecting facilities and machinery, observing worksites for hazards, and interviewing workers during accident investigations. Demand elasticity is constrained because safety engineering volume is driven largely by regulatory requirements and facility counts rather than cost; cheaper safety analysis unlocks only modest additional demand (e.g., smaller firms adopting formal safety programs). With disruption at a moderate 5, the occupation is resilient — AI will streamline paperwork and hazard analysis but won't replace the on-site inspection, investigation, and interpersonal aspects that define the role.

title: Health education specialists
rationale: A large share of the work — developing educational materials, designing campaigns, writing grants, analyzing community health data — is digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and generative AI already accelerates content and program development significantly. However, the core value also depends on in-person facilitation, community trust-building, one-on-one patient interaction, and navigating local politics and stakeholder resistance, keeping disruption at the high end of moderate rather than very high. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper program development could expand preventive health outreach, but demand is largely constrained by government budgets and grant funding rather than production cost. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands as resilient — AI will reshape the desk work substantially, but the community-facing core keeps humans central.

title: Health information technologists and medical registrars
rationale: Core tasks — abstracting clinical data from records, assigning classification codes, maintaining registries, validating data integrity, and generating reports — are almost entirely digital and language-based, placing them squarely in AI's path; LLMs can already abstract pathology reports and assign codes with high accuracy. Elasticity is moderate: healthcare data volume is exploding and cheaper analytics would expand quality tracking, research registries, and outcomes monitoring, but registry abstraction demand is ultimately capped by patient volumes, and privacy/regulatory constraints limit unbounded expansion. The occupation will shift from manual abstraction and coding toward AI oversight, data validation, systems implementation, and analytics interpretation — workers who adapt to those roles will thrive while routine abstractors are displaced, fitting the restructure category.

title: Heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers
rationale: HVAC work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on — installing equipment, brazing pipes, handling refrigerants, and working in cramped spaces — none of which AI can perform; AI assists only at the periphery through diagnostic tools, smart-system monitoring, scheduling, and documentation. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper diagnostics and predictive maintenance could expand service volume somewhat, and electrification/efficiency retrofits drive real demand growth, but the physical installation work itself isn't made 10x cheaper by AI. With disruption well below the threshold and BLS projecting much-faster-than-average growth, this occupation is clearly resilient — AI may even increase demand by making climate-control systems more sophisticated and networked, requiring skilled technicians to install and maintain them.

title: Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers
rationale: Truck driving is physical, real-world work, but it is uniquely exposed to embodied AI: autonomous trucking is already in limited commercial deployment on highway corridors, and long-haul interstate driving is the most automatable driving domain. Still, over a 10-year horizon, regulatory hurdles, weather, first/last-mile complexity, cargo securing, inspections, and hazmat rules mean most drivers' core tasks remain human-performed, warranting a moderate disruption score. Freight demand is driven by overall goods consumption rather than transport cost, so a 10x cheaper trucking mile yields only modest expansion in shipped volume — some induced demand from cheaper logistics, but nothing like software's latent demand. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient in the near decade, though the tail-end risk from autonomous long-haul trucking is real and could accelerate beyond this window.

title: Heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians
rationale: The core work is intensely physical and hands-on — disassembling engines, replacing hydraulic pumps, welding, and lifting heavy parts in shops and at remote field sites — placing it far outside AI's direct path. AI assists at the periphery through smarter computerized diagnostics, predictive maintenance alerts, and AI-guided troubleshooting of increasingly software-driven equipment, but the repair itself still requires a skilled human with tools. Elasticity is moderate: predictive maintenance could shift some demand from breakdown repair to scheduled service, while a growing equipment stock and increasingly complex machinery sustain steady need for technicians. With disruption this low, the occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS's faster-than-average growth projection.

title: High school teachers
rationale: A substantial share of teachers' knowledge work — lesson planning, grading, assessment creation, differentiated materials, parent communication — is already being reshaped by AI tools, but the core of the job remains in-person instruction, classroom management, motivation, and custodial supervision of minors, which AI cannot replace and which anchors disruption at the moderate-high boundary. Elasticity is low: staffing is driven by student enrollment (projected to decline), student-teacher ratios, and public budgets rather than the cost of instructional output, so making a teacher 10x more productive at planning and grading does not lead society to hire more teachers. Because the irreducibly human, in-person supervisory core keeps disruption at 6 rather than 7+, the occupation is resilient — AI streamlines the peripheral workload while headcount is governed by demographics and budgets, not automation.

title: Historians
rationale: The core tasks of historians — gathering documents, analyzing texts, tracing developments, and writing reports and books — are language- and research-based knowledge work squarely in AI's path; LLMs already accelerate archival search, document interpretation, translation of foreign-language sources, and drafting, though physical artifact handling and public engagement retain some human elements. Demand is largely inelastic: employment depends on donations and government funding, not on the price of historical research, so making the work 10x faster does not meaningfully expand the number of funded positions, and some latent demand (corporate histories, genealogy) is small and increasingly served by AI directly. With institutional budgets capping headcount and AI absorbing the research and writing core, productivity gains translate into fewer positions rather than more output, fitting the replace category.

title: Home health and personal care aides
rationale: The core work — bathing, dressing, lifting, feeding, housekeeping, companionship, and in-person monitoring — is almost entirely physical and interpersonal, requiring unpredictable real-world presence in clients' homes; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling and documentation. Elasticity is moderate-to-high in principle given the aging population and demand suppressed by cost, but the productivity gains from AI are minimal because AI cannot substitute for hands-on care. With BLS projecting 17% growth driven by demographics, this is a textbook resilient occupation: disruption is minimal regardless of demand dynamics.

title: Human resources specialists
rationale: The core tasks — screening resumes, scheduling interviews, checking references, answering policy questions, processing paperwork, and maintaining records — are digital and language-based work squarely in AI's path, with AI recruiting and HR chatbot tools already widely deployed; only interviews and sensitive employee-relations work require genuine human presence. Elasticity is low because demand for HR services scales with organizational headcount, not with the price of HR work — companies do not hire 10x more employees or run 10x more benefits enrollments because HR became cheaper, so productivity gains translate largely into leaner HR teams. Some latent demand exists in better candidate matching and more thorough compliance, but it is structurally capped. High disruption combined with inelastic demand points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category, though specialists focused on strategic and interpersonal work will be more insulated.

title: Hydrologists
rationale: Hydrologists split their time between field data collection (streamflow measurement, water and soil sampling in remote locations) and desk-based modeling, forecasting, and report writing. AI already meaningfully accelerates the modeling, data analysis, and report-drafting portions, but the physical fieldwork, site evaluation, and stakeholder coordination require human presence, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is low: demand is driven by regulatory mandates and government budgets (over 60% work for federal, state, or local government), so cheaper analysis won't unlock much latent demand — BLS already projects 0% growth citing budget constraints. With disruption at 5, the core occupation remains resilient even as its analytical toolkit shifts toward AI-assisted modeling.

title: Industrial designers
rationale: Core tasks—sketching, rendering, 3D CAD modeling, generating design alternatives—are digital and directly in the path of generative AI and AI-assisted CAD tools that can already produce concepts, renderings, and design variations rapidly. However, physical prototyping, materials/manufacturing feasibility judgment, and client collaboration keep humans central, capping disruption at 7. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design would let more small manufacturers and startups afford professional industrial design and enable faster iteration cycles, but total demand is ultimately tethered to physical product manufacturing volumes, which don't scale 10x just because design gets cheaper. The occupation will survive but shift toward AI-driven concept generation, curation, and manufacturing integration skills—a classic restructure profile.

title: Industrial engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: A substantial share of the work — statistical production studies, cost analysis, workflow charting, and documentation — is digital and analytical, squarely in AI's path, and increasingly automated by sensor-driven analytics and AI-powered process optimization tools. However, the core role requires physical presence on factory floors: observing workers, collecting data on machinery, testing prototypes, and conferring with production staff, which caps disruption at moderate-high. Elasticity is moderate — cheaper process analysis would let more manufacturers pursue continuous improvement, but total demand is bounded by the size of the domestic manufacturing base rather than latent unmet demand. With disruption at the boundary of 6, the physical, plant-based nature of the observational and hands-on work tips this toward resilient, though the analytical portions of the job will shift heavily toward AI-assisted tooling.

title: Industrial engineers
rationale: A large share of industrial engineering — data analysis, simulation, process optimization, and report writing — is squarely in AI's path, and AI-powered optimization tools already materially assist this work. However, the core role requires physical presence on factory floors and in hospitals, observing workers, understanding physical constraints, and driving organizational change through cross-departmental collaboration, keeping disruption at the moderate-high boundary. Elasticity is high because demand for efficiency improvement is essentially unbounded — as optimization becomes cheaper, far more processes, supply chains, and facilities become economical to analyze, consistent with BLS's projected 11% growth. Since disruption sits at 6 with the hands-on, in-the-field core intact, the occupation is resilient, with AI amplifying rather than absorbing the work.

title: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers, and millwrights
rationale: The core work — disassembling machinery, replacing parts, welding, aligning, and physically moving heavy equipment — is hands-on and occurs in unpredictable industrial environments where AI and robotics cannot substitute. AI does affect the diagnostic layer: predictive maintenance, vibration analysis, and AI-assisted troubleshooting will streamline problem detection, but the repair itself remains manual. Elasticity is moderate-to-high because increased factory automation actually creates more machinery needing maintenance, and BLS projects 13% growth driven by this dynamic. With disruption clearly low, this occupation is resilient — AI augments diagnostics at the periphery while demand for skilled hands grows.

title: Industrial production managers
rationale: A meaningful portion of the role — production scheduling, analyzing production data, budget tracking, report review, quality analytics — is squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven planning and predictive quality tools will materially change those tasks. However, the core work requires physical presence on the plant floor, leading and motivating workers, handling emergencies, safety oversight, and cross-department coordination, which keeps disruption moderate. Elasticity is low because headcount is tied to the number of plants and manufacturing output, not the cost of management — making managers 10x more efficient doesn't create 10x more factories, and BLS already projects near-flat growth. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI augments the analytical side but the hands-on leadership core remains intact.

title: Information clerks
rationale: The core tasks — preparing routine reports, answering standard inquiries, filing records, processing orders and applications — are precisely the routine digital and language-based work that current AI chatbots, form-processing, and self-service systems already handle well; only subsegments like hotel front desk clerks retain a physical/hospitality component. Demand for record maintenance, order processing, and answering routine questions is essentially fixed by the volume of underlying transactions — making these tasks 10x cheaper doesn't cause organizations to file 10x more records or answer 10x more inquiries, so productivity gains flow directly to headcount reduction. BLS already projects decline, with the sharpest drops in the most automatable subgroups (file clerks, order clerks, interviewers). High disruption combined with inelastic demand makes this a clear replace case, with significant contraction expected beyond BLS's conservative projections.

title: Information security analysts
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital — monitoring logs, scanning for vulnerabilities, writing reports, and developing security policies — and AI-driven SOC tools already automate alert triage, threat detection, and incident response, placing core tasks directly in AI's path. However, demand is highly elastic: cyberattacks are growing in volume and sophistication (partly fueled by AI itself), and cheaper security services would let millions of small and mid-sized organizations afford protection they currently forgo. This is an adversarial domain where AI attackers escalate the need for AI-augmented defenders, so productivity gains get absorbed by dramatically expanded coverage rather than headcount cuts. High disruption plus high elasticity — consistent with BLS's projected 29% growth — makes this a clear augment case.

title: Instructional coordinators
rationale: Core tasks — curriculum development, analyzing student test data, reviewing educational materials, and creating teacher training content — are language-heavy knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and generative AI can already draft curricula, standards-aligned lesson frameworks, and data analyses; only classroom observation and in-person coaching resist automation. Elasticity is low because demand is capped by fixed public education budgets and district staffing structures — even if curriculum design becomes 10x cheaper, schools won't hire more coordinators, and the BLS's own 1% projected growth citing budget constraints confirms this. With one coordinator plus AI able to serve the curriculum and data-analysis needs previously requiring several, headcount pressure is downward. High disruption combined with structurally constrained demand places this occupation in the replace category.

title: Insulation workers
rationale: Insulation work is almost entirely physical and manual — cutting, fitting, stapling, and spraying insulation in confined spaces, attics, and around pipes — with AI relevant only to peripheral tasks like estimating material quantities or reading blueprints. Robotics for unpredictable construction environments remains far from practical deployment over a 10-year horizon. Elasticity is modest: cheaper insulation services would unlock some latent demand for energy-efficiency retrofits, but demand is tied to construction cycles and building stock rather than being heavily cost-suppressed. With disruption near minimal, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Insurance sales agents
rationale: The core tasks — explaining policy features, comparing options, quoting, customizing coverage, and handling renewals — are language-based knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and direct-to-consumer online purchasing plus AI advisory chatbots are already eroding the intermediary role. Elasticity is low: insurance demand is driven by assets, income, and legal mandates, not agent cost — people won't buy meaningfully more policies just because sales advice becomes 10x cheaper, and any modest expansion into underinsured segments will likely be captured by automated channels rather than more agents. Trust-based relationship selling for complex commercial and high-net-worth cases will persist, but the large volume of routine personal-lines sales faces direct substitution. High disruption combined with structurally capped demand points to significant headcount contraction, fitting 'replace'.

title: Insurance underwriters
rationale: Underwriting is almost entirely digital knowledge work — analyzing application data, assessing risk factors, and setting premiums — and automated underwriting software already handles simple policies end-to-end, with AI rapidly extending into complex commercial and specialty lines. Demand elasticity is low: people and businesses don't buy meaningfully more insurance because underwriting becomes faster or cheaper, since demand is driven by assets, regulation, and risk exposure rather than underwriting cost. BLS already projects a 3% decline driven explicitly by automation, and AI will accelerate this by shrinking the residual pool of complex cases requiring human judgment. High disruption combined with structurally capped demand makes this a clear replace scenario.

title: Interior designers
rationale: Much of the core workflow — concept sketches, CAD/BIM drawings, 3D visualizations, material specification, cost estimation, and project scheduling — is digital and directly in AI's path, with generative tools already producing photorealistic room designs from text prompts; however, client relationships, site visits, contractor coordination, and code compliance oversight keep disruption from reaching the top tier. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design services would unlock latent demand from homeowners and small businesses who currently forgo professional design, but much of that demand may be captured by consumers using AI tools directly rather than hiring designers, and renovation volume is ultimately capped by construction budgets. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the occupation restructures — designers who leverage AI to serve more clients and pivot toward project management, client advisory, and code expertise will thrive, while those competing on rendering and drafting output will be displaced.

title: Interpreters and translators
rationale: Translation is almost entirely digital language work sitting directly in AI's path — machine translation already handles most routine text at near-human quality, and real-time speech translation is rapidly closing the gap on interpreting, leaving humans mainly as post-editors and quality checkers. While cheaper translation unlocks enormous latent demand (far more content gets localized), that expanded volume flows overwhelmingly to AI systems directly rather than to human translators, so headcount demand for the occupation itself is largely capped to high-stakes niches like courts, medical settings, literary work, and sign language interpreting. These protected segments are regulated or liability-driven but too small to offset displacement in the commercial translation market. High disruption with low effective demand elasticity for human workers makes this a clear replace category.

title: Ironworkers
rationale: Ironworkers' core tasks — erecting steel girders, tying rebar, welding, walking beams at height, and signaling cranes on unpredictable outdoor jobsites — are almost entirely physical and unstructured, placing them far outside AI's near-term reach; AI touches only peripheral tasks like blueprint interpretation and scheduling. Elasticity is modest: construction demand is driven by capital spending, infrastructure funding, and land availability rather than the labor cost of ironwork, so even large productivity gains would not dramatically expand steel erection volume. With minimal disruption to the hands-on core, the occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS's steady 4% growth projection.

title: Janitors and building cleaners
rationale: Janitorial work is almost entirely physical — mopping, emptying trash, cleaning restrooms, minor repairs — in varied, unpredictable environments where language-based AI is irrelevant; even robotic floor scrubbers handle only a narrow slice of tasks. Elasticity is low: buildings need cleaning on a fixed schedule regardless of cost, so cheaper cleaning would not meaningfully expand total square footage cleaned, though marginally more frequent cleaning is possible. With disruption near the floor, the occupation is resilient — AI may assist scheduling and supply ordering at the margins but does not touch the core work.

title: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers
rationale: Core work is hands-on craft — soldering, stone setting, polishing, repair — requiring fine dexterity that AI cannot perform; AI touches only peripheral tasks like CAD design generation, appraisal research, and gemstone grading (which computer vision may partially automate for gemologists). Elasticity is low: jewelry is a discretionary luxury good whose demand is driven by fashion, income, and sentiment rather than the cost of bench labor, so cheaper design or grading would not meaningfully expand consumption, and imports plus 3D printing already pressure headcount. The occupation faces gradual decline from automation of manufacturing and offshoring rather than AI displacement of core skills, fitting the resilient category since disruption is well below the threshold.

title: Judges and hearing officers
rationale: Much of the work — legal research, evaluating briefs and motions, and drafting opinions — is language-based knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and AI tools will substantially accelerate these tasks. However, the core function is exercising legally-vested human authority: presiding over live hearings, weighing credibility, and issuing binding rulings, which is constitutionally and institutionally reserved for human officeholders whose numbers are set by statute and budget appropriations rather than productivity. Elasticity is low because judgeships don't multiply when adjudication gets cheaper — caseloads per judge might rise and backlogs shrink, but governments won't hire dramatically more judges, and budget constraints already suppress headcount. With disruption at the boundary but the irreducibly human, gatekept core of the role dominating, the occupation is resilient: AI augments chambers work (much of it currently done by clerks) without displacing the judges themselves.

title: Kindergarten and elementary school teachers
rationale: AI meaningfully assists with lesson planning, grading, differentiated materials, and parent communication, but the core of this job is in-person supervision, socialization, behavior management, and emotional development of young children — functions that require physical presence and cannot be delegated to software. Demand is structurally tied to child population and enrollment, which is projected to decline, and productivity gains don't cause society to consume 'more kindergarten'; at best, cheaper AI tutoring might supplement but also modestly pressure staffing ratios. Because disruption stays moderate — AI reshapes the paperwork periphery, not the classroom core — the occupation is resilient, with headcount driven by demographics and school budgets rather than automation.

title: Labor relations specialists
rationale: AI can already assist with drafting policies, analyzing collective bargaining agreements, compliance checking, and grievance documentation, but the core work — face-to-face negotiation, building trust with workers and management, mediating tense disputes, and conducting misconduct investigations — depends on interpersonal rapport and real-time human judgment that AI cannot substitute. Elasticity is low because demand is structurally tied to union membership rates and the volume of labor disputes, not to the cost of the service; cheaper contract drafting won't generate more union negotiations. With disruption at a moderate 5, the occupation is resilient: AI streamlines the paperwork-heavy periphery while the relational core remains intact, consistent with BLS's flat employment projection driven by union trends rather than automation.

title: Landscape architects
rationale: A large share of the work—CADD drafting, GIS analysis, renderings, cost estimates, and specifications—is digital and squarely in AI's path, with generative design and AI rendering tools already compressing production time. However, the core role also requires site visits, construction inspection, region-specific plant/soil/climate judgment, stakeholder negotiation, and a state license to stamp plans, keeping disruption at the moderate-high boundary rather than very high. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper design could unlock latent demand from homeowners, small municipalities, and green-infrastructure projects, but design fees are a small fraction of total project cost, so construction budgets and land availability cap expansion. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands as resilient—AI transforms the drafting and visualization workflow but the licensed, site-embedded core survives largely intact.

title: Lawyers
rationale: Legal research, document drafting, contract review, and brief preparation are core lawyer tasks squarely in AI's path, and current tools already handle much of this work; however, courtroom advocacy, negotiation, and client counseling retain human requirements, keeping disruption at 7 rather than higher. Elasticity is limited: while significant latent demand for legal services exists among individuals and small businesses priced out of the market, growth is capped by court capacity, bar licensing, regulatory constraints, and the fact that much legal demand (litigation, transactions) is driven by external events rather than price. Productivity gains will likely be absorbed through leaner staffing at firms rather than proportional demand expansion, particularly hitting junior associates whose research and drafting work AI absorbs. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 4, the occupation faces net headcount pressure despite surviving as a profession, fitting the replace category.

title: Librarians and library media specialists
rationale: The reference and research core of librarianship — helping patrons find and evaluate information — is directly in AI's path, and cataloging/collection curation is increasingly automated; special and corporate librarians face acute exposure. However, roughly two-thirds of these workers are in public and school settings where the job has already shifted toward in-person programming, teaching, community services, and managing physical spaces, which anchors disruption at the high end of moderate rather than high. Elasticity is low because libraries are publicly and institutionally funded with fixed budgets — cheaper information retrieval does not cause communities to hire more librarians, and AI actually substitutes for the public's need to consult one. On the boundary between resilient and replace, resilient fits best because the surviving core of the role (community engagement, youth programming, teaching, facility stewardship) requires physical presence and is not reshaped by AI, though the pure information-specialist segment will contract.

title: Library technicians and assistants
rationale: A substantial share of the work — cataloging, database maintenance, answering routine reference questions, and clerical processing — is squarely in AI's path, and self-checkout/automated circulation systems already erode core tasks; however, reshelving materials, staffing service desks, running story times, and hands-on patron assistance keep the occupation anchored in physical presence, holding disruption at the moderate-high boundary. Elasticity is very low: library usage is declining, services are already free to patrons, and headcount is set by constrained local government and school budgets, so productivity gains translate directly into fewer positions rather than expanded service. With disruption at 6, the category is resilient by definition, though this is a borderline case — the occupation faces steady contraction from budget pressure and declining library use, with AI accelerating the erosion of its clerical and reference components rather than transforming the in-person core.

title: Licensed practical and licensed vocational nurses
rationale: The core work of LPNs/LVNs is hands-on and physical: checking vital signs, changing bandages, bathing and feeding patients, and providing bedside comfort — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like documentation, charting, and care-plan summaries, which may free up time but doesn't change the essence of the job. Demand elasticity is fairly high given the aging population, chronic disease prevalence, and persistent caregiver shortages — cheaper, faster support would be readily absorbed by home health and long-term care. With disruption low, the occupation is clearly resilient: AI streamlines paperwork while the physical caregiving core remains fully human.

title: Loan officers
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — gathering and verifying financial documents, analyzing credit data, reviewing compliance, and underwriting — are digital and language-based, and underwriting software already automates much of the decision; AI extends this to document intake, verification, customer Q&A, and even sales outreach. Demand for loans is driven by real economic needs (homes, cars, business investment) and constrained by borrowers' creditworthiness and interest rates, not by processing cost, so making loan origination 10x cheaper does not generate proportionally more loans — some latent demand exists in small-business and underserved lending, but regulation and credit risk cap expansion. Productivity gains therefore translate mostly into fewer officers processing the same loan volume, with residual roles concentrated in complex commercial deals and relationship-based sales. High disruption with low elasticity places this squarely in the replace category, consistent with BLS's own note that technology is already suppressing growth.

title: Lodging managers
rationale: A meaningful share of lodging management involves knowledge work that AI is already transforming — revenue management, occupancy forecasting, dynamic pricing, scheduling, guest communications, and budgeting — but the core of the job requires on-site presence: inspecting rooms, supervising and motivating staff, resolving guest conflicts face-to-face, and coordinating physical operations 24/7. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: cheaper management doesn't create dramatically more hotel stays, since demand is driven by travel patterns and physical room supply, though AI-enabled efficiency may let smaller properties afford professional-grade management or one manager to oversee multiple properties. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI will absorb the analytical back-office portions (especially revenue manager sub-roles) while the general management core, rooted in physical presence and interpersonal leadership, remains human.

title: Logging workers
rationale: Logging is almost entirely physical, outdoor work in rugged, unpredictable terrain — felling trees, operating heavy machinery, and handling logs — which is far outside AI's near-term reach; only peripheral tasks like log grading/scaling and route or harvest planning are digitally assisted. Demand for timber is driven by construction and paper markets, not by the labor cost of logging, so productivity gains would mostly reduce crew sizes rather than expand harvesting (mechanization has already been shrinking headcount for decades). With disruption near the minimum, the occupation is clearly resilient to AI, though it remains exposed to ongoing mechanization and slow structural decline.

title: Logisticians
rationale: Logisticians' core tasks — demand forecasting, supply-demand alignment, cost optimization, risk monitoring, and systems management — are analytical, data-heavy, and digital, precisely where AI-driven optimization and predictive tools are already highly capable, though liaison work with suppliers and on-site problem-solving retain a human element. Elasticity is moderate: e-commerce growth and supply chain complexity create real appetite for more granular, continuous optimization, and cheaper analysis lets smaller firms buy sophisticated logistics planning, but total demand is ultimately anchored to physical goods flows that don't multiply just because analysis gets cheaper. The occupation will persist and likely grow overall, but the role shifts from routine planning and tracking toward exception handling, AI system oversight, and strategic supplier relationships. This combination of high disruption and moderate demand expansion fits restructure: workers who master AI-augmented supply chain tools thrive, while those doing routine coordination are displaced.

title: Machinists and tool and die makers
rationale: The core work — setting up machines, aligning cutting tools, fixturing workpieces, monitoring feeds and speeds, and hand-finishing dies to .0001-inch tolerances — is physical and requires shop-floor presence, though AI meaningfully assists the digital portions like CAD/CAM interpretation and CNC programming (a larger share of tool and die makers' work, hence their steeper projected decline). Elasticity is moderate: cheaper precision machining unlocks some latent demand for custom parts, prototyping, and reshored manufacturing, but total demand is tied to broader manufacturing output and capped by capital equipment costs. Automation and CNC efficiency gains will continue to slowly compress headcount, but AI itself touches the programming periphery rather than the hands-on core. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient, though tool and die makers face more skill-shift pressure than machinists.

title: Management analysts
rationale: The core tasks — gathering and analyzing data, synthesizing findings, writing reports, and building recommendations — are almost entirely digital and language-based, squarely in AI's current path; LLMs already draft strategy decks, analyze financials, and benchmark processes. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis unlocks latent demand from small and mid-size firms that couldn't afford consulting, and AI adoption itself generates new advisory work, but demand is capped by trust dynamics — clients pay for accountability, relationships, and change management, not just analysis, and some clients will use AI to bypass consultants entirely. The occupation persists but shifts sharply toward client relationship management, judgment, implementation oversight, and AI-augmented delivery, while junior analysts doing pure research and slide production face displacement. This high-disruption, moderate-elasticity profile fits restructure.

title: Manicurists and pedicurists
rationale: Nail care is almost entirely hands-on physical work requiring fine motor dexterity, direct skin contact, and in-person presence — AI has essentially no path into the core tasks of cleaning, trimming, polishing, and applying nail art. AI might marginally help with scheduling, marketing, or design suggestions, but these are peripheral. Elasticity is moot since AI cannot deliver the productivity gains; demand is driven by disposable income and grooming trends rather than technology costs. With disruption near zero, this occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS's above-average growth projection.

title: Marine engineers and naval architects
rationale: A substantial share of the work — hull design, system schematics, performance simulations, cost estimates, and technical reports — is digital knowledge work where AI-assisted CAD, generative design, and simulation tools are already advancing, but the core also includes overseeing prototype construction, physical testing, shipyard presence, offshore work, and regulatory sign-off requiring PE licensure and human accountability. Elasticity is limited: ship and offshore platform demand is driven by capital-intensive procurement cycles, defense budgets, and trade volumes rather than engineering labor costs, so 10x cheaper design would only modestly expand the number of vessels built. With disruption at the boundary but held to 6 by the significant physical, safety-critical, and on-site components, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the design workflow while the role itself persists.

title: Market research analysts
rationale: Nearly every core task — survey design, data gathering, statistical analysis, report writing, chart creation, and trend forecasting — is digital and language-based, placing this occupation squarely in AI's direct path; current LLMs and analytics tools can already draft surveys, synthesize consumer sentiment from big data, and generate polished reports. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper research would let small businesses and product teams consume far more market insight than today, but much demand is bundled into fixed corporate marketing budgets and decision-making bandwidth, so consumption won't scale 10x with cost reductions. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the field survives but shifts toward strategic interpretation, research design, and stakeholder advising while AI handles data collection and synthesis — a classic restructure where non-adapting analysts are displaced.

title: Marriage and family therapists
rationale: Therapy is language-based on the surface, but its core value lies in human rapport, trust, and navigating live emotional dynamics between multiple people in a room — something clients specifically seek from a human, and licensure/liability rules reinforce this. AI will assist with intake, session notes, treatment planning, billing, and may siphon off some low-acuity support via chatbots, but it does not replace the therapeutic relationship at the core. Elasticity is high because mental health demand is heavily suppressed by cost, stigma, and provider shortages — cheaper, faster support would be absorbed by enormous unmet need. With disruption at the moderate level, the occupation is resilient: AI trims administrative burden and possibly expands access, while the core work remains human.

title: Masonry workers
rationale: Masonry is almost entirely physical, hands-on work performed in unpredictable outdoor construction environments — lifting materials, laying brick, finishing concrete — where current AI has essentially no purchase; peripheral tasks like estimating materials from blueprints or scheduling could see minor AI assistance. Bricklaying robots exist but remain niche and are better classified as automation hardware than AI, and adoption over 10 years will be limited. Elasticity is modest: cheaper construction would spur some additional building, but demand is constrained by land, permitting, materials cost, and the shift toward prefabricated panels noted by BLS. With disruption near the floor, the occupation is clearly resilient — headcount will be shaped by construction cycles and prefab trends, not AI.

title: Massage therapists
rationale: Massage therapy is almost entirely hands-on physical work requiring skilled manipulation of soft tissue, real-time tactile feedback, and human presence — AI cannot perform any of the core tasks, and only peripheral activities like scheduling, marketing, and client documentation are touched. Elasticity is moderate: demand for wellness services is growing and somewhat price-sensitive, but the service itself cannot be made cheaper or faster by AI since the therapist's time is the product. With minimal disruption to core work and strong projected employment growth (15%), this occupation is clearly resilient to AI.

title: Material moving machine operators
rationale: The core work is physical machine operation, but it occurs largely in structured, controlled environments like warehouses — precisely where AI-driven automation (autonomous forklifts, AGVs, automated conveyor and crane systems) is advancing fastest, so disruption is moderate rather than low. Elasticity is limited: e-commerce growth increases material volume somewhat, but cheaper material handling doesn't unlock vast latent demand for moving goods — productivity gains mostly translate to fewer operators per warehouse. The net effect is resilient over the 10-year horizon because embodied automation deploys slowly due to capital costs, safety regulation, and heterogeneous worksites (construction sites, ports, dredging), though the warehouse-based forklift segment faces the greatest long-term erosion.

title: Material recording clerks
rationale: The core work—recordkeeping, inventory tracking, report compilation, scheduling, and invoicing—is routine digital data processing squarely in AI's path, and RFID sensors plus automated warehouse management systems already eliminate much manual counting and entry; only the residual physical tasks (handling packages, spot-inspecting goods) temper the score. Demand for inventory tracking is derived entirely from the volume of goods moving through supply chains, which won't grow because tracking becomes cheaper—productivity gains flow directly to headcount reduction, as BLS's own -6% projection reflects. With high disruption and near-inelastic demand, this is a clear replace scenario, with automation absorbing the recordkeeping core while remaining physical tasks get consolidated into fewer warehouse roles.

title: Materials engineers
rationale: AI is already transforming the computational side of this field — ML models for property prediction, generative materials discovery (e.g., candidate alloy and polymer screening), and simulation acceleration hit the design and analysis portions of the job directly. However, the core work still requires physical synthesis, lab testing, failure analysis of real components, and integration with manufacturing processes, which keeps disruption at the high end of moderate rather than very high. Elasticity is moderate-to-good: cheaper, faster materials discovery unlocks latent demand in aerospace, semiconductors, batteries, and sustainability applications, but the small occupation size and long physical validation cycles cap how much headcount expands. With disruption at 6, the physical-experimental core anchors this as resilient, though the skill mix will shift heavily toward computational and AI-driven materials workflows.

title: Mathematicians and statisticians
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — designing analyses, building statistical models, writing code, interpreting data, producing reports — are digital cognitive work squarely in AI's path, and current LLMs and automated modeling tools already handle substantial portions of routine statistical analysis. Demand for statistical insight expands meaningfully as it gets cheaper — more businesses, healthcare studies, and policy questions get rigorous analysis — but much of that expanded demand flows through general-purpose AI tools or adjacent roles like data scientists rather than credentialed statisticians, and regulated domains (clinical trials, federal statistics) cap headcount growth. The occupation persists but shifts toward study design, causal reasoning, validation of AI-generated analyses, and communication, displacing those who only execute routine modeling. This high-disruption, moderate-elasticity profile fits restructure.

title: Mechanical engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: The work is genuinely mixed: CAD layouts, drawings, data recording, test analysis, and cost calculations are squarely in AI's path, but a substantial core involves physically setting up test rigs, assembling parts, operating machinery like lathes and grinders, and troubleshooting equipment on factory floors — tasks requiring hands-on presence. Elasticity is modest because demand is tied to manufacturing and product development activity, which cheaper drafting and analysis does not dramatically expand; BLS already projects flat employment as automation of routine design work offsets any growth. With disruption around 5, AI erodes the digital half of the job (making the drafting-heavy technologist role more vulnerable) but leaves the hands-on testing and fabrication core intact, fitting the resilient category despite meaningful skill-shift pressure.

title: Mechanical engineers
