rationale: A large share of mechanical engineering work — CAD design, simulation, analysis, generating specifications — is digital and increasingly assisted by generative design and AI-accelerated simulation tools, but the core job also involves building and testing physical prototypes, diagnosing equipment failures on-site, and overseeing manufacturing, which keeps disruption at the moderate-high boundary rather than fully digital. Elasticity is high because cheaper, faster engineering design would unlock substantial latent demand: more products iterated, more automation deployed, more robotics and energy systems built — and ironically, AI-driven automation itself creates demand for mechanical engineers to integrate it. Because the irreducibly physical portions (prototyping, testing, factory-floor oversight) anchor the occupation against full AI absorption, disruption lands at 6 and the occupation is best classified as resilient, though its knowledge-work half will be heavily reshaped and engineers who adopt AI design tools will be far more productive.

title: Medical and health services managers
rationale: Much of the work — budgeting, scheduling, compliance monitoring, reporting, and records oversight — is digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, but core responsibilities like leading clinical staff, resolving on-site operational crises, negotiating with boards and physicians, and being present in 24/7 facilities keep the role anchored in human presence and interpersonal authority, placing disruption at the boundary of moderate and high. Elasticity is moderate: healthcare demand is structurally growing with an aging population, and cheaper administration lets more clinics and departments afford professional management, but the number of managers is ultimately tied to the number of facilities and staff, not to how cheap management becomes. With disruption at 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI will absorb much of the analytical and administrative workload, but the coordination and leadership core survives, consistent with BLS's projected 23% growth.

title: Medical assistants
rationale: Core clinical tasks — taking vital signs, drawing blood, preparing specimens, assisting with exams, giving injections — require physical presence and hands-on patient contact that AI cannot perform, though the administrative side (scheduling, records entry, insurance coding, billing) is squarely in AI's path and may be substantially automated. Elasticity is moderate: an aging population and cost-constrained healthcare access mean cheaper clinical support would be absorbed by growing demand, as reflected in the 12% projected growth. Because disruption is confined to the administrative periphery while the in-person clinical core remains intact, the occupation is resilient — though roles may tilt further toward clinical duties as AI absorbs the paperwork.

title: Medical dosimetrists
rationale: The core work — reviewing scans, calculating radiation doses, and designing treatment plans on a computer — is almost entirely digital and is already being transformed by AI-driven auto-planning and deep-learning dose optimization tools (e.g., knowledge-based planning, adaptive radiotherapy systems), placing it squarely in AI's path. Demand for radiation treatment planning is driven by cancer incidence, not by the cost or speed of planning; patients won't receive 10x more radiotherapy courses because plans become cheaper, though daily adaptive replanning offers some modest volume expansion. With only 4,800 workers and projected flat employment, productivity gains from AI planning tools will likely translate into fewer dosimetrists per clinic rather than expanded demand. High disruption combined with structurally inelastic demand makes this a replace scenario, with remaining roles shifting toward QA and plan review under physicist oversight.

title: Medical equipment repairers
rationale: The core work — physically installing, disassembling, calibrating, and repairing electromechanical and hydraulic medical equipment on-site — requires hands-on presence, dexterity, and physical strength that AI cannot replace. AI meaningfully assists peripheral tasks like fault diagnosis, pulling technical manual guidance, predictive maintenance scheduling, and record-keeping, but these are complements rather than substitutes for the manual repair itself. Demand is largely driven by the installed base of medical equipment and healthcare utilization rather than repair cost, so even faster diagnostics would only modestly expand total work. With low disruption to core tasks and strong projected employment growth from expanding healthcare demand, this occupation is resilient.

title: Medical records specialists
rationale: The core tasks — reviewing records, assigning standardized diagnosis and procedure codes, and entering data into EHR systems — are entirely digital, rule-based classification work that sits directly in AI's path, and autonomous coding tools are already deployed and improving rapidly. Demand for medical coding is driven by patient encounter volume and payer requirements, not by cost or speed of coding, so making the work 10x cheaper does not generate meaningfully more records to code. While healthcare volume grows modestly with an aging population, that growth cannot absorb the productivity gains from AI coding systems, so headcount contraction is likely despite BLS's current positive projection. High disruption combined with inelastic demand places this occupation squarely in the replace category.

title: Medical scientists
rationale: A large share of a medical scientist's core work — literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, experimental design, statistical analysis of trial data, and grant/manuscript writing — is directly in AI's path, and tools like protein-structure prediction and AI-driven drug discovery are already reshaping the field; hands-on wet lab work tempers the score but is often delegated to technicians. Demand elasticity is high because the appetite for cures and treatments is effectively unbounded — cheaper, faster research means more diseases investigated, more compounds screened, and more trials run, with an aging population and chronic disease burden fueling funding. Productivity gains are likely absorbed by dramatically expanded research output rather than headcount cuts, consistent with BLS's much-faster-than-average growth projection. High disruption paired with high elasticity makes this a clear augment case.

title: Medical transcriptionists
rationale: Medical transcription is fully routine digital language processing — AI speech recognition and LLM-based ambient documentation tools already perform the core task (converting dictation to formatted medical reports) with high accuracy, and the residual editing/QA role is rapidly shrinking as models improve. Demand is inelastic: the volume of clinical documentation is driven by patient encounters, not by transcription cost, so a 10x cheaper transcription process does not generate 10x more dictation — it simply requires fewer humans. BLS already projects decline, and ambient AI scribes are accelerating this beyond the official forecast. With maximum disruption and near-zero demand elasticity, this is a textbook replace occupation.

title: Meeting, convention, and event planners
rationale: A substantial portion of the work — vendor research, soliciting bids, budgeting, scheduling, attendee communications, and post-event billing — is digital coordination work that AI tools can already accelerate significantly, but the core still requires physical site inspections, in-person negotiation, relationship management with venues and clients, and real-time on-site troubleshooting during live events. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper planning services could unlock some latent demand (smaller businesses and individuals hiring planners for events they'd otherwise self-organize), but the total number of weddings, conventions, and corporate gatherings is bounded by social and budgetary factors, not planning costs. With disruption at the 6 boundary — the human-presence and trust components anchoring the role — this occupation fits resilient: AI will streamline the back-office half of the job while the experiential, logistical, and interpersonal core remains human-driven.

title: Metal and plastic machine workers
rationale: The core work is physical — loading materials, tending machines, replacing tooling, and inspecting parts on a factory floor — which limits direct AI disruption, though AI-driven CNC programming, machine vision inspection, and predictive monitoring will erode the cognitive slices of the job (setup, quality checks, program generation). Elasticity is low: demand for machined parts is driven by downstream manufacturing output and foreign competition, not by the cost of operator labor, so productivity gains from automation translate into fewer operators per machine rather than more parts consumed. The occupation's decline (BLS projects -7%) stems mainly from robotics and CNC automation rather than AI reshaping knowledge work, and the hands-on setter/operator core remains outside AI's direct path over the next decade. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient to AI specifically, even as long-run automation pressure shrinks headcount.

title: Microbiologists
rationale: Microbiologists' work is a mix of hands-on wet-lab tasks — culturing, isolating, and maintaining microorganisms, running physical experiments — and knowledge work like data analysis, report writing, and grant applications. AI substantially accelerates the analytical and writing portions (genomic analysis, literature review, experimental design hypotheses), but the core laboratory bench work requires physical presence and is only partially addressed by lab automation, yielding moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster microbial research would expand drug discovery, biofuels, and environmental applications, though funding cycles and lab infrastructure cap how quickly demand scales. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the desk-work half while the lab-work core remains human-driven.

title: Middle school teachers
rationale: AI already materially assists the knowledge-work portions of teaching—lesson planning, grading, differentiated materials, parent communication—but the core of middle school teaching is in-person: managing classrooms of adolescents, supervision, motivation, and social-emotional guidance, which keeps disruption at the boundary of moderate-high. Elasticity is low because demand is set by student demographics (projected to decline) and public budgets, not price; making teaching 10x more productive doesn't create more middle schoolers, though it may modestly reduce class sizes or teacher counts. The custodial and relational core of the job is not in AI's path, so despite substantial workflow changes, the occupation is best characterized as resilient with a shifting toolkit rather than restructured or replaced.

title: Military careers
rationale: Military careers span combat, transportation, healthcare, and administration, but the core of most roles requires physical presence, deployment readiness, and operation in unpredictable, dangerous environments where AI assists rather than substitutes; AI and autonomous systems will meaningfully reshape some specialties (intelligence analysis, logistics, drone operations) but not the bulk of enlisted and officer work. Elasticity is unusual here because force size is set by policy, budget, and geopolitical strategy rather than market price — productivity gains from AI do not straightforwardly translate into either more 'consumption' of military service or headcount cuts, though pressure toward smaller, tech-heavy forces exists. With disruption at a moderate level and demand determined politically, the occupation as a whole is resilient, even as specific specialties shift toward AI-enabled systems operation.

title: Mining and geological engineers
rationale: Mining and geological engineers split their time between digital knowledge work (mine design, geological modeling, technical reports, production analysis) that AI tools can increasingly accelerate, and irreplaceable on-site work such as supervising shaft construction, inspecting mine walls and equipment, and ensuring regulatory safety compliance in unpredictable physical environments. The elasticity score is low-to-moderate because demand is driven by commodity markets, deposit availability, and permitting regimes rather than the cost of engineering labor — cheaper engineering analysis does not meaningfully expand the number of viable mines, though critical mineral demand for EVs and electronics provides some tailwind. With disruption at 5, the physical, safety-critical, and site-bound core of the work keeps this occupation resilient, even as AI reshapes the modeling and reporting portions of the job.

title: Models
rationale: Although modeling involves a physical human body, the actual product is a digital image or video — precisely what generative AI can now produce. AI-generated virtual models, image reuse licensing, and virtual try-on technology can substitute for many photo shoots, catalog work, and e-commerce imagery, putting the core output squarely in AI's path. Elasticity is low: even though cheap imagery means brands produce far more visual content, that expanded demand is largely satisfied by synthetic models rather than more human bookings, and premium demand for celebrity or runway models is fixed and concentrated. With high disruption and little demand absorption for human workers specifically, the occupation faces significant headcount contraction outside a small live-event and high-fashion niche.

title: Music directors and composers
rationale: This occupation splits into two halves: music directors, whose core work is leading live rehearsals and performances with human ensembles (largely in churches, schools, and performing arts companies employing ~70% of workers) and is minimally AI-exposed, and composers, whose work is directly in the path of generative music AI that can already produce jingles, background scores, and stock music. The blended disruption lands at moderate-high, pulled down by the in-person conducting majority but up sharply for commercial composition. Elasticity is limited: while cheaper music production expands content volume somewhat, AI-generated music tends to substitute for commissioned composition rather than expand paid composer demand, and live directing demand is capped by nonprofit and school funding constraints. Because the dominant employment base is hands-on, presence-required directing work, the occupation as a whole is resilient — though commercial composers specifically face significant displacement risk.

title: Musicians and singers
rationale: AI music generation directly threatens studio-based segments — session work, backing tracks, jingles, and background/stock music — but the core of this occupation is live, embodied performance where audiences specifically value human presence and authenticity, which AI cannot substitute. Elasticity is modest: cheaper music production mostly benefits AI-generated output rather than expanding demand for human performers, and live performance demand is constrained by leisure time and venue economics, though the 'human-made' premium may strengthen as synthetic music floods the market. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient overall — recording-centric musicians face real displacement, but performers in churches, live venues, and touring acts will see AI touch only the periphery of their work.

title: Natural sciences managers
rationale: Much of this role's paperwork—drafting operational reports, budgeting, project monitoring, literature and research review—is squarely in AI's path, and AI research tools will change how scientific work is planned and evaluated. However, the core of the job is leadership: hiring, motivating, and evaluating scientists, coordinating across units, and overseeing physical labs, which remains human-centered and gives a disruption score at the top of the moderate band rather than high. Elasticity is moderate: AI-accelerated science could expand R&D activity and thus the teams needing oversight, but managers are flexible in span of control, and AI-driven flattening of hierarchies could offset that expansion. With disruption at 6, the occupation is resilient—AI streamlines the administrative periphery while the interpersonal and organizational core persists.

title: Network and computer systems administrators
rationale: The core work — configuring systems, managing permissions, diagnosing issues, monitoring performance — is predominantly digital and cognitive, and AI-driven automation (AIOps, self-healing infrastructure, LLM-assisted troubleshooting and scripting) is already absorbing routine administration; only residual physical hardware tasks resist automation, and cloud migration is eliminating even those. Elasticity is low because an organization's need for network and system administration scales with its infrastructure footprint, not with the cost of administration — companies won't consume 10x more sysadmin work if it gets cheaper, and cloud consolidation plus Networks-as-a-Service further concentrate the remaining work with fewer providers. BLS already projects a 4% decline, consistent with productivity gains translating directly into headcount reduction. High disruption with inelastic demand puts this squarely in the replace category.

title: News analysts, reporters, and journalists
rationale: Writing, summarizing, updating stories, and analyzing information are directly in AI's path, and routine coverage (earnings reports, sports recaps, weather, aggregation) is already being automated; only original reporting requiring source relationships and field presence resists, warranting a disruption of 7. Demand elasticity is low because news consumption is not cost-suppressed — the industry's constraint is collapsing advertising revenue and consolidation, not production capacity, so 10x cheaper content production does not translate into proportionally more paid journalist jobs. BLS already projects a 4% decline before accounting for accelerating AI-driven content generation. High disruption combined with structurally weak demand places this occupation in the replace category, with surviving roles concentrated in investigative, relationship-driven, and on-camera work.

title: Nuclear engineers
rationale: Much of nuclear engineering is analytical knowledge work — dose calculations, reactor simulations, technical documentation, and compliance review — where AI tools will materially assist, but the core work is bound to physical facilities, safety-critical oversight, security clearances, and NRC licensing regimes that require accountable human judgment and on-site presence. Demand for nuclear engineers is governed less by engineering cost than by capital-intensive plant construction, regulatory approval timelines, and energy policy; even a 10x productivity gain would not unlock proportionally more reactors, though renewed interest in SMRs and data-center power provides some upside. With disruption at 5, the occupation's core is not reshaped by AI even as its computational and documentation tasks are augmented, making it resilient — consistent with BLS projections of roughly flat employment driven by industry structure rather than automation.

title: Nuclear medicine technologists
rationale: The core work—preparing and administering radiopharmaceuticals, physically positioning patients, operating imaging equipment, and enforcing radiation safety—is hands-on and requires human presence with hazardous materials; AI assists mainly with peripheral tasks like image quality checks, protocol optimization, and record-keeping. Elasticity is low because nuclear imaging volume is driven by clinical indications, physician referrals, radiopharmaceutical supply, and reimbursement rather than technologist labor cost, so faster workflows would not unlock dramatically more scans. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI may streamline scheduling, dosing calculations, and documentation, but the essential patient-facing, physical, and safety-critical duties remain human work.

title: Nuclear technicians
rationale: Nuclear technicians' core work involves physically calibrating and maintaining radiation detection equipment, collecting environmental samples onsite, and responding to contamination incidents — tasks requiring hands-on presence in reactors and field locations. AI can assist with the knowledge-work portions like anomaly detection in sensor data, radiation calculations, and monitoring dashboards, but heavy nuclear safety regulation mandates human oversight and verification. Elasticity is low because demand is tied to the fixed number of nuclear facilities and regulatory requirements, not the cost of technician labor — cheaper monitoring does not create more reactors, and BLS already projects decline due to fewer plant constructions. With moderate disruption and structurally constrained demand, the occupation is resilient to AI itself, though it faces headwinds from broader energy-sector trends.

title: Nurse anesthetists, nurse midwives, and nurse practitioners
rationale: The core work — physical exams, administering anesthesia, delivering babies, monitoring patients, hands-on procedures — requires physical presence and cannot be done by AI, though diagnostic support, documentation, care-plan drafting, and clinical decision support will meaningfully assist the knowledge-work portions. Elasticity is high because primary care demand is heavily suppressed by cost and provider shortages, an aging population and chronic disease burden create near-unlimited latent demand, and BLS already projects 35% growth. With disruption at the moderate level, the net effect is resilient: AI augments diagnosis and paperwork but the hands-on clinical core remains firmly human, and expanding demand ensures strong headcount growth.

title: Nursing assistants and orderlies
rationale: The core work — bathing, feeding, toileting, lifting, and transferring patients — is intensely physical, hands-on, and requires human presence and compassion in unpredictable environments, placing it almost entirely outside AI's path. AI may marginally assist with documentation, vital-sign monitoring, and care scheduling, but these are peripheral to daily tasks. Demand is driven by an aging population and is somewhat cost-constrained (nursing home budgets, Medicaid reimbursement), so moderate latent demand exists, but elasticity is largely irrelevant given the negligible disruption. This is a textbook resilient occupation: AI touches the edges while the physical caregiving core remains untouched.

title: Occupational health and safety specialists and technicians
rationale: Core work requires physical presence at worksites — inspecting equipment, testing air quality, observing worker behavior, demonstrating protective gear — which AI cannot replicate, though AI substantially assists the knowledge-work portions like report writing, regulatory compliance checks, incident data analysis, and training material development. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper safety analysis could expand coverage to smaller businesses currently underserved, but demand is largely driven by regulatory mandates and workforce size rather than cost, capping expansion. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI streamlines documentation and analytics but the fieldwork, enforcement, and human interaction at the core remain intact, consistent with BLS's projected 12% growth.

title: Occupational therapists
rationale: Occupational therapy is fundamentally hands-on and interpersonal: observing patients perform physical tasks, demonstrating exercises, fitting adaptive equipment, and building rapport with people who have disabilities all require in-person human presence. AI can assist with documentation, billing, treatment plan drafting, and home assessment analysis, but these are peripheral to the core clinical work. Elasticity is moderate — an aging population and unmet rehab needs create real latent demand, but insurance reimbursement and the labor-intensive nature of sessions limit how much productivity gains expand consumption. With disruption low, the occupation is resilient; BLS's 14% projected growth reinforces strong structural demand insulated from AI displacement.

title: Occupational therapy assistants and aides
rationale: The core work is hands-on and physical: guiding patients through therapeutic exercises, lifting and transferring clients, demonstrating adaptive equipment, and preparing treatment spaces — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like progress documentation, scheduling, and billing paperwork, which are a small fraction of the job. Demand elasticity is modest since occupational therapy is driven by demographic need (aging population) and constrained by insurance reimbursement rather than cost of the assistant's labor. With minimal disruption to the core work and BLS projecting 18% growth, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Oil and gas workers
rationale: Oil and gas work is overwhelmingly physical — assembling rigs, operating drills, moving pipe, and repairing equipment in harsh outdoor environments — leaving little for language-based AI to displace, though automated drilling and remote monitoring (robotics rather than AI per se) may trim some roles at the margin. Elasticity is low because demand for extraction labor is driven by commodity prices and energy policy, not the cost of labor itself; cheaper labor would not meaningfully increase drilling activity. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient to AI, with any headcount pressure coming from industry automation and energy transition dynamics rather than AI tools.

title: Operations research analysts
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — collecting and analyzing data, building quantitative models, writing analytical reports and recommendations — are digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and AI tools can already draft optimization models, run simulations, and summarize findings. However, demand for optimization and decision analytics is heavily cost-suppressed: most mid-sized firms, hospitals, and logistics operations currently can't afford dedicated OR analysis, so dramatically cheaper modeling would extend it to pricing, scheduling, and supply chain problems across far more organizations (BLS already projects 21% growth). High disruption paired with high elasticity means each analyst produces far more, but expanding applications absorb the productivity gains — a classic augment profile, though the role shifts toward problem framing and stakeholder persuasion over hand-building models.

title: Opticians
rationale: The core work — physically measuring faces, adjusting and repairing frames with hand tools, helping customers insert contact lenses — requires in-person presence and manual dexterity that AI cannot replicate, though AI-assisted measurement apps, automated work-order generation, and online retail with virtual try-on will erode peripheral and some frame-selection tasks. Demand elasticity is modest: eyewear demand is driven by prescriptions and demographics (aging population, myopia rates), not by service cost, so cheaper fitting services would not meaningfully expand consumption. The bigger long-term threat is e-commerce channel shift rather than AI absorbing core tasks. With disruption well below 7, the occupation fits the resilient category.

title: Optometrists
rationale: Core optometry work requires in-person examination, physical manipulation of equipment, minor procedures, and hands-on patient care, though AI is already strong at the diagnostic-interpretation portion (retinal image analysis for glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, macular degeneration) and could automate refraction analysis, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper diagnostics could expand screening in underserved populations and an aging, myopic, diabetic population supplies growing demand, but eye exams are largely need-driven rather than cost-suppressed, so people won't consume 10x more exams. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient — AI augments diagnosis and workflow but does not displace the licensed, hands-on clinical core.

title: Orthotists and prosthetists
rationale: The core work — physically examining patients, taking impressions, fitting devices, and hands-on fabrication and adjustment — requires human presence and manual dexterity, though AI-assisted 3D scanning and generative design tools will streamline the design and documentation portions. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster device design could expand access for underserved populations, but demand is fundamentally driven by medical need (amputations, orthopedic conditions) rather than cost suppression, and reimbursement structures limit expansion. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — AI augments design workflows at the periphery while demographic trends (aging, diabetes) independently drive strong employment growth.

title: Painters, construction and maintenance
rationale: Painting is almost entirely physical, hands-on work in unpredictable real-world environments — surface prep, scaffolding, applying coatings in occupied homes and on bridges — which AI cannot perform; at most AI assists with estimating, color matching, and scheduling, and robotic painting remains limited to controlled industrial settings. Elasticity is modest: cheaper painting would induce some homeowners to repaint more often or hire out DIY jobs, but demand is fundamentally tied to building stock and maintenance cycles rather than suppressed by information costs. With disruption at the minimal end, the occupation is clearly resilient — AI touches only the peripheral admin work while the core trade remains untouched.

title: Painting and coating workers
rationale: Core work is physical—preparing surfaces, operating spray equipment, dipping, masking, and inspecting finishes—which AI language and analysis tools cannot perform; the relevant threat is industrial robotics and automated painting lines, which predates modern AI and mainly affects large-scale manufacturing rather than repair and small-batch work. Elasticity is low because demand for painting and coating is derived from manufacturing output and repair volume, which would not expand meaningfully even if the work were cheaper. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient to AI, though gradual factory automation will continue to limit growth as BLS projects.

title: Paralegals and legal assistants
rationale: Nearly all core paralegal tasks — legal research, document drafting, file organization, transcript review, and correspondence — are digital, language-based work squarely in AI's current capabilities, with legal-specific AI tools already handling research and first-draft documents. While cheaper legal services would unlock some latent demand, growth is capped by regulatory structures, court capacity, and the fact that attorneys using AI directly can bypass paralegal support entirely, so productivity gains largely convert to headcount reduction rather than expanded output. BLS itself flags AI as a demand suppressor, projecting flat employment. High disruption combined with low-to-moderate elasticity places this occupation in the replace category.

title: Personal financial advisors
rationale: The analytical core of this job — portfolio construction, tax and retirement scenario modeling, investment research, and account monitoring — is digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and robo-advisors plus LLM-based planning tools already automate much of it; however, the trust-building, sales, and behavioral coaching components require human relationships, keeping disruption at 7 rather than higher. On elasticity, substantial latent demand exists since comprehensive financial planning is currently unaffordable for most middle-income households, but much of that unlocked demand will be captured by fully automated tools rather than human advisors, and demographics (retiring boomers, self-directed retirement accounts) provide only moderate expansion for humans, yielding a 6. The occupation survives but shifts decisively toward relationship management, complex life-event planning, and behavioral coaching, with AI handling the analytics — a classic restructure where advisors who don't move up the value chain are displaced.

title: Pest control workers
rationale: Pest control is overwhelmingly physical, hands-on work — inspecting crawl spaces, applying pesticides, setting traps, and sealing structures in unpredictable real-world environments that AI and robotics cannot address in the near term. AI helps only peripherally with scheduling, routing, pest identification from photos, and record-keeping. Demand is driven by actual infestations rather than cost or speed, so productivity gains would not unlock large latent demand, though modest expansion is possible as diagnostics get cheaper. With disruption at 2, the occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Petroleum engineers
rationale: A substantial portion of petroleum engineering — reservoir simulation, production data analysis, well design optimization — is computational and squarely in AI's path, but core duties also require field presence, overseeing drilling operations, troubleshooting equipment, and coordinating with rig crews, keeping disruption moderate. Demand for petroleum engineers is driven by global oil and gas prices and production volumes, not by the cost of engineering labor, so making engineering work 10x cheaper would not meaningfully increase drilling activity or headcount — demand is largely inelastic to engineering productivity. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI will augment the analytical side (reservoir modeling, production optimization) while the field-facing core and commodity-driven employment dynamics remain largely unchanged. The bigger risk to this occupation is energy transition, not AI.

title: Pharmacists
rationale: A substantial portion of pharmacist work — checking drug interactions, verifying dosages, maintaining records, resolving insurance issues — is cognitive and already heavily assisted by software, with AI poised to automate much of the verification and counseling knowledge layer. However, the core role remains anchored by legal requirements for licensed pharmacist sign-off, physical dispensing and compounding, vaccinations, and in-person patient interaction, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is low because prescription volume is driven by disease prevalence, not price — making pharmacist services 10x cheaper does not lead people to take 10x more medications, though some expansion in clinical medication management and underserved-area counseling is plausible. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient, though retail dispensing roles face more pressure than clinical ones.

title: Pharmacy technicians
rationale: A meaningful share of the work—prescription data entry, insurance claim processing, refill authorizations, and phone handling—is digital and squarely in AI's path, and automated dispensing robots already handle counting and packaging in larger operations. However, core duties like physically handling medications, compounding, sterile IV prep in hospitals, and in-person customer interaction still require human presence, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is low because prescription volume is driven by demographics and disease prevalence, not the cost of technician labor—making the work 10x cheaper doesn't cause people to consume more medications. The moderate disruption score places this in resilient: AI and automation will streamline the administrative layer, but the physical dispensing and patient-facing core persists, consistent with BLS's projected growth as technicians absorb tasks shifted from pharmacists.

title: Phlebotomists
rationale: Phlebotomy is almost entirely hands-on physical work — inserting needles into veins, handling samples, and calming anxious patients — none of which AI can perform; only peripheral tasks like labeling databases and sample tracking are digital. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper diagnostics and an aging population would drive more blood testing volume, though each draw still requires a human present. With core tasks untouched by AI and demand growth already projected faster than average, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Physical therapist assistants and aides
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical care — guiding exercises, manual therapy, transferring patients, and setting up equipment — which AI cannot perform; AI only touches peripheral tasks like documentation, scheduling, and progress notes. Elasticity is moderate: an aging population and chronic disease create substantial latent demand for rehabilitation, though insurance reimbursement rules constrain how much cheaper delivery translates into more consumption. With disruption at 2, the occupation is clearly resilient — BLS projects much-faster-than-average growth, and AI-driven documentation tools would if anything free assistants for more patient contact rather than displace them.

title: Physical therapists
rationale: Physical therapy is fundamentally hands-on work — manual therapy, guiding exercises, observing movement, and physically assisting patients — that AI cannot perform; AI's role is limited to documentation, treatment plan suggestions, and motion-analysis tools that assist rather than replace the core work. Elasticity is moderate: an aging population, chronic disease prevalence, and nonopioid pain management create real latent demand, though insurance coverage and time-per-patient constraints limit unbounded expansion. With disruption low, productivity tools at most free up time for more patient contact rather than reducing headcount. This fits squarely in the resilient category — AI touches the administrative periphery while the physical, interpersonal core remains human.

title: Physician assistants
rationale: PAs perform substantial hands-on clinical work — physical exams, suturing, setting bones, immunizations, surgical assistance — that requires in-person human presence and is beyond AI's reach; AI meaningfully assists the cognitive portions like diagnosis, test interpretation, documentation, and treatment research, yielding moderate disruption. Elasticity is high because healthcare demand is heavily suppressed by cost and provider shortages, especially in rural and underserved areas where PAs are already primary providers, and an aging, chronically ill population creates near-continuous latent demand. With disruption at 5, the core clinical work remains fundamentally human, making this occupation resilient — AI will augment charting and diagnostic support while headcount grows strongly, consistent with BLS's 20% projected growth.

title: Physicians and surgeons
rationale: AI is already meaningfully changing the cognitive portions of medicine — diagnostic reasoning, image interpretation, clinical documentation, and chart review — but the core of most physician work requires physical presence: exams, procedures, surgery, and high-stakes patient interaction under licensure requirements that mandate a human in the loop. Elasticity is high because healthcare demand is heavily suppressed by cost, physician shortages, and long wait times; cheaper and faster physician time would be readily absorbed by an aging population with rising chronic disease burden. Certain subspecialties like radiology and pathology face much higher disruption, but the aggregate occupation is anchored in embodied, regulated care. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI augments the knowledge work while the hands-on, patient-facing core remains human.

title: Physicists and astronomers
rationale: Much of physicists' and astronomers' daily work — mathematical modeling, writing analysis code, processing datasets, drafting papers and grant proposals — is exactly the digital, cognitive work AI is rapidly absorbing, and AI research assistants are already accelerating theory and simulation work; however, experimental design, hands-on instrument work, and lab operations keep disruption below the highest tier. Elasticity is moderate: while there is essentially unlimited scientific inquiry to pursue, headcount is tightly coupled to federal research budgets and grant funding rather than to the unit cost of analysis, so a 10x productivity gain likely means more science per scientist rather than proportionally more scientists. This combination fits restructure — the field persists but shifts toward researchers who direct AI-driven analysis, design experiments, and validate results, while those doing routine computation and data-processing work are displaced.

title: Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters
rationale: The core work — installing pipes, soldering, troubleshooting leaks, maneuvering in crawl spaces — is physical, hands-on, and performed in unpredictable real-world environments far from AI's reach; AI helps only peripherally with estimates, scheduling, code lookup, and BIM planning. Demand for plumbing is driven by construction volume and physical system failures, not by the cost of the knowledge work AI could speed up, so productivity gains from AI tools would unlock only modest additional demand. This is a textbook resilient trade: low disruption means the occupation's core remains intact regardless of elasticity, and BLS projections confirm steady, average-paced growth.

title: Podiatrists
rationale: Podiatrists' core work — physical exams, surgery, wound care, and hands-on treatment of feet and ankles — requires physical presence and manual dexterity that AI cannot replicate; AI assists only with peripheral tasks like imaging interpretation, documentation, and practice administration. Demand for foot care is driven by demographics (aging, diabetes, obesity) rather than price, so making the diagnostic or administrative portions cheaper would not meaningfully expand the number of surgeries or treatments consumed, especially since patients can already substitute other physicians. With low disruption to the hands-on core, this occupation is clearly resilient to AI over the next decade.

title: Police and detectives
rationale: Core police work — patrolling, responding to emergencies, making arrests, de-escalating conflicts, testifying in court — requires physical presence in unpredictable real-world situations that AI cannot perform, though AI meaningfully assists report writing, records searches, evidence analysis, and investigative work (especially for detectives). Demand for policing is set by public budgets, crime levels, and political decisions rather than cost per unit of output, so productivity gains won't dramatically expand headcount, though modest latent demand exists for faster case clearance. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient: AI will speed up paperwork and investigations but the sworn-officer role remains fundamentally hands-on and human-facing.

title: Political scientists
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — researching political topics, analyzing survey data, monitoring events, forecasting trends, and writing reports — are digital, language-based knowledge work squarely in AI's path, with current LLMs already capable of drafting policy analyses and synthesizing large document sets. Demand elasticity is low: two-thirds of these jobs sit in the federal government where headcount is budget-driven rather than price-driven, and while cheaper analysis could unlock some latent demand from advocacy groups and think tanks, the institutional appetite for political science research is structurally capped rather than cost-suppressed. BLS already projects a -3% decline before accounting for AI acceleration. High disruption combined with low elasticity points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.

title: Postal service workers
rationale: The bulk of this workforce (mail carriers, 64%) does physical delivery work that AI cannot perform without autonomous vehicle/robotics maturity; however, sorters and clerks face real pressure from AI-powered OCR sorting machines and self-service kiosks, putting overall disruption at moderate. Elasticity is very low: mail volume is structurally declining due to digital communication, and making sorting or delivery cheaper does not induce people to send more letters — productivity gains translate directly into fewer workers, as BLS's -5% projection reflects. The net effect is 'resilient' because disruption stays below 7 — the core delivery work is physical and AI touches mainly the sorting/processing periphery — though headcount will still shrink gradually due to secular volume decline rather than AI displacement per se.

title: Postsecondary education administrators
rationale: Much of this occupation's routine digital work — processing applications, maintaining records, scheduling courses, producing transcripts and enrollment data — is squarely in AI's path, and registrar and admissions-processing functions face substantial automation. However, the occupation also includes deans, provosts, and student affairs roles centered on institutional leadership, tenure and budget decisions, student advising, and in-person relationship-building, which keeps overall disruption at the moderate-high boundary rather than clearly high. Elasticity is low: demand is tied to student enrollment and constrained state budgets, and cheaper administration will not cause universities to consume dramatically more administrators — institutions have a fixed number of deanships and will pocket efficiency gains. The net effect is resilient overall, though the more clerical subfunctions (registrar, admissions processing) will likely see headcount pressure while leadership and student-facing roles persist.

title: Postsecondary teachers
rationale: Core tasks—lesson planning, lecturing, grading, syllabus design, advising, and research writing—are predominantly cognitive and language-based, and current AI tools already materially assist with content creation, assessment, and literature synthesis, driving a high disruption score. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper instruction could expand access to lifelong learning and underserved students, but demand is structurally capped by credentialing systems, demographic enrollment trends, tuition models, and constrained public budgets, so institutions are more likely to absorb productivity gains through larger course loads and more adjuncts than through proportional headcount growth. The role will persist because mentorship, credential-granting, and in-person research supervision remain human-centered, but the skill mix shifts sharply toward AI-augmented course design, personalized coaching, and assessment oversight. High disruption with moderate elasticity places this squarely in restructure.

title: Power plant operators, distributors, and dispatchers
rationale: Much of the work is control-room monitoring, meter reading, and switching orders—tasks that smart-grid automation and AI-enhanced control systems are already absorbing—but the core role remains anchored by physical equipment rounds, safety-critical human-in-the-loop requirements, and strict NRC/regulatory staffing mandates that prevent full digital displacement. Elasticity is very low: demand for operators is tied to the number of plants and grid nodes, not to the cost of operation, so productivity gains translate directly into leaner control rooms (consistent with the BLS -10% projection) rather than more consumption of operator labor. With disruption at a moderate 5, the occupation falls into the resilient category, though it is a shrinking-resilient case where automation gradually thins headcount while the remaining roles stay fundamentally similar.

title: Preschool and childcare center directors
rationale: Directors' administrative tasks — budgeting, scheduling, compliance documentation, parent communications — are AI-assistable, but the core work of supervising staff on-site, managing safety, handling live parent and child interactions, and providing physical leadership presence requires being there in person. AI can trim office hours but not replace the onsite management function. Demand elasticity is low because demand is tied to the number of childcare centers, which is constrained by birth rates, staffing costs (mostly teachers, not directors), and physical facilities — cheaper administration doesn't create more children needing care. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient; the BLS-projected slight decline stems from demographics, not AI.

title: Preschool teachers
rationale: Preschool teaching is fundamentally in-person, physical, and relational work — supervising active young children, managing behavior, providing emotional support, and ensuring safety — none of which AI can perform. AI helps only with peripheral tasks like lesson planning, progress records, and parent communications, which are a small fraction of the day. Elasticity is low because demand is driven by the number of young children and staffing ratios mandated by regulation, not by the cost of the teacher's cognitive output; AI productivity gains cannot reduce required adult-to-child ratios. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Private detectives and investigators
rationale: The desk-research portion of this work — searching public records, court databases, social media, and writing reports — is squarely in AI's path and already being automated by background-check and skip-tracing tools. However, core tasks like physical surveillance, in-person interviews, undercover store detective work, and lawful evidence collection require unpredictable real-world presence, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is moderate-to-high: cheaper investigations would unlock latent demand from small businesses, attorneys, and individuals who currently can't afford investigative services, though physical fieldwork limits how much output can scale. Because disruption is at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI accelerates the research layer but the field-based core of the job remains human.

title: Probation officers and correctional treatment specialists
rationale: A meaningful portion of the work — case reports, prehearing investigations, risk assessments, and case file maintenance — is language-based and squarely in AI's path, and algorithmic risk-scoring tools are already used in pretrial and parole decisions. However, the core of the job is in-person supervision: home visits, drug testing, court testimony, and building rapport with often hostile clients in unpredictable environments, which keeps disruption moderate. Elasticity is low because demand is set by caseloads, sentencing policy, and state/local government budgets rather than by the cost or speed of the service; faster report-writing won't create more probationers. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient — AI streamlines paperwork and risk assessment but does not reshape the fundamentally relational, field-based core.

title: Producers and directors
rationale: Producers and directors do predominantly cognitive and creative coordination work—script evaluation, budgeting, scheduling, editing oversight—and generative AI video, script analysis, previsualization, and post-production tools are already compressing production workflows, though on-set leadership, casting, and interpersonal direction retain a human core, placing disruption at the boundary of high. Elasticity is high because demand for video content is heavily cost-suppressed: as production costs collapse, businesses, brands, streamers, and independent creators will commission dramatically more video, advertising, and episodic content, expanding the total market. The net effect is augmentation—each producer/director orchestrates far more output with AI tools, and the exploding content market absorbs the productivity gains, keeping headcount stable or growing even as the required skill set shifts toward AI-assisted production.

title: Project management specialists
rationale: Much of a project manager's daily work — status reports, scheduling, budget tracking, risk logs, documentation, meeting summaries — is digital and already directly addressable by AI tools, which can automate the coordination and reporting layer that consumes most PM hours; however, stakeholder negotiation, accountability, and interpersonal conflict resolution remain human anchors, capping disruption at 7. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper project coordination lets one PM oversee more concurrent projects and lowers the threshold for formally managing smaller initiatives, but the number of projects is ultimately driven by organizational investment budgets, not PM cost, so demand won't explode. The occupation fits restructure — the role survives but shifts from administrative tracking toward stakeholder management, judgment, and exception handling, and PMs who remain report-generators will be displaced.

title: Property appraisers and assessors
rationale: The core of appraisal work — analyzing comparables, verifying records, and writing valuation reports — is data-driven knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and automated valuation models (Zillow-style AVMs) already handle much of routine residential valuation; only site inspections remain physical, and even those are being reduced by desktop and hybrid appraisals. Demand is derived from real estate transactions, tax assessments, and lending requirements, which are driven by market activity and regulation rather than appraisal cost — making appraisals 10x cheaper does not generate meaningfully more home sales or tax rolls to value. Regulatory licensing requirements provide some protective friction, but lenders and GSEs are actively expanding appraisal waivers, signaling institutional willingness to substitute automation. With high disruption and inelastic demand, headcount contraction is likely, fitting the replace category.

title: Property, real estate, and community association managers
rationale: A substantial share of the work — rent collection, record keeping, budget preparation, posting vacancies, dispatching maintenance requests, and drafting communications — is administrative and already being automated by property-tech platforms, but core duties like physical inspections, showing units, supervising contractors, and mediating tenant and board disputes require in-person presence and interpersonal judgment. Demand is anchored to the fixed stock of buildings and housing units; making management 10x cheaper does not create more properties to manage, though it may pull some self-managed properties into professional management. With disruption in the moderate range, the occupation is resilient: managers will handle larger portfolios with AI handling the back office, but the human-facing, on-site core of the job persists.

title: Psychiatric technicians and aides
rationale: The core work is hands-on, physically demanding patient care: bathing, feeding, escorting, restraining, and directly observing patients in unpredictable, sometimes volatile environments — tasks AI cannot perform. AI touches only the periphery through documentation, charting, and behavior-monitoring tools, warranting a low disruption score. Elasticity is moderate: mental health care demand is substantial and cost-suppressed (reflected in BLS's projected 16% growth), but staffing is constrained by facility budgets and state funding rather than purely by price. Because disruption is well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI may assist with record-keeping but will not reshape the fundamentally human, physical nature of this care work.

title: Psychologists
rationale: Much of a psychologist's work is language-based — assessment write-ups, test scoring and interpretation, research analysis, and even talk therapy are in AI's technical path, and AI chatbots already handle low-acuity mental health support. However, the core of clinical practice rests on the therapeutic alliance, licensure requirements, in-person school and hospital roles, and strong client preference for human trust and empathy, which keeps disruption at the moderate-high boundary rather than fully transformative. Elasticity is high because mental health demand is massively suppressed by cost, stigma, and provider shortages — cheaper, faster psychological services would unlock enormous latent demand. With disruption at 6, the occupation falls into resilient: AI will absorb documentation, testing, and triage work while the human core of treatment persists, and expanding demand supports stable or growing headcount.

title: Public relations and fundraising managers
rationale: Much of the core work — writing press releases, drafting speeches, media monitoring, donor prospect research, grant applications, and campaign content — is language-based knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and AI tools already materially accelerate these tasks. However, high-stakes relationship work (in-person major gift solicitation, media relationships, crisis judgment, executive counsel) remains human, and managerial supervision moderates full automation, keeping disruption at 7 rather than higher. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper PR and fundraising capacity lets smaller nonprofits and businesses run professional campaigns they couldn't previously afford, but total donor dollars and media attention are finite, capping demand expansion. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the role survives but shifts toward relationship management, strategy, and AI-orchestration skills — a restructure.

title: Public relations specialists
rationale: The core daily output of PR specialists — press releases, speeches, social media content, sentiment monitoring — is language-based digital work squarely in AI's path, and current tools already draft and analyze this material competently, driving a high disruption score. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper PR could let more small businesses and nonprofits invest in communications, but total media attention is finite and much of the value lies in journalist relationships, judgment during crises, and trust — demand won't scale 10x with 10x cheaper output. With disruption at 8 and elasticity at 5, the occupation restructures: routine content production collapses in value while strategy, relationship management, and crisis judgment become the differentiating skills. Specialists who remain content-writers face displacement; those who pivot to strategic counsel and media relationships will thrive.

title: Public safety telecommunicators
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language-based — answering calls, triaging severity, logging data, relaying instructions — placing it directly in AI's path; AI systems are already handling nonemergency call intake, real-time transcription, translation, and location determination in PSAPs, though life-critical liability and government procurement will keep humans in the loop for emergency calls. Demand is essentially inelastic: emergency call volume is driven by population and incident rates, not by the cost or speed of dispatch, so productivity gains translate into fewer seats needed per shift rather than more calls answered. With state and local budget pressure explicitly noted as a constraint, agencies have strong incentive to let AI absorb nonemergency and routine triage work and shrink staffing. High disruption combined with very low elasticity fits the replace category, even though the transition will be slowed by regulation and public-safety risk aversion.

title: Purchasing managers, buyers, and purchasing agents
rationale: Core tasks — analyzing price proposals, comparing suppliers, monitoring contract compliance, maintaining purchasing records, and processing routine orders — are digital, data-driven work squarely in AI's path, and procurement software with AI-driven spend analysis and automated sourcing is already deployed; only supplier relationship-building, plant visits, and high-stakes negotiation resist automation. Elasticity is low because procurement volume is derived from an organization's underlying need for goods and services — making purchasing 10x cheaper doesn't cause companies to buy meaningfully more inputs, so productivity gains translate into fewer buyers handling more spend. With high disruption and inelastic demand, the routine agent/buyer layer contracts significantly, fitting the replace category, though senior negotiators and category strategists persist.

title: Quality control inspectors
rationale: The core task — visually and dimensionally detecting defects against specifications — is squarely in the path of AI-powered machine vision systems, which already outperform humans on speed and consistency for many inspection tasks; the remaining physical handling and equipment monitoring is a shrinking share of the role. Elasticity is low because inspection demand is tied to production volume, not inspection cost — cheaper inspection leads to 100% automated inspection rather than sampling, but that additional coverage is absorbed by vision systems, not more human inspectors. BLS already projects zero growth, and as automated inspection scales, productivity gains translate directly into fewer inspectors monitoring more lines. High disruption with inelastic demand fits the replace category, though a residual cadre will remain to audit systems and conduct random physical checks.

title: Radiation therapists
rationale: The core work — physically positioning patients, operating linear accelerators, monitoring for adverse reactions, and providing in-person emotional support across weeks of treatment — requires human presence, though AI is increasingly assisting adjacent tasks like tumor localization, auto-contouring, and treatment planning (work largely done by dosimetrists and physicists). Elasticity is very low: radiation therapy volume is driven by cancer incidence, not cost or speed, and more efficient hypofractionated protocols actually reduce visit counts rather than expand demand. Productivity gains from AI-assisted planning may modestly compress headcount at the margins, but the hands-on treatment delivery role remains intact. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the periphery, not the core.

title: Radiologic and MRI technologists
rationale: The core work — positioning patients, operating scanners hands-on, injecting contrast, lifting and comforting patients — requires physical presence and cannot be done by AI; AI mainly assists at the periphery through automated protocol selection, image quality optimization, and faster scan sequences. Elasticity is modest: while an aging population drives more imaging, exam volume is throttled by physician ordering, insurance reimbursement, and scanner capacity rather than technologist labor cost, so AI-driven efficiency won't unleash massive new demand. Note that AI disruption in this field falls on radiologists (image interpretation), not technologists (image acquisition). With disruption well below 7 and demand growth steady per BLS projections, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Railroad workers
rationale: Train operation occurs on fixed rails in a controlled environment, making it a comparatively tractable automation target — Positive Train Control, remote yard locomotives, and autonomous freight pilots (e.g., in Australian mining) show the trajectory, though FRA regulation, union crew-size agreements, and the physical coupling, inspection, and safety work keep near-term AI disruption moderate rather than high. Elasticity is low: cheaper train operation would not meaningfully increase freight or passenger rail volume, which is driven by overall economic activity and infrastructure capacity, so productivity gains largely translate to smaller crews (as already seen in the shift toward one-person crew proposals). With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient over a 10-year horizon — AI and automation will chip at crew sizes and yard operations, but regulatory friction and physical duties prevent core reshaping in the near term.

title: Real estate brokers and sales agents
rationale: A large share of the work — comparative market analysis, listing generation, marketing copy, document preparation, and lead screening — is already being absorbed by AI and platforms like Zillow, but core value drivers (in-person showings, trust-building, local relationships, and high-stakes negotiation on the largest purchase most people ever make) remain human-centered, putting disruption at the top of the moderate band. Elasticity is very low: the number of real estate transactions is determined by housing stock, life events, and interest rates, not by agent cost — cheaper agents do not cause people to buy 10x more homes, and commission compression would shrink incomes rather than expand volume. The net effect is resilient, though with a caveat: the occupation will face fee pressure and consolidation toward top producers, and marginal part-time agents may exit even as the role itself persists.

title: Receptionists
rationale: Core tasks — answering phones, scheduling appointments, taking messages, entering data, handling correspondence — are exactly what AI voice agents, chatbots, and automated scheduling systems already do well, though the in-person greeting and security-escort component provides a partial physical anchor. Demand for reception services is fixed by the number of physical locations and visitor volume; making reception 10x cheaper doesn't cause organizations to consume 10x more of it, so productivity gains translate directly into fewer front-desk hires or consolidated coverage. With BLS already projecting zero growth amid automation, high disruption plus inelastic demand points to significant headcount contraction concentrated in phone- and scheduling-heavy roles, with residual jobs surviving mainly where physical presence and hospitality are valued.

title: Recreation workers
rationale: The core of this occupation is in-person group leadership—leading activities, supervising participants, ensuring safety, and providing human motivation and social connection, none of which AI can substitute. AI touches only peripheral admin tasks like scheduling, newsletters, and program planning, which are a small share of the workday. Elasticity is modest: demand is driven by demographic and social factors (aging population, community programming budgets) rather than being suppressed by the cost of the knowledge-work component, so AI productivity gains would not meaningfully expand or contract headcount. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Recreational therapists
rationale: The core of recreational therapy is in-person, physically and emotionally engaged work — leading activities, motivating patients, providing hands-on assistance, and building therapeutic rapport — none of which AI can substitute for. AI meaningfully helps only with peripheral tasks like documentation, progress tracking, and treatment plan drafting. Elasticity is modest: an aging population creates some latent demand, but reimbursement and funding constraints in nursing homes and healthcare settings cap expansion regardless of cost. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is clearly resilient — AI streamlines admin work but leaves the therapeutic core intact.

title: Registered nurses
rationale: Nursing is the canonical moderate-disruption occupation: core work — administering medications, physical assessments, lifting and moving patients, operating equipment, providing emotional support — requires human presence, while AI meaningfully assists documentation, charting, care planning, patient monitoring alerts, and triage. Demand elasticity is moderate-to-high given an aging population, chronic disease burden, persistent nursing shortages, and latent demand for home-based and preventive care that cheaper coordination could unlock, though staffing budgets and reimbursement structures cap expansion. With disruption at 4, the net effect is resilient: AI will offload administrative burden and augment clinical decision-making, but the hands-on, empathetic core of nursing remains firmly human, and BLS already projects faster-than-average growth.

title: Rehabilitation counselors
rationale: The core of rehabilitation counseling is empathetic, in-person relationship work with clients facing disabilities — counseling sessions, advocacy, and trust-building that resist automation, though AI can meaningfully assist with client assessments, rehabilitation plan drafting, resource matching, and case documentation. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: latent need among the aging population and people with disabilities exists, but demand is largely funded by constrained state budgets and mandated programs rather than price-sensitive consumers, so cheaper service delivery mostly relieves caseload backlogs rather than dramatically expanding headcount. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — AI streamlines the administrative periphery while the human counseling core remains intact.

title: Respiratory therapists
rationale: Respiratory therapists perform hands-on bedside care—administering treatments, managing ventilators, chest physiotherapy, drawing blood, and physically monitoring critically ill patients—which requires physical presence and cannot be done by AI. AI will assist with peripheral tasks like documentation, ventilator setting optimization, and diagnostic interpretation, but the core work remains manual and clinical. Elasticity is moderate: demand is driven by demographics and disease prevalence (aging population, COPD) rather than cost, though cheaper monitoring could expand home-care and outpatient respiratory services somewhat. With low disruption, the occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS's projected 12% growth.

title: Retail sales workers
rationale: The core of retail sales work requires physical presence in stores — greeting customers, demonstrating products, stocking shelves, and processing in-person transactions — which AI cannot directly perform, though AI-powered product recommendation, chatbots, and self-checkout erode the knowledge and transactional portions of the role. Elasticity is low because cheaper sales assistance does not meaningfully expand how much merchandise people buy in physical stores; the bigger structural pressure is e-commerce substitution, not AI-driven productivity absorption. Even if AI made each worker more efficient, retailers would trim headcount rather than expand service, but since disruption stays at moderate levels the occupation is resilient — pressured more by channel shift to online shopping than by AI reshaping the in-person work itself.

title: Roofers
rationale: Roofing is almost entirely physical, hands-on work performed at heights in unpredictable outdoor conditions — removing old roofs, hauling 60-pound shingle bundles, cutting and installing materials — which AI cannot perform and near-term robotics cannot handle economically. AI's role is limited to peripheral tasks like drone-based measurement, estimating, and scheduling, which is why disruption is the explicit benchmark example of minimal (0-1). Elasticity is low because roof replacement demand is driven by weather damage, material lifespan, and construction cycles rather than labor cost; cheaper roofing wouldn't cause people to re-roof much more often. With disruption far below the threshold, the occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Sales engineers
rationale: A large share of sales engineers' supporting work—preparing technical presentations, answering RFPs, product configuration, troubleshooting documentation, and market research—is digital and squarely in AI's path, but the core of the job remains high-stakes, trust-based persuasion, relationship building, and negotiation with enterprise buyers, which AI cannot replace. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper technical pre-sales support doesn't dramatically expand the number of complex B2B deals, though lower cost-of-sale could let vendors pursue more mid-market customers with dedicated technical selling. With disruption at 6, AI restructures the workflow (fewer hours on decks and documentation, more on customer-facing strategy) without displacing the relational core, making the occupation resilient. BLS's projected 5% growth is consistent with continued demand for humans who translate increasingly complex technology into buyer trust.

title: Sales managers
rationale: AI already materially assists the analytical portions of this job — sales forecasting, pipeline analysis, territory planning, quota setting, and CRM-driven reporting are squarely in AI's path. However, the core of the role is interpersonal: recruiting, coaching, and motivating sales reps, resolving escalated customer issues, and building relationships with dealers and distributors, which keeps disruption at the top of the moderate band rather than higher. Elasticity is moderate — headcount is largely tied to the size of sales teams and span of control rather than the cost of analysis, so faster analytics alone won't dramatically expand demand for managers, though cheaper sales operations may modestly grow sales organizations. With disruption at 6, the occupation is resilient: the analytical toolkit will shift substantially, but the leadership core keeps the role intact.

title: School and career counselors and advisors
rationale: A meaningful portion of this work — career exploration, college matching, résumé and application help, aptitude assessment interpretation, and information delivery — is language-based and already well within AI's reach, which pushes disruption up. However, the core of school counseling involves in-person relationship-building, social-emotional support with minors, crisis intervention, mandated reporting, and collaboration with families and teachers, which anchors the human presence requirement and keeps disruption at the moderate-high boundary rather than above it. Elasticity is moderate: there is genuine latent demand (student-to-counselor ratios are far above recommended levels, and cheap career guidance would be consumed widely), but school budgets and staffing structures cap headcount expansion. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands in resilient — AI will absorb the informational advising tasks, but the interpersonal counseling core remains human work.

title: Secretaries and administrative assistants
rationale: The core tasks — scheduling, drafting memos and emails, editing documents, transcription, managing calendars and databases, basic bookkeeping — are almost entirely digital, language-based work squarely in AI's current capabilities, and AI assistants already handle much of this today; only reception duties and in-person office coordination resist automation. Demand for administrative support is derived from organizational headcount, not suppressed by cost — making admin work 10x cheaper does not lead firms or executives to consume dramatically more of it, and the trend of managers self-serving with digital tools further caps demand. Some structural friction (healthcare front-office growth, personal-relationship value in executive roles) provides limited elasticity but not enough to absorb productivity gains. High disruption with low elasticity places this occupation firmly in the replace category, consistent with BLS projecting declines in three of four subcategories.

title: Securities, commodities, and financial services sales agents
rationale: The core tasks — monitoring markets, analyzing securities, executing trades, and generating investment recommendations — are almost entirely digital and cognitive, and are already heavily eroded by algorithmic trading, robo-advisors, and self-directed online platforms; AI accelerates this trajectory, leaving relationship-building and trust as the main human moat. Elasticity is limited because cheaper analysis and execution do not proportionally expand the pool of investable wealth or the number of transactions requiring a human intermediary — retail investors increasingly bypass agents entirely when costs drop, and institutional trading volume gains flow to automated systems, not headcount. Some latent demand exists for personalized financial advice among underserved households, but robo-advisors capture much of that at near-zero marginal cost rather than employing more agents. With high disruption and productivity gains largely translating to fewer intermediaries rather than more consumption of their services, this occupation faces contraction, consistent with the historical pattern of floor brokers and traders already displaced by electronic trading.

title: Security guards and gambling surveillance officers
rationale: The core of security guard work — physical presence, patrolling, controlling access, deterring and responding to incidents — requires being on-site in unpredictable environments, though the surveillance-monitoring portion (watching camera feeds, flagging anomalies, writing reports) is squarely in AI's path via video analytics, and the small gambling-surveillance subset is more exposed. Elasticity is low: while cheaper AI-enabled monitoring could extend security coverage to more properties, that expanded coverage largely substitutes cameras and software for human watchers rather than hiring more guards, and demand for physical guard presence is driven by liability and crime concerns rather than cost suppression. With disruption in the moderate range, the occupation is resilient overall — AI erodes the desk-monitoring roles at the margins but does not reshape the physical-presence core that employs the vast majority of the 1.3 million workers.

title: Semiconductor processing technicians
rationale: The core work requires physical presence in cleanrooms — loading wafers, adjusting and repairing equipment, and hands-on quality control — which AI cannot perform, though AI-powered defect detection, process monitoring, and predictive maintenance are already reshaping the inspection and data-analysis portions of the job. Elasticity is moderate-to-high: semiconductor demand is booming and cheaper, faster fab operations would expand output, but headcount per fab is constrained by increasing automation of the fabs themselves. With disruption in the moderate range, the occupation is resilient — AI augments monitoring and testing tasks but the hands-on equipment operation and maintenance core remains human, and industry growth (CHIPS Act investment, projected 11% growth) supports stable employment.

title: Set and exhibit designers
rationale: The conceptual and drafting portions of the work—script analysis, mood boards, CAD drawings, renderings, and budgeting—are squarely in AI's path, as generative tools can already produce concept art and 3D visualizations rapidly; however, the core job also involves physical spaces, materials, on-site installation oversight, and intensive real-time collaboration with directors, curators, and craftspeople, which caps disruption at moderate-high.
