Elasticity is low-to-moderate: cheaper design does not dramatically expand the number of theatrical productions, films, or museum exhibits, since those are constrained by production budgets, venues, and audience demand rather than design costs—and AI-generated virtual backgrounds may even substitute for physical sets in film. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands as resilient: AI will reshape the visualization workflow and squeeze the rendering-heavy portion of the job, but the physical, site-specific, and collaborative core keeps humans central.

title: Sheet metal workers
rationale: The core work — measuring, cutting, bending, installing, and welding sheet metal on construction sites and in shops — is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on, keeping AI disruption low; the main technology pressure comes from automated fabrication machinery and prefabrication rather than AI per se, and AI touches only peripheral tasks like CADD assistance, estimating, and scheduling. Demand elasticity is modest: HVAC and construction demand is driven by building activity, not by the cost of sheet metal labor, so productivity gains would not unlock large latent demand, though energy-efficiency retrofits offer some expansion. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — the bigger long-term risk is factory automation and prefab systems, not AI language or cognitive tools.

title: Skincare specialists
rationale: The core work — facials, waxing, peels, massage, makeup application — is entirely hands-on and requires physical presence with the client, placing it well outside AI's reach. AI touches only peripheral tasks like skin analysis (AI imaging tools may assist product recommendations), scheduling, marketing, and bookkeeping for self-employed practitioners. Elasticity is modest: demand for skincare services is growing but is driven by disposable income and appearance culture rather than being suppressed by cognitive-labor costs, so AI productivity gains would barely move total demand. With minimal disruption to the physical core of the job, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Small engine mechanics
rationale: Small engine mechanics perform overwhelmingly hands-on work — disassembling engines, replacing parts, and manipulating components with hand tools — which AI cannot do; AI's role is limited to peripheral tasks like diagnostic assistance, parts lookup, scheduling, and record-keeping. Elasticity is low because repair demand is driven by the installed base of equipment and breakage rates, not by repair cost or speed; cheaper diagnostics would not lead people to service their lawnmowers or boats dramatically more often, and electrification may even shrink the repair market. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient — AI touches only the administrative periphery of a fundamentally physical trade.

title: Social and community service managers
rationale: A substantial portion of this role is knowledge work squarely in AI's path — grant proposal writing, program data analysis, effectiveness reporting, budget administration, and outreach content — but the core involves stakeholder relationships, community trust-building, staff supervision, and in-person representation that AI cannot substitute. Elasticity is constrained: demand for social services is driven by grant funding, government budgets, and philanthropic giving rather than the cost of management labor, so productivity gains don't unlock much latent demand, though some small nonprofits might sustain programs they otherwise couldn't. With disruption at the boundary of 6, the relational and supervisory core keeps this occupation resilient — AI reshapes the administrative periphery while managers who leverage it for grant writing and evaluation will simply be more effective, consistent with BLS's projected 6% growth.

title: Social and human service assistants
rationale: A meaningful share of the work — researching benefit programs, completing application paperwork, coordinating services, and documentation — is digital and squarely in AI's path, but the core involves face-to-face relationship-building with vulnerable populations (homeless individuals, people in addiction recovery, the elderly), home visits, and crisis situations that require human presence and trust. Demand for social services is substantially suppressed by public funding constraints, and cheaper case-handling could allow agencies to serve more of the large unmet need, though government budgets rather than price elasticity ultimately cap expansion. With disruption at 5, AI streamlines the administrative periphery while the human-contact core remains intact, making this occupation resilient — consistent with BLS's faster-than-average growth projection driven by an aging population.

title: Social workers
rationale: The core of social work — building trust with vulnerable clients, crisis intervention, home visits, child welfare investigations, and therapeutic relationships — requires human presence and empathy that AI cannot substitute, though AI will meaningfully streamline case documentation, resource matching, benefits navigation, and risk assessment, which consume a large share of social workers' time. Demand is substantially suppressed today by underfunded public budgets and chronic understaffing with large caseloads, so productivity gains would mostly be absorbed by serving more clients better rather than cutting headcount, though government budget constraints cap expansion. With disruption at a moderate 4, the occupation is resilient: AI relieves administrative burden at the periphery while the relational core of the work remains firmly human.

title: Sociologists
rationale: Sociologists' core tasks — designing studies, analyzing survey and interview data, running statistical models, and writing reports — are predominantly digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, though fieldwork like establishing rapport in interviews retains a human element. Demand is largely constrained by grant funding, academic budgets, and government appropriations rather than by the cost of research itself, so a 10x productivity gain would mostly mean fewer researchers per study rather than 10x more sociological research being commissioned. Some latent demand exists in policy and business applications, but funding structures cap expansion. With high disruption and low elasticity in an already tiny occupation (3,400 jobs), headcount contraction is the likely outcome.

title: Software developers, quality assurance analysts, and testers
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — writing code, designing systems, generating test plans, executing automated tests, documenting software — are digital and squarely in AI's direct path, with coding assistants and AI-driven test generation already materially changing daily workflows. Demand elasticity is high because software demand has historically been suppressed by development cost: cheaper, faster development unlocks a large backlog of custom software, integrations, and applications that were previously uneconomical, as evidenced by decades of productivity gains (compilers, frameworks, open source) coinciding with employment growth. The net effect is augment: each developer becomes dramatically more productive while total software output expands, keeping headcount stable or growing, though the QA/tester subgroup faces greater displacement risk as testing is more routinized and its demand is derivative rather than independent.

title: Solar photovoltaic installers
rationale: The core work is physical installation on rooftops and at ground-level solar farms — lifting panels, mounting structures, wiring, sealing — which AI cannot perform; AI touches only peripheral tasks like system design layout, site assessment via imagery, and scheduling, warranting a low disruption score. Elasticity is high because demand for solar installation is strongly cost-driven and expanding rapidly (BLS projects 42% growth), and cheaper design/permitting via AI would accelerate adoption further. Since disruption is well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI may streamline planning and quoting, but the hands-on installation work remains firmly human for the foreseeable future.

title: Special education teachers
rationale: AI can meaningfully assist with IEP drafting, lesson adaptation, progress tracking, and personalized learning materials, but the core work — in-person instruction, behavioral management, emotional support, and hands-on work with students who have physical, emotional, or severe cognitive disabilities — requires human presence and relationship-building that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is moderate: there is genuine unmet demand for special education services (chronic teacher shortages, caseload caps, earlier identification of disabilities), but growth is constrained by public school funding and enrollment rather than service cost. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient — AI will lighten the substantial paperwork burden (a major pain point) and could actually improve retention rather than reduce headcount.

title: Special effects artists and animators
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital — modeling, rendering, compositing, and animating are directly in the path of generative image and video AI, which can already produce effects and animation that previously required teams of specialists, driving a very high disruption score. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper animation unlocks real latent demand (indie games, small-studio films, advertising, mobile content), but total consumption of visual media is capped by audience attention, and generative tools increasingly let directors and non-specialists produce effects without dedicated artists, so demand expansion won't fully absorb the productivity gains. The occupation will survive but shift dramatically toward AI-directed workflows, prompt-driven asset generation, and creative supervision rather than frame-by-frame craft. Artists who master AI pipelines can thrive on higher output; those relying on traditional technical execution face displacement, making restructure the fitting category.

title: Speech-language pathologists
rationale: SLP work is language-centered, so AI speech recognition, pronunciation analysis, and practice apps can meaningfully assist assessment, documentation, and at-home drilling — but core treatment requires in-person clinical judgment, hands-on swallowing therapy, real-time adaptation to clients with impaired communication, and counseling of families, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is high because demand is heavily suppressed by cost and therapist shortages (long school waitlists, underserved stroke and autism populations), so cheaper AI-assisted therapy delivery would expand total service consumption substantially. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI augments practice sessions and paperwork while the licensed clinician remains central, consistent with BLS's 15% projected growth.

title: Stationary engineers and boiler operators
rationale: The core of this occupation is hands-on mechanical work — repairing valves, replacing bearings, crawling inside boilers, lubricating parts — which AI cannot perform; only the monitoring, gauge-reading, and log-keeping portions are in AI's path, and much of that is already automated via computerized controls. Elasticity is low because demand for boiler and HVAC operation is fixed by the building stock and equipment installed base — cheaper monitoring does not lead facilities to consume more steam or hire more operators, and remote monitoring may slightly reduce headcount per facility. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient: AI-enhanced sensors and predictive maintenance tools will assist workers but the physical maintenance, safety inspection, and licensed-operator requirements keep humans central to the role.

title: Substance abuse, behavioral disorder, and mental health counselors
rationale: Counseling is language-based work in principle, and AI chatbots and documentation tools will assist with treatment plans, progress notes, and between-session support — but the core value lies in human trust, empathy, crisis intervention, and therapeutic alliance, which clients and regulators largely will not accept from machines, especially for addiction and court-mandated treatment. Elasticity is very high: mental health and substance abuse care demand is massively suppressed by cost, provider shortages, and access barriers, so cheaper adjunct capacity would be absorbed by enormous unmet need (BLS already projects 17% growth). With disruption at a moderate 5, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes documentation and peripheral tasks while the counselor-client relationship remains the irreducible core, and strong latent demand further protects headcount.

title: Surgical assistants and technologists
rationale: The core work — sterilizing equipment, positioning patients, passing instruments, holding retractors, suturing — is entirely physical, hands-on, and performed in a sterile operating room where real-time dexterity and presence are essential; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, inventory tracking, and documentation. Surgical robotics may change workflows over time but still requires human technologists to set up and support equipment, and full automation of instrument handling is far beyond a 10-year horizon. Demand for surgery is driven by clinical need and an aging population rather than the cost of assistant labor, so productivity gains in this role would not dramatically expand surgical volume. With minimal disruption to core tasks and projected employment growth, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Survey researchers
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — designing questionnaires, testing question wording, correcting for nonresponse bias, running statistical analysis, and summarizing results in tables and reports — are digital, language-based, and squarely in the path of current AI tools, which can already draft surveys, code responses, and analyze data end to end. Elasticity is low because demand for traditional survey research is being actively substituted away by data mining, passive behavioral data, and social media analytics; making surveys 10x cheaper unlocks only modest latent demand (small organizations running more polls) and cannot offset the structural shift, as reflected in BLS's projected -5% decline even before aggressive AI adoption. With disruption of 8 and elasticity of 3, productivity gains translate into fewer researchers rather than more surveys, making 'replace' the fitting category.

title: Surveying and mapping technicians
rationale: The occupation splits between physical fieldwork (setting markers, operating instruments in rugged terrain, drone operation on site) and digital processing (GIS data assembly, map editing, CAD work). AI plus automated photogrammetry can heavily absorb the office-based mapping and data-processing tasks, but the on-site measurement, marker location, and equipment work require physical presence, capping disruption at moderate. Elasticity is moderate-to-high because cheaper geospatial data unlocks meaningful latent demand — utilities, construction, infrastructure, and autonomous systems all consume more mapping when it's faster and cheaper — but legal boundary surveys are tied to fixed real-estate transaction volumes. With disruption at 5, the core field-based work remains largely intact, making this occupation resilient, though technicians focused purely on desk-based GIS work will face more pressure than field crews.

title: Surveyors
rationale: Surveying blends office-based knowledge work (records research, GIS analysis, map and report preparation) that AI can substantially accelerate with essential fieldwork requiring physical presence on rugged terrain to set monuments and verify conditions — plus legal licensure requirements that mandate a human certify boundaries. Drones, robotic total stations, and AI-assisted data processing already boost productivity, but demand is largely tethered to construction activity and real estate transactions, which are driven by external economic factors rather than survey cost; cheaper surveys unlock only modest latent demand (e.g., more frequent monitoring, smaller projects getting surveyed). With disruption at 5, the core field-and-certification work remains human-anchored, making this occupation resilient despite meaningful AI assistance in the office portion.

title: Tax examiners and collectors, and revenue agents
rationale: The core work — reviewing tax returns, verifying deductions against tax law, cross-referencing financial records, and flagging discrepancies — is rule-based digital document analysis squarely in AI's current capability path, with only field audits and sensitive collection negotiations requiring human presence. Elasticity is low because demand is set by government budgets and legislative priorities rather than price: cheaper auditing does not mean society consumes 10x more tax enforcement, and while there is latent demand to close the tax gap, headcount is structurally capped by public funding and political constraints (BLS already projects a 2% decline). High disruption combined with budget-constrained inelastic demand means productivity gains will translate directly into fewer examiners needed, making 'replace' the appropriate category.

title: Taxi drivers, shuttle drivers, and chauffeurs
rationale: Unlike most physical occupations, driving is the direct target of embodied AI: robotaxis (Waymo, and expanding competitors) are already operating commercially in the same dense metro markets where taxi and ride-hail employment is concentrated, putting the core task squarely in AI's path over a 10-year horizon. Elasticity is low for the occupation itself—while cheaper rides would expand total ride volume substantially, autonomous vehicles capture that expanded demand without drivers, so productivity gains flow to fewer human workers rather than more driving jobs. Segments requiring human presence (paratransit assistance, wheelchair lifts, executive chauffeur duties, luggage handling) provide partial insulation, but they represent a minority of the workforce. High disruption combined with demand growth that bypasses human drivers points to significant headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.

title: Teacher assistants
rationale: The instructional-reinforcement portion of the job (reviewing lessons, drilling material) is squarely in AI tutoring's path, and admin tasks like grading and attendance are easily automated, but the core of the role — physical supervision, behavior management, and hands-on care for special education students including feeding and hygiene — requires human presence that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper individualized instruction via AI could shift some tutoring demand away from aides, but demand for adult supervision is tied to student headcount and school budgets, not instruction cost, with special-needs support providing a structural demand floor. Because most daily work is physical and interpersonal rather than digital, disruption stays at 4, making this occupation resilient even as its tutoring-adjacent tasks migrate to AI tools.

title: Technical writers
rationale: Technical writing is almost entirely digital, language-based knowledge work — drafting manuals, FAQs, and how-to guides is squarely in the path of current LLMs, which can already generate first-draft documentation directly from code, specs, or engineer interviews. Demand for documentation is largely derivative of product output rather than price: companies will not consume 10x more manuals just because they are cheaper, and much documentation may be replaced by AI-generated, on-demand answers rather than static docs, capping elasticity at low levels despite some latent demand for better localization and coverage. With high disruption and low demand expansion, productivity gains translate into fewer writers needed, with remaining roles shifting toward content strategy, review, and prompt/knowledge-base curation. BLS's near-zero projected growth already hints at this contraction pressure.

title: Telecommunications technicians
rationale: The core work — climbing towers, splicing fiber, installing lines, and physically repairing equipment in homes, central offices, and outdoor sites — is hands-on and requires unpredictable real-world presence, keeping AI's impact limited to peripheral tasks like diagnostics, remote monitoring, scheduling, and documentation. Elasticity is modest: telecom infrastructure demand is driven by build-out cycles (5G, broadband expansion) and durable low-maintenance technologies like fiber, not by the cost of technician labor, so cheaper knowledge work won't unlock much additional installation demand. AI-enhanced remote diagnostics and self-healing networks may trim some truck rolls, but the physical installation and repair core remains intact. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient — its projected decline stems from infrastructure maturity, not AI displacement.

title: Tellers
rationale: Teller work is dominated by routine transaction processing, account queries, and record-keeping — tasks already heavily absorbed by mobile banking, enhanced ATMs, and AI-powered customer service, with the remaining physical cash handling also increasingly automated. Demand is highly inelastic: making transactions faster or cheaper does not cause people to visit bank branches more; in fact, consumers are actively migrating away from in-person banking regardless of cost. BLS already projects a 13% decline, and AI chatbots plus automated kiosks will accelerate the reduction of tellers per branch and branch counts overall. High disruption combined with fixed-to-shrinking demand places this squarely in the replace category.

title: Top executives
rationale: Top executives do predominantly cognitive work — analyzing financials, drafting strategy, reviewing reports — where AI is already a powerful assistant, but the core of the role is accountability, negotiation, board relations, organizational leadership, and high-stakes judgment that stakeholders require a human to own; this keeps disruption at the boundary of moderate and high. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: organizations need roughly one CEO and a bounded layer of general managers regardless of how cheap analysis becomes, though AI-lowered barriers to starting and running small businesses could modestly expand the number of executive roles. With AI compressing the analytical staff work beneath executives more than the executive role itself, the occupation's core — deciding, leading, and being accountable — remains intact. Disruption at 6 places this in resilient, though executives who fail to leverage AI for decision support will be at a competitive disadvantage.

title: Tour and travel guides
rationale: The core work — physically escorting groups, reading the room, managing pacing, and providing engaging in-person interaction — requires human presence and social rapport that AI cannot replicate. AI meaningfully assists peripheral tasks like itinerary planning, research, marketing, and booking logistics, and AI audio guides may substitute for the lowest-value tours, but people who pay for guided experiences are largely buying human connection and entertainment. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper trip-planning could expand tourism volume somewhat, and the experience economy is growing, but demand is bounded by travel time and disposable income rather than guide cost. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — BLS's projected 8% growth reflects that leisure demand outweighs any AI substitution at the margins.

title: Training and development managers
rationale: The core work — designing curricula, creating and selecting training content, assessing needs, and evaluating program effectiveness — is predominantly digital knowledge work where AI already generates instructional materials, personalizes learning paths, and analyzes training outcomes, though the managerial, budgeting, and stakeholder-alignment aspects retain human elements. Elasticity is moderate-to-good: AI-driven workplace transformation itself creates enormous continuous reskilling demand, and cheaper training production lets organizations train more people more often, but headcount growth is capped because AI simultaneously shrinks the specialist teams these managers oversee and consolidates content production. The role survives but shifts from managing instructional designers and course production toward orchestrating AI-powered learning platforms and strategic workforce capability planning, fitting the restructure category.

title: Training and development specialists
rationale: A large share of core tasks — designing training manuals, creating e-learning modules, drafting course materials, and building assessments — is digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, with generative tools already producing instructional content and even AI-driven adaptive learning; live facilitation and needs assessment retain human elements, keeping disruption at 7 rather than higher. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper training production and the accelerating need to reskill workers (ironically driven by AI itself) unlock meaningful latent demand for more frequent, personalized upskilling, but AI tutors and self-serve learning platforms can absorb much of that expanded volume without proportional headcount growth. The occupation persists but shifts from content authoring toward curating AI-generated materials, learning strategy, and change management. High disruption with moderate elasticity fits the restructure category — specialists who master AI-augmented instructional design will thrive while traditional content developers face displacement.

title: Transportation, storage, and distribution managers
rationale: A substantial share of this job — route planning, inventory tracking, scheduling, compliance monitoring, and supply chain optimization — is analytical and already being transformed by AI-driven logistics software, warehouse management systems, and predictive analytics. However, the core still requires physical presence in warehouses and yards, direct supervision of frontline workers, hiring, safety enforcement, and real-time crisis resolution in the physical world, keeping disruption at the high end of moderate. Elasticity is moderate: e-commerce growth and more complex supply chains create some expanded need for coordination, but each manager overseeing an AI-optimized operation can span a larger scope, so headcount doesn't scale with output. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands as resilient — AI reshapes the planning tools but not the fundamentally on-site, people-management core.

title: Travel agents
rationale: Travel agents' core tasks — researching options, comparing fares, building itineraries, booking reservations, and advising on destinations — are almost entirely digital, language-based information work squarely in AI's current capability path; AI trip-planning tools and booking agents already perform much of this today. Elasticity is low because travel demand is driven by disposable income and leisure time, not by the cost of agent services, and the occupation already lost most of its market to self-service online booking; making agent-style planning 10x cheaper mostly means consumers use AI directly rather than hiring more agents. A niche will persist for high-touch luxury, group, and complex corporate travel, but this is a small share of current headcount. High disruption combined with inelastic demand points clearly to replacement and continued contraction.

title: Tutors
rationale: Tutoring is almost entirely language-based cognitive work — explaining concepts, generating practice problems, giving feedback — all squarely in the path of current generative AI, which can already deliver personalized instruction at near-zero marginal cost. However, demand for personalized education has been massively suppressed by cost: at $40-60/hour, most families and students cannot afford regular tutoring, so a 10x cost reduction unlocks enormous latent demand across K-12 support, test prep, adult learning, and language instruction. Human tutors who leverage AI for lesson prep, drills, and progress tracking can serve more students, and demand for accountability, motivation, and human connection (especially for younger and special-needs students) keeps humans in the loop even as pure content delivery shifts to software. The combination of high disruption and very high demand elasticity fits 'augment' — the role transforms into an AI-supervised coaching model, with the expanded market absorbing productivity gains, though tutors offering only rote content review face displacement.

title: Umpires, referees, and other sports officials
rationale: While AI-assisted officiating technology (automated ball-strike systems, Hawk-Eye line calling) is advancing at elite professional levels, the vast majority of officials work youth, high school, and recreational games where installing camera and sensor infrastructure is cost-prohibitive, and the core job requires physical presence, game management, safety oversight, and de-escalating disputes with players and coaches. Demand elasticity is low because the number of officials needed is fixed by the number of games played — cheaper officiating technology doesn't cause society to play meaningfully more games. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI may assist calls at the margins in televised sports, but on-field human authority remains central.

title: Urban and regional planners
rationale: Much of planners' analytical work — data gathering, GIS analysis, feasibility studies, report writing, zoning code research — is squarely in AI's path and will be heavily automated. However, the core of the job is political and interpersonal: negotiating with elected officials, developers, and residents, running public hearings, and building consensus around contested land-use decisions, which keeps disruption at the top of the moderate band rather than high. Elasticity is low because 84% of planners work in government where headcount is set by budgets and political processes, not by the marginal cost of planning analysis; cheaper analysis does not mean cities approve 10x more plans. The net effect is resilient — AI transforms the analytical toolkit but the stakeholder-facing, judgment-and-legitimacy core of the occupation remains human, though planners who don't adopt AI-driven GIS and analysis tools will lose ground.

title: Veterinarians
rationale: Veterinary work is fundamentally hands-on — physical exams, surgery, dental work, euthanasia, and handling unpredictable animals cannot be done by AI, though diagnostic support, imaging interpretation, record-keeping, and client communication will be meaningfully assisted by AI tools (this is the prompt's own benchmark example for moderate disruption). Elasticity is moderate-to-high: pet healthcare demand is clearly cost-suppressed, and cheaper diagnostics and admin efficiency would let more owners pursue advanced care, but the physical clinical bottleneck limits how much throughput AI alone can unlock. Because the core work requires human presence and manual dexterity, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the diagnostic and administrative periphery while the vet's hands-on role remains intact, consistent with BLS's strong projected growth.

title: Veterinary assistants and laboratory animal caretakers
rationale: The core work — feeding, bathing, restraining animals, cleaning kennels, sterilizing instruments, and providing hands-on post-surgical care — is almost entirely physical and requires unpredictable real-world presence with living animals, placing AI's impact at the periphery (perhaps scheduling or record-keeping). Elasticity is moderate since pet-care spending is growing and cheaper veterinary services would expand procedure volume, but the assistants' labor itself isn't what AI would make cheaper. With disruption near the minimum, the occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS's projected 9% growth driven by rising pet spending.

title: Veterinary technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work — restraining animals, administering anesthesia, drawing blood, taking x-rays, providing nursing care — is hands-on and physically demanding, requiring presence with unpredictable live animals; AI helps mainly with peripheral tasks like record-keeping, diagnostic test interpretation, and client communication. Elasticity is moderate: pet ownership and willingness to spend on animal health are growing, and cheaper diagnostics could expand veterinary care consumption, but the physical labor bottleneck means productivity gains from AI are limited anyway. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient — BLS projects much-faster-than-average growth driven by rising pet spending, and AI will not reshape the hands-on core of the job.

title: Waiters and waitresses
rationale: The core work is physical and interpersonal — carrying food, setting tables, reading customers, and providing in-person hospitality — which AI cannot perform; digital touchpoints like order-taking and payment are already partially handled by kiosks and QR menus, but this is automation at the margins rather than AI transforming the role. Elasticity is modest: dining out is somewhat price-sensitive, but table service demand is driven more by lifestyle and disposable income than by labor cost of servers, and self-service adoption tends to shrink server headcount per restaurant rather than expand it. With disruption at 2, the occupation is clearly resilient — the human hospitality element remains central even as ordering technology chips away at some tasks. The BLS's own projection of near-flat employment reflects technology substitution at the periphery, not AI reshaping the core work.

title: Water and wastewater treatment plant and system operators
rationale: The monitoring, data logging, sample analysis, and regulatory reporting portions of this job are increasingly automated via SCADA systems and AI-driven process optimization, but core duties—manual equipment operation during malfunctions, physical maintenance, chemical handling, and on-site emergency response—require human presence at 24/7 facilities. Demand is fundamentally inelastic: communities need a fixed amount of water treated regardless of cost, so productivity gains translate to leaner staffing rather than expanded output, consistent with BLS's projected -7% decline. Because disruption is moderate (the physical, safety-critical core remains human) despite automation eroding headcount at the margins, the occupation is resilient in character even as it slowly shrinks.

title: Water transportation workers
rationale: Water transportation work is overwhelmingly physical and location-bound — maintaining engines, handling deck equipment, mooring, and standing watch in unpredictable maritime conditions. AI aids peripheral tasks like route optimization, navigation, logbooks, and predictive maintenance, and autonomous vessel technology is emerging but remains distant given regulatory (USCG/IMO), safety, and liability constraints over a 10-year horizon. Demand is driven by trade volumes in bulk commodities and passenger travel, not by the cost of crew labor, so productivity gains would not unlock meaningful latent demand. With low disruption to core tasks, the occupation is resilient over the next decade.

title: Web developers and digital designers
rationale: Nearly every core task — writing HTML/JavaScript code, creating layouts, generating graphics, prototyping interfaces, and testing usability — is fully digital and squarely in the path of current AI coding assistants and generative design tools, which can already produce functional websites from natural-language prompts. Elasticity is moderate rather than high: while cheaper development unlocks some latent demand (more small businesses and individuals getting custom sites, more frequent redesigns), routine website creation was already commoditized by template platforms, and AI increasingly lets end users bypass developers entirely for standard sites, capping headcount expansion. The occupation will survive but shift toward complex custom applications, integration work, brand strategy, and orchestrating AI tools rather than hand-coding pages. This combination of very high disruption with moderate demand absorption fits restructure — practitioners who move up the value chain thrive while those doing routine build-out work face displacement.

title: Welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers
rationale: Welding is fundamentally hands-on physical work requiring manual dexterity, real-world presence in varied and often unpredictable environments (construction sites, scaffolds, confined spaces), placing it largely outside AI's direct path; AI helps mainly with peripheral tasks like blueprint interpretation, weld inspection via computer vision, and job scheduling. Robotic welding automation is a real pressure in high-volume manufacturing, but that displacement route runs through machine operators rather than AI-driven knowledge work, and field/repair welding resists automation. Elasticity is modest — infrastructure and fabrication demand is driven by capital spending cycles, not welding labor cost, so cheaper welding wouldn't unlock massive latent demand. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient: the core work remains human for the foreseeable decade, with gradual erosion only in the most routinized factory segments.

title: Wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives
rationale: Much of this work — prospecting via directories, cold outreach, answering product questions, preparing quotes and contracts, order processing, sales reporting, and follow-up communication — is digital and language-based, squarely in the path of AI sales agents, chatbots, and B2B e-commerce self-service portals; only the relationship-building field visits for complex or technical products resist automation. Elasticity is low because demand for sales reps is derived from the volume of physical goods traded: making selling 10x cheaper does not make businesses buy meaningfully more industrial equipment, food, or office supplies, so productivity gains flow to fewer reps covering more accounts. The large transactional segment (routine reorders, nontechnical products, inside sales) faces direct headcount contraction as buyers shift to AI-assisted self-service. Relationship-intensive technical sales will persist, but the occupation overall fits 'replace' — high disruption with demand that cannot expand to absorb the productivity gains.

title: Wind turbine technicians
rationale: The core work is intensely physical — climbing 200-foot towers, rappelling to blades, replacing heavy components in confined nacelles at remote or offshore sites — which AI cannot perform. AI's role is peripheral: predictive maintenance analytics, remote diagnostics, and drone-based inspections may improve fault detection and reduce unnecessary trips, but a human must still travel to the site to make repairs. Elasticity is moderate-to-high since electricity demand growth and wind buildout (BLS projects 50% employment growth) mean any efficiency gains are readily absorbed by an expanding turbine fleet. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is clearly resilient, and structural demand tailwinds reinforce that.

title: Woodworkers
rationale: Woodworking is fundamentally physical work — cutting, sanding, assembling, finishing, and handling heavy materials — where AI's direct impact is limited to peripheral tasks like generating CNC programs, interpreting drawings, and design assistance. The larger displacement pressure comes from traditional automation (CNC machines and robotics), not AI language or cognitive tools, which is why disruption scores low. Elasticity is modest: demand for furniture and cabinets is tied to housing and consumer spending, with some latent demand for custom work if design-to-fabrication costs drop, but it won't expand dramatically. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient to AI specifically, though slow structural decline from automation continues.

title: Writers and authors
rationale: Writing is almost entirely digital, language-based work that sits directly in the path of large language models — drafting copy, blog posts, marketing content, and even fiction are tasks AI already performs at commercially usable quality, driving a disruption score of 9. While total demand for written content will expand as production costs collapse, much of that expanded output can be generated by AI directly or by non-writers using AI tools, meaning the marginal demand does not flow back to professional human writers; commodity segments like content writing and copywriting face outright substitution, keeping elasticity low at 3. Some premium demand persists for distinctive voice, brand-name authors, and high-stakes creative work (screenwriting, speechwriting), but this is too small a share to offset contraction in the bulk of the occupation. High disruption combined with low effective elasticity for human labor places this occupation in the replace category.

title: Zoologists and wildlife biologists
rationale: The occupation is a genuine mix: data analysis, population modeling, GIS work, and report writing are squarely in AI's path (and AI-powered camera traps, acoustic monitoring, and image classification are already transforming wildlife data collection), but core fieldwork — handling animals, traveling to remote habitats, conducting physical sampling — requires human presence in unpredictable outdoor environments. Elasticity is low because ~69% of employment is government-funded, and demand is set by agency budgets and conservation policy rather than by cost or speed of the science; cheaper analysis will not translate into proportionally more funded positions. With moderate disruption and budget-capped demand, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the analytical portion of the work but does not displace the field-based core, and headcount will remain roughly flat as BLS projects.

title: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — replacing parts, soldering, torquing bolts, inspecting airframes — which AI cannot perform; AI mainly assists with diagnostics, predictive maintenance scheduling, and documentation lookup, so disruption is low. Demand is driven by flight hours and FAA-mandated maintenance schedules rather than by the cost of maintenance labor, so even 10x faster diagnostics wouldn't cause airlines to consume dramatically more maintenance, keeping elasticity low-to-moderate (some expansion from growing air traffic and space industry). With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient: AI-enhanced diagnostics may improve productivity at the margins, but certified human mechanics remain regulatorily and physically essential.

title: Airline and commercial pilots
rationale: Flight decks are already highly automated, and AI will further assist with flight planning, weather analysis, fuel optimization, and monitoring — but FAA regulations, certification regimes, and public safety expectations firmly anchor human pilots in the cockpit for at least the next decade, keeping core disruption moderate. Single-pilot or autonomous operations for passenger airlines face enormous regulatory, insurance, and social acceptance barriers within a 10-year horizon, though cargo and some commercial niches may see earlier automation pressure. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper air operations would expand travel and freight demand somewhat, but pilot headcount is tied to flight volume rather than knowledge-work throughput. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes cockpit tools and back-office tasks but not the fundamental requirement for certified humans flying aircraft.

title: Animal care and service workers
rationale: Nearly all core tasks — feeding, grooming, exercising, training, and physically handling live animals — require hands-on presence with unpredictable creatures, placing this work almost entirely outside AI's reach; AI touches only peripheral scheduling, record-keeping, and customer communication. Elasticity is moderate: pet care demand is growing with pet humanization trends, but demand is driven by pet ownership rather than service cost, so cheaper admin wouldn't dramatically expand consumption. With disruption this low, the occupation is clearly resilient — BLS projects 11% growth, and AI is largely irrelevant to the physical, animal-facing core of the job.

title: Announcers and DJs
rationale: The broadcast announcer/radio DJ segment (about 60% of the occupation) is squarely in AI's path: voice synthesis, automated script writing, music selection algorithms, and AI DJs are already being deployed by radio stations, as BLS itself notes. The live-event DJ/emcee segment is more resilient because clients pay for human presence and crowd interaction, which moderates the overall disruption score. Elasticity is low: radio airtime slots and station counts are fixed or shrinking due to consolidation, so making announcing 10x cheaper mostly means fewer paid human voices rather than more radio consumption, and wedding/party demand is driven by events, not announcing costs. High disruption with inelastic demand points to headcount contraction concentrated in broadcast roles, fitting 'replace'.

title: Anthropologists and archeologists
rationale: Core work is split between irreplaceable in-person activities — excavation, site surveys, ethnographic fieldwork, artifact handling — and knowledge tasks like data analysis, GIS interpretation, and report writing where AI is already materially useful (e.g., drafting compliance reports, pattern analysis in datasets). This mixed profile puts disruption in the moderate range. Demand is largely fixed by federal preservation regulations, government budgets, and research grant funding rather than cost, so faster/cheaper analysis would not unlock a much larger market — perhaps modest expansion in corporate cultural research or CRM compliance work. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI will speed up the lab and writing portions but the fieldwork core and regulatory demand structure remain intact.

title: Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators
rationale: The analytical portions of the work — reviewing documents, applying laws and precedents, drafting settlement agreements, scheduling — are squarely in AI's path, and online dispute resolution platforms already automate simple, low-stakes cases. However, the core of the occupation is live facilitation between emotional, often confrontational parties, where perceived neutrality, trust, and human authority are essential to gaining voluntary consent, keeping disruption at the high end of moderate rather than high. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster dispute resolution could unlock latent demand from parties who currently forgo mediation or default to litigation, though contract clauses and court referrals structurally cap growth. With disruption at 6, the occupation is resilient — AI streamlines case preparation and document work but does not displace the human-centered negotiation at its core.

title: Architects
rationale: The bulk of an architect's daily work — drafting, rendering, spec writing, code compliance checking, and documentation via CADD/BIM — is digital and squarely in the path of generative design AI, which already produces schematics, visualizations, and code-checked layouts; only site visits, client relations, and licensed sign-off resist automation. Elasticity is moderate: design fees are a small fraction of total construction cost, so cheaper design doesn't proportionally increase building activity, though some latent demand exists (custom homes, renovations, and small projects that currently skip architects could afford professional design). With high disruption but only moderate demand expansion, the profession will survive but shift substantially — away from production drafting toward AI-directed design curation, client advising, and construction oversight, displacing drafting-heavy roles while licensed, adaptable architects retain value through legal liability and stamp requirements.

title: Architectural and engineering managers
rationale: Core tasks — project planning, budgeting, scheduling, resource allocation, quality oversight, and reporting — are cognitive and document-heavy work that AI tools already materially assist, though people leadership, hiring, stakeholder negotiation, and accountability for physical outcomes (construction, manufacturing) keep humans central. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper engineering and design work does unlock more projects (infrastructure repair, energy transition), but manager headcount scales with team size, and AI-augmented engineers may mean flatter organizations with fewer supervisory layers. The occupation persists but shifts from administrative coordination toward strategic judgment, AI-tool orchestration, and cross-organizational leadership, so restructure fits: managers who leverage AI for the planning/analysis load will thrive while purely administrative managers are squeezed out.

title: Archivists, curators, and museum workers
rationale: The digital-cognitive portions of this work — cataloging, metadata creation, classification, transcription of archival materials, and records management — are squarely in AI's path, but a large share of the occupation involves physical handling: conserving fragile artifacts, building and installing exhibits, transporting objects, and hands-on chemical/lab restoration work that AI cannot perform. Elasticity is moderate: vast backlogs of undigitized and uncataloged archival material represent real latent demand that cheaper processing could unlock, but overall headcount is capped by museum budgets, philanthropy, and government funding rather than by processing cost. With disruption around 5, the core hands-on and curatorial-judgment work remains human, making this occupation resilient even as AI reshapes the cataloging and records-management tasks within it.

title: Art directors
rationale: Art direction is almost entirely digital knowledge work — concept development, visual style selection, layout review, and design approval — and generative AI image, video, and design tools already directly perform much of the production the role oversees, collapsing the traditional pipeline of directing teams of designers and photographers. Elasticity is moderate-to-high: dramatically cheaper visual content unlocks substantial latent demand (more campaigns, more brands producing high-end visuals, more video content), but the supervisory nature of the role means fewer human artists to coordinate and clients may increasingly self-serve visual direction with AI tools. The core skill set shifts from managing human creative staff to curating, prompting, and quality-controlling AI outputs while retaining taste, brand judgment, and client communication. This combination of high disruption and moderate demand expansion makes restructure the best fit — the occupation persists but its daily work and required competencies change substantially.

title: Assemblers and fabricators
rationale: Assembly work is fundamentally physical and manual, requiring dexterity, strength, and hands-on manipulation of components, which keeps direct AI (language/cognitive) disruption low; however, AI-enhanced robotics and machine vision for quality inspection are advancing rapidly and repetitive, structured factory-floor tasks are among the most robot-tractable physical jobs, warranting a moderate score. Elasticity is limited: cheaper assembly does expand some manufactured goods consumption and reshoring, but automated facilities absorb that growth with capital rather than headcount, as BLS's -1% projection reflects. Because the disruption comes from robotics adoption over a longer horizon rather than software AI reshaping daily tasks in the near term, the occupation falls into the resilient category, though workers should expect gradual erosion in routine, high-volume segments while skilled, low-volume, and precision hand-assembly niches persist.

title: Athletes and sports competitors
rationale: The core work of athletes is inherently physical human performance — competing, training, and entertaining spectators — which AI cannot substitute; the entire value proposition is watching humans compete. AI touches only peripheral aspects like video analysis, training optimization, and opponent scouting, which are largely handled by coaching and analytics staff anyway. Elasticity is low because the number of professional athlete roles is structurally capped by league sizes and team rosters, not by cost or productivity constraints. With disruption near the minimum, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Athletic trainers
rationale: Athletic trainers' core work is intensely physical and in-person: taping, bracing, on-field emergency response, hands-on injury evaluation, and supervised rehabilitation cannot be done remotely or by software. AI assists only peripheral tasks like injury documentation, rehab program design suggestions, and administrative recordkeeping, and may add value via wearable-based injury prediction analytics — but the trainer still delivers the physical intervention. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper injury-prevention analytics and growing youth/aging-adult sports participation could expand demand somewhat, but the constraint is physical presence, not information cost. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient, consistent with BLS's projected 11% growth.

title: Atmospheric scientists, including meteorologists
rationale: Core work — running computer models, analyzing atmospheric data, generating forecasts and graphics — is almost entirely digital, and AI weather models like GraphCast already match or beat traditional numerical prediction at a fraction of the compute cost, putting forecasting directly in AI's path. Elasticity is low because forecasts are largely a public good: a single better model serves everyone simultaneously, so 10x cheaper forecasting doesn't require 10x more forecasters, and the largest employer (federal government at 31%) is budget-constrained rather than demand-constrained. Some latent demand exists for tailored business weather analytics, but it's insufficient to offset automation of routine forecasting. High disruption paired with limited demand expansion in a small (9,400-worker), funding-capped occupation fits the replace category.

title: Audiologists
rationale: Audiologists' core work is hands-on and in-person: examining ears, administering audiometric tests, fitting and adjusting hearing aids, and counseling patients with communication difficulties. AI assists the diagnostic-interpretation and documentation portions, and OTC hearing aids with AI-driven self-fitting may erode some routine dispensing work, but physical examination, device fitting, and vestibular treatment require human presence. Elasticity is moderate — an aging population and vast untreated hearing loss mean cheaper screening could expand who seeks care, though licensure and clinical capacity limit explosive growth. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient; AI reshapes the periphery, not the core.

title: Automotive body and glass repairers
rationale: The core work — hammering out dents, welding replacement parts, realigning frames, and installing windshields — is intensely physical, hands-on labor performed in unpredictable conditions on uniquely damaged vehicles, which is far beyond AI or near-term robotics. AI only assists peripheral tasks like damage estimation, parts ordering, and scheduling. Demand elasticity is low because collision and glass repair volume is driven by accident rates (which ADAS technology is actually reducing), not by repair cost or speed. With minimal disruption to core tasks, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Automotive service technicians and mechanics
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — disassembling components, replacing parts, working in cramped positions with heavy objects — which AI cannot perform; AI mainly enhances the diagnostic portion via smarter computerized diagnostics and repair documentation, warranting a low disruption score. Demand elasticity is limited because vehicle repair is driven by miles driven, fleet size, and wear rather than repair cost — cheaper diagnostics won't cause people to consume 10x more repairs, and the EV transition may actually reduce maintenance needs. Since disruption is well below 7, the occupation is resilient: AI speeds up troubleshooting on increasingly electronic vehicles but does not reshape the fundamentally manual core of the job.

title: Bakers
rationale: Baking is overwhelmingly physical, hands-on work — mixing, kneading, shaping, monitoring ovens — where AI language and analysis tools are largely irrelevant to core tasks; the main automation risk comes from industrial machinery in commercial facilities, not AI, and that automation is already mature. AI may assist peripherally with recipe scaling, inventory ordering, and demand forecasting for bakery owners. Demand for baked goods is fairly stable and tied to food consumption, so even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatic new demand, though artisanal and specialty segments have some room to grow. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI touches admin edges but does not reshape the craft.

title: Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists
rationale: The core work—cutting, coloring, and styling hair—is entirely hands-on, physical, and performed on a human body in person, placing it far outside AI's reach; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, marketing, and style visualization consultations. Elasticity is low because demand for haircuts is bounded by how often people need or want them, not by cost of the knowledge-work components, so AI-driven productivity gains barely change service throughput. With disruption near the minimum, the occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS projections of faster-than-average growth driven by demographic and grooming demand rather than technology.

title: Bartenders
rationale: Bartending is overwhelmingly physical and social work — mixing and pouring drinks, engaging customers, monitoring intoxication, and managing the physical bar space — none of which AI software touches meaningfully; automated cocktail machines exist but the social hospitality role is the core value proposition, especially in tipped venues. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper drink service wouldn't dramatically expand alcohol consumption, though the experiential nature of bars keeps human bartenders in demand. With disruption at 2, this occupation is clearly resilient — AI may help with inventory management and POS peripherals, but the core work is untouched, consistent with BLS projecting faster-than-average growth.

title: Bill and account collectors
rationale: Nearly every core task—skip tracing via databases, scripted phone outreach, negotiation of repayment plans, record-keeping, and compliance disclosures—is digital and language-based, squarely in the path of AI voice agents and automated workflows that already exist in collections today. Demand is fundamentally capped by the stock of delinquent debt, which does not grow because collection becomes cheaper; at best, marginally smaller debts become economical to pursue, but regulation (FDCPA contact limits) and social pressure constrain expanded collection activity. Productivity gains therefore translate directly into fewer human collectors handling more accounts, consistent with BLS's projected 10% decline. High disruption with inelastic demand makes this a clear replace case.

title: Biochemists and biophysicists
rationale: A significant share of the work — literature review, grant writing, data analysis, and especially molecular structure prediction (e.g., AlphaFold-style tools) — is squarely in AI's path and already being transformed, but core wet-lab experimentation, protein synthesis, and hands-on validation still require physical presence and are only partially addressed by lab automation. Elasticity is high because drug discovery, biotech, and agricultural research have deep latent demand: cheaper, faster hypothesis generation and computational screening means more candidate molecules get investigated and more research programs become fundable. Because disruption sits at the moderate-high boundary with the hands-on experimental core intact, the occupation lands as resilient — AI dramatically accelerates the computational portions while human researchers remain essential for experimental design, bench work, and validation. Scientists who integrate AI tools will be far more productive, but headcount is likely to hold or grow given expanding biotech demand.

title: Bioengineers and biomedical engineers
rationale: A substantial share of the work — statistical modeling, simulation, software design, technical writing, and data analysis — is squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven protein folding and generative design tools are already accelerating biomedical R&D. However, the core work remains anchored in physical prototyping, wet-lab experimentation, clinical validation in hospitals, regulatory testing, and hands-on equipment support, which caps disruption at the boundary of the high category. Elasticity is high because demand for medical devices, implants, and biological therapies is heavily suppressed by R&D cost and time — cheaper development would expand the pipeline of devices and treatments dramatically. With disruption at 6, this lands as resilient (bordering augment): AI supercharges the analytical portions while the physical and regulatory core keeps humans essential, and expanding demand supports stable-to-growing headcount.

title: Human resources managers
rationale: A substantial share of HR management work — drafting policies, screening candidates, benefits administration, compliance documentation, workforce analytics — is knowledge work squarely in AI's path, and AI tools are already reshaping recruiting and payroll functions the role oversees. However, the core managerial duties — mediating disputes, negotiating labor contracts, advising executives, and leading staff — depend on interpersonal trust, organizational politics, and accountability that AI cannot substitute for, keeping disruption at the high end of moderate. Elasticity is low because HR demand scales with organizational headcount rather than cost: companies won't consume 10x more HR management if it becomes cheaper, so productivity gains mostly thin out supporting layers rather than expand the market. With disruption at 6, the occupation is resilient at the managerial level, though the specialist work beneath it will be significantly automated and the manager's toolkit will shift toward overseeing AI-driven HR systems.

title: Photographers
rationale: The core act of capturing real people, events, and moments — weddings, portraits, news, sports — requires physical presence and cannot be generated, but AI heavily disrupts post-production editing and directly threatens commercial, stock, and product photography where generative images substitute for shoots. Elasticity is low: demand for photos is already saturated by smartphones and cheap stock libraries, so making professional photography faster and cheaper does not unlock much latent demand — people won't hire 10x more wedding or portrait photographers. The occupation lands at moderate disruption because the majority of employment (event, portrait, journalism) is anchored in unpredictable real-world presence, making it resilient overall, though the commercial/stock segment specifically faces significant contraction as generative AI absorbs that work.
